translations.an10.13:1: “These, bhikkhus, are the ten fetters. What are the ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: “As far as beings go, bhikkhus—whether footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet, whether having form or formless, percipient or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared supreme among them, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one; so too, bhikkhus, all wholesome qualities have heedfulness as their root, converge on heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared supreme among them.
translations.an10.15:2: “Just as, bhikkhus, whatever footprints of living beings there are in the jungle, all of them converge on the elephant’s footprint, and the elephant’s footprint is declared supreme among them by reason of its great size; so too, bhikkhus, all wholesome qualities have heedfulness as their root, converge on heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared supreme among them.
translations.an10.15:3: “Just as, bhikkhus, all the rafters of a roofed building slope toward the peak, incline toward the peak, converge on the peak, and the peak is declared supreme among them; so too, bhikkhus, all wholesome qualities have heedfulness as their root, converge on heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared supreme among them.
translations.an10.15:7: “Just as, bhikkhus, whatever minor kings there are, all of them become followers of the wheel-turning monarch, and the king, the wheel-turning monarch, is declared supreme among them; so too, bhikkhus ….
translations.an10.15:8: “Just as, bhikkhus, whatever radiance there is from the stars, none of them outshines the moon’s radiance by even one-sixteenth part, and the moon’s radiance is declared supreme among them; so too, bhikkhus ….
translations.an10.15:9: “Just as, bhikkhus, when the autumn sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, rising into the sky, dispels all darkness in space and shines, glows, and radiates; so too, bhikkhus ….
translations.an10.17:1: “Dwell, bhikkhus, with refuge, not without refuge. It is suffering, bhikkhus, to dwell without refuge. These ten, bhikkhus, are the qualities that provide refuge. What are the ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained by the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, training in the training rules. Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is virtuous … training in the training rules, this quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.17:2: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is learned, retaining what he has heard, accumulating what he has heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the fully complete and pure brahmacariya—such teachings he has learned well, retained in mind, examined with wisdom, and seen clearly with right view. Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is learned … seen clearly with right view, this quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.17:3: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate. Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate, this quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.18:10: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and alertness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago. ‘This bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and alertness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago,’—the elder bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed, the middle bhikkhus … the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, compassionate toward juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.18:11: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is wise, endowed with wisdom that arises and ceases, noble, penetrative, leading rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. ‘This bhikkhu is wise, endowed with wisdom that arises and ceases, noble, penetrative, leading rightly to the complete destruction of suffering,’—the elder bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed, the middle bhikkhus … the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed. For one who is compassionate toward elders … not decline. This quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.18:2: “Dwell, bhikkhus, with refuge, not without refuge. It is suffering, bhikkhus, to dwell without refuge. These ten, bhikkhus, are the qualities that provide refuge. What are the ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous … training in the training rules. ‘This bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained by the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, training in the training rules,’—the elder bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed, the middle bhikkhus … the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, compassionate toward juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.18:4: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate. ‘This bhikkhu is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate,’—the elder bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed, the middle bhikkhus … the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, compassionate toward juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.18:5: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is easy to admonish, endowed with qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, receptive to instruction. ‘This bhikkhu is easy to admonish, endowed with qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, receptive to instruction,’—the elder bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed, the middle bhikkhus … the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be advised and instructed. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, compassionate toward juniors, growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. This quality too is a refuge-providing quality.
translations.an10.18:6: Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is skilled and diligent in whatever duties, high or low, that need to be done by his fellow practitioners; he is endowed with inquiry and investigation into methods, capable of doing and arranging. 'This bhikkhu is indeed skilled, diligent, endowed with inquiry and investigation into methods, capable of doing and arranging in whatever duties, high or low, that need to be done by his fellow practitioners' — thus the elder bhikkhus, the middle bhikkhus, and even the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be instructed and advised. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, and compassionate toward the juniors, growth in wholesome qualities may be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that provides protection.
translations.an10.18:7: Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is fond of the Dhamma, takes delight in the words of the Teacher, and has great joy in the higher Dhamma and discipline. 'This bhikkhu is indeed fond of the Dhamma, takes delight in the words of the Teacher, and has great joy in the higher Dhamma and discipline' — thus the elder bhikkhus, the middle bhikkhus, and even the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be instructed and advised. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, and compassionate toward the juniors, growth in wholesome qualities may be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that provides protection.
translations.an10.18:8: Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he is steadfast, vigorous, and unrelenting in maintaining wholesome qualities. 'This bhikkhu indeed dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he is steadfast, vigorous, and unrelenting in maintaining wholesome qualities' — thus the elder bhikkhus, the middle bhikkhus, and even the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be instructed and advised. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, and compassionate toward the juniors, growth in wholesome qualities may be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that provides protection.
translations.an10.18:9: Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicine for the sick. 'This bhikkhu is indeed content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicine for the sick' — thus the elder bhikkhus, the middle bhikkhus, and even the junior bhikkhus consider him worthy to be instructed and advised. For one who is compassionate toward elders, compassionate toward the middle ones, and compassionate toward the juniors, growth in wholesome qualities may be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that provides protection.
translations.an10.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kuru people in a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadamma.
translations.an10.20:10: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one with tranquillized bodily formation? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one with tranquillized bodily formation.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one with well-liberated mind? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one with well-liberated mind.
translations.an10.20:2: These ten, bhikkhus, are the noble abodes in which the noble ones have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell. What are the ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is free from the five hindrances, endowed with six qualities, one-guarded, four-restrained, free from individual speculative views, at peace with the goal, free from defiled thoughts, tranquillized in bodily formation, well-liberated in mind, and well-liberated in wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu free from the five hindrances? Here, bhikkhus, sensual desire is abandoned in a bhikkhu, ill will is abandoned, sloth and torpor are abandoned, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, doubt is abandoned. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is free from the five hindrances.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither joyful nor sorrowful; he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly aware. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible with the body... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither joyful nor sorrowful; he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly aware. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with six qualities.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one-guarded? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with mindfulness as his guard. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one-guarded.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu four-restrained? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu accepts one thing, approves one thing, avoids one thing, and dispels one thing. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is four-restrained.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu free from individual speculative views? Here, bhikkhus, all the various individual speculative views held by various ascetics and brahmins—such as: 'The world is eternal,' or 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world is finite,' or 'The world is infinite,' 'The soul and the body are the same,' or 'The soul is one thing, the body another,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' or 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—all these are rejected, abandoned, relinquished, and given up by him. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is free from individual speculative views.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu at peace with the goal? Here, bhikkhus, sensual desire is abandoned in a bhikkhu, desire for existence is abandoned, and the desire for a holy life is calmed. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is at peace with the goal.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu free from defiled thoughts? Here, bhikkhus, sensual thought is abandoned in a bhikkhu, thought of ill will is abandoned, and thought of harm is abandoned. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is free from defiled thoughts.
translations.an10.24:1: On one occasion Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There Venerable Mahācunda addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus!' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Mahācunda. Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: For example, a friend, if a man were wealthy and spoke of wealth, if he were rich and spoke of riches, if he were prosperous and spoke of prosperity, then whenever any financial matter arose, he would be able to bring forth money, grain, silver, or gold. People would know of him thus: 'This venerable one is indeed wealthy, that's why he speaks of wealth; he is indeed rich, that's why he speaks of riches; he is indeed prosperous, that's why he speaks of prosperity. Why is that? Because this venerable one, whenever any financial matter arises, is able to bring forth money, grain, silver, or gold.'
translations.an10.24:2: "A monk who claims knowledge, saying, 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma,' but is overcome and dominated by greed, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, envy, miserliness, ill will, or unwholesome desire—such a monk should be recognized as follows: 'This venerable one does not truly understand as one who knows, for if he did, greed would not overcome him; indeed, greed overcomes this venerable one. This venerable one does not truly understand as one who knows, for if he did, hatred would not overcome him... delusion... anger... resentment... hypocrisy... envy... miserliness... ill will... unwholesome desire would not overcome him; indeed, unwholesome desire overcomes this venerable one.'"
translations.an10.24:3: "A monk who claims cultivation, saying, 'I have developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, developed wisdom,' but is overcome and dominated by greed, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, envy, miserliness, ill will, or unwholesome desire—such a monk should be recognized as follows: 'This venerable one does not truly understand as one who knows, for if he did, greed would not overcome him; indeed, greed overcomes this venerable one. This venerable one does not truly understand as one who knows, for if he did, hatred would not overcome him... delusion... anger... resentment... hypocrisy... envy... miserliness... ill will... unwholesome desire would not overcome him; indeed, unwholesome desire overcomes this venerable one.'"
translations.an10.24:5: For example, a friend, if a man were poor and spoke of wealth, if he were penniless and spoke of riches, if he were destitute and spoke of prosperity, then whenever any financial matter arose, he would not be able to bring forth money, grain, silver, or gold. People would know of him thus: 'This venerable one is indeed poor, yet speaks of wealth; he is indeed penniless, yet speaks of riches; he is indeed destitute, yet speaks of prosperity. Why is that? Because this venerable one, whenever any financial matter arises, is not able to bring forth money, grain, silver, or gold.'
translations.an10.24:9: "A monk who claims both knowledge and cultivation, saying, 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I have developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, developed wisdom,' and is not overcome or dominated by greed, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, envy, miserliness, ill will, or unwholesome desire—such a monk should be recognized as follows: 'This venerable one truly understands as one who knows, for greed does not overcome him; indeed, greed does not overcome this venerable one. This venerable one truly understands as one who knows, for hatred does not overcome him... delusion... anger... resentment... hypocrisy... envy... miserliness... ill will... unwholesome desire does not overcome him; indeed, unwholesome desire does not overcome this venerable one.'"
translations.an10.29:1: "Monks, as far as the realm of Kāsi and Kosala extends, as far as King Pasenadi of Kosala's dominion reaches, King Pasenadi of Kosala is renowned as supreme. Yet even for King Pasenadi of Kosala, there is change and alteration in his position. Seeing this, monks, a well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with the highest position, let alone the lowly ones."
translations.an10.29:10: Internally perceiving the formless, one sees external forms as blue, of blue color, with blue appearance, and blue hue. Just as a blue utpala flower, blue in color, with blue appearance, and blue hue, or as a Benares-dyed cloth, evenly dyed on both sides, blue in color, with blue appearance, and blue hue—so too, internally perceiving the formless, one sees external forms as blue, of blue color, with blue appearance, and blue hue; with the thought, 'I perceive and know them beyond them,' such a perception arises. This is the fifth mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: Internally perceiving the formless, one sees external forms as yellow, of yellow color, with yellow appearance, and yellow hue. Just as a kaṇikāra flower, yellow in color, with yellow appearance, and yellow hue, or as a Benares-dyed cloth, evenly dyed on both sides, yellow in color, with yellow appearance, and yellow hue—so too, internally perceiving the formless, one sees external forms as yellow, of yellow color, with yellow appearance, and yellow hue; with the thought, 'I perceive and know them beyond them,' such a perception arises. This is the sixth mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: Internally perceiving formless perception, one perceives external forms as red, reddish, red in appearance, red in hue. Just as a red bandujīvaka flower is red, reddish, red in appearance, red in hue, or as a Benares-dyed cloth, polished on both sides, is red, reddish, red in appearance, red in hue; so too, internally perceiving formless perception, one perceives external forms as red, reddish, red in appearance, red in hue; with the thought, 'I perceive and overcome them,' such is their perception. This is the seventh mastery base.
translations.an10.29:13: Internally perceiving formless perception, one perceives external forms as white, whitish, white in appearance, white in hue. Just as the stars are white, whitish, white in appearance, white in hue, or as a Benares-dyed cloth, polished on both sides, is white, whitish, white in appearance, white in hue; so too, internally perceiving formless perception, one perceives external forms as white, whitish, white in appearance, white in hue; with the thought, 'I perceive and overcome them,' such is their perception. This is the eighth mastery base. These, bhikkhus, are the eight mastery bases.
translations.an10.29:14: The highest of these eight mastery bases, bhikkhus, is when one, internally perceiving formless perception, perceives external forms as white, whitish, white in appearance, white in hue; with the thought, 'I perceive and overcome them,' such is their perception. There are beings, bhikkhus, who have such perception. Even in beings with such perception, bhikkhus, there truly is change and alteration. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the higher, just as toward the lower.
translations.an10.29:15: These four, bhikkhus, are the paths. What four? The path of suffering with slow knowledge, the path of suffering with swift knowledge, the path of ease with slow knowledge, the path of ease with swift knowledge—these, bhikkhus, are the four paths.
translations.an10.29:16: The highest of these four paths, bhikkhus, is the path of ease with swift knowledge. There are beings, bhikkhus, who practice thus. Even in beings who practice thus, bhikkhus, there truly is change and alteration. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the higher, just as toward the lower.
translations.an10.29:17: These four, bhikkhus, are perceptions. What four? One perceives as limited, one perceives as expansive, one perceives as measureless, one perceives as the base of nothingness, thinking 'There is nothing.' These, bhikkhus, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The highest of these four perceptions, bhikkhus, is when one perceives as the base of nothingness, thinking 'There is nothing.' There are beings, bhikkhus, who have such perception. Even in beings with such perception, bhikkhus, there truly is change and alteration. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the higher, just as toward the lower.
translations.an10.29:2: As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the directions, so great is the thousandfold world. In that thousandfold world there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Western continents, a thousand Northern continents, a thousand Eastern continents, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand Cātummahārājika heavens, a thousand Tāvatiṁsa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tusita heavens, a thousand Nimmānaratī heavens, a thousand Paranimmitavasavattī heavens, and a thousand Brahmā worlds. As far as the thousandfold world system, the Great Brahmā is declared supreme. Even in the Great Brahmā, bhikkhus, there truly is change and alteration. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the higher, just as toward the lower.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, bhikkhus, some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim ultimate purity. The highest of those who proclaim ultimate purity, bhikkhus, is one who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, attains and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. They teach the Dhamma for realizing that through direct knowledge. There are beings, bhikkhus, who speak thus. Even in beings who speak thus, bhikkhus, there truly is change and alteration. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the higher, just as toward the lower.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, bhikkhus, when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, most beings are reborn in the Ābhassara Brahmā realm. There they exist mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, abiding in glory, and remaining for a long, extended period. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, the Ābhassara devas are declared supreme. Even in the Ābhassara devas, bhikkhus, there truly is change and alteration. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the higher, just as toward the lower.
translations.an10.29:4: These ten, bhikkhus, are the kasiṇa bases. What ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa as above, below, and across, unbounded and measureless; one perceives the water kasiṇa … one perceives the fire kasiṇa … one perceives the air kasiṇa … one perceives the blue kasiṇa … one perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one perceives the red kasiṇa … one perceives the white kasiṇa … one perceives the space kasiṇa … one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa as above, below, and across, unbounded and measureless. These, bhikkhus, are the ten kasiṇa bases.
translations.an10.29:5: This is the highest point, bhikkhus, of these ten kasiṇa bases, namely the sphere of consciousness: one perceives it as boundless, above, below, across, without distinction. Even so, bhikkhus, there are beings with such perception. Even in beings with such perception, there is indeed difference, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest, just as toward the lowest.
translations.an10.29:6: There are, bhikkhus, eight mastery bases. What are the eight? One, having form-perception internally, sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly; with the thought 'I know and see them after mastering them,' such is his perception. This is the first mastery base.
translations.an10.29:7: One, having form-perception internally, sees forms externally, boundless, beautiful and ugly; with the thought 'I know and see them after mastering them,' such is his perception. This is the second mastery base.
translations.an10.29:8: One, without form-perception internally, sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly; with the thought 'I know and see them after mastering them,' such is his perception. This is the third mastery base.
translations.an10.29:9: One, without form-perception internally, sees forms externally, boundless, beautiful and ugly; with the thought 'I know and see them after mastering them,' such is his perception. This is the fourth mastery base.
translations.an10.51:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in the ways of his own mind? Just as, bhikkhus, a woman or a man, young and fond of adornment, would examine her or his own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or in a clear bowl of water: if she or he saw dust or grime there, she or he would make an effort to remove that dust or grime; but if she or he saw no dust or grime, she or he would be glad and satisfied, thinking: 'Gain indeed for me, pure indeed for me.' So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's self-examination is very helpful for wholesome qualities: 'Do I usually dwell with covetousness or without covetousness? With ill will or without ill will? Overcome by dullness and drowsiness or free from dullness and drowsiness? Distracted or undistracted? Doubtful or free from doubt? Angry or not angry? With defiled mind or with undefiled mind? Faithful or lacking faith? Lacking energy or energetic? Unconcentrated or concentrated?'
translations.an10.51:4: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu examining himself knows: 'I usually dwell with covetousness, with ill will, overcome by dullness and drowsiness, distracted, doubtful, angry, with defiled mind, lacking faith, lazy, unconcentrated,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make strong effort, zeal, energy, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil, unwholesome qualities. Just as, bhikkhus, if one's clothes or head were on fire, one would make strong effort, zeal, energy, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish them. So too, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make strong effort, zeal, energy, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil, unwholesome qualities.
translations.an10.54:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in the ways of his own mind? Just as, bhikkhus, a woman or a man, young and fond of adornment, would examine her or his own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or in a clear bowl of water: if she or he saw dust or grime there, she or he would make an effort to remove that dust or grime; but if she or he saw no dust or grime, she or he would be glad and satisfied, thinking: 'Gain indeed for me, pure indeed for me.' So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's self-examination is very helpful for wholesome qualities: 'Am I one who has attained internal mental tranquility? Or am I not one who has attained internal mental tranquility? Am I one who has attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena? Or am I not one who has attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena?'
translations.an10.54:5: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu examining himself knows: 'I have not attained internal mental tranquility, I have not attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make strong effort, zeal, energy, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of those very wholesome qualities. Just as, bhikkhus, if one's clothes or head were on fire, one would make strong effort, zeal, energy, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish them. So too, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should make strong effort, zeal, energy, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of those very wholesome qualities. In time, he will become one who has attained internal mental tranquility and one who has attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.
translations.an10.54:6: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu examining himself knows: 'I have attained internal mental tranquility, I have attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should establish himself in those very wholesome qualities and strive for the destruction of the taints.
translations.an10.58:1: “Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you: ‘What is the root of all phenomena, what is their source, what gives rise to them, what is their gathering point, what is their chief, what governs them, what is their superior, what is their essence, what is their support, what is their final end?’, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, taking refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good indeed if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Then, bhikkhus, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.59:1: “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our mind will be well developed in the renunciation of the life of home and the homelessness; and arisen evil unwholesome states will not persist to overwhelm the mind; our mind will be well developed in perception of impermanence, in perception of not-self, in perception of foulness, in perception of danger, having known the world’s balance and imbalance, our mind will be well developed in that perception; having known existence and non-existence in the world, our mind will be well developed in that perception; having known the arising and passing away in the world, our mind will be well developed in that perception; our mind will be well developed in perception of abandoning, in perception of dispassion, in perception of cessation.’ Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.
translations.an10.60:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. At that time, Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Seated there, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.an10.60:10: What, Ānanda, is perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, cessation, nibbāna.’ This is called, Ānanda, perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: What, Ānanda, is perception of non-delight in the whole world? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu abandons all attachments, mental fixations, clingings, and underlying tendencies in the world, dwelling without grasping. This is called, Ānanda, perception of non-delight in the whole world.
translations.an10.60:12: What, Ānanda, is perception of non-desire in all formations? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu feels revulsion, withdrawal, and disgust toward all conditioned phenomena. This is called, Ānanda, perception of non-desire in all formations.
translations.an10.60:13: What, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, straightening his body, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: ‘I breathe in long.’ Breathing out long, he knows: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he knows: ‘I breathe in short.’ Breathing out short, he knows: ‘I breathe out short.’ ‘Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Calming the bodily formation, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Calming the bodily formation, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing rapture, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing rapture, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Calming the mental formation, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Calming the mental formation, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing the mind, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Experiencing the mind, I will breathe out,’ he trains. ‘Gladdening the mind…’ ‘Steadying the mind…’ ‘Liberating the mind…’ ‘Contemplating impermanence…’ ‘Contemplating dispassion…’ ‘Contemplating cessation…’ ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in,’ he trains. ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out,’ he trains. This is called, Ānanda, mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If you, Ānanda, were to teach these ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that upon hearing these ten perceptions, the bhikkhu Girimānanda’s illness would subside.”
translations.an10.60:2: “Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Girimānanda is sick, suffering, gravely ill. May the Blessed One go to him out of compassion.” “If you, Ānanda, were to teach ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that upon hearing the ten perceptions, the bhikkhu Girimānanda’s illness would subside.
translations.an10.60:3: What are the ten? Perception of impermanence, perception of not-self, perception of foulness, perception of danger, perception of abandoning, perception of dispassion, perception of cessation, perception of non-delight in the whole world, perception of non-desire in all formations, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: What, Ānanda, is perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates subject to clinging. This is called, Ānanda, perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: What, Ānanda, is the perception of not-self? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'The eye is not-self, forms are not-self, the ear is not-self, sounds are not-self, the nose is not-self, smells are not-self, the tongue is not-self, tastes are not-self, the body is not-self, tangibles are not-self, the mind is not-self, mental phenomena are not-self.' Thus he dwells contemplating not-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of not-self.
translations.an10.60:6: What, Ānanda, is the perception of unattractiveness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu examines this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the hair downward, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurity: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, urine.' Thus he dwells contemplating unattractiveness in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of unattractiveness.
translations.an10.60:7: What, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'This body is indeed full of suffering, full of danger. In this body, various kinds of illness arise, such as: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, head-disease, ear-illness, mouth-illness, tooth-illness, lip-illness, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach-illness, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, scabies, itch, ringworm, nail-fungus, ringworm of the scalp, blood-disorders, bile-disorders, diabetes, shoulder-aches, scrofula; illnesses originating from bile, illnesses originating from phlegm, illnesses originating from wind, illnesses arising from the combination of these, illnesses caused by change of season, illnesses caused by irregular behavior, illnesses caused by violence, illnesses resulting from kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.' Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: What, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not accept an arisen sensual thought; he abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it, and makes it cease. He does not accept an arisen thought of ill will; he abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it, and makes it cease. He does not accept an arisen thought of cruelty; he abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it, and makes it cease. He does not accept arisen and recurring evil, unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and makes them cease. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: "Bhikkhus, the former limit of ignorance is not discernible: 'Ignorance was not before, then later it came to be.' Even so, bhikkhus, although it is said, still it is discernible: 'With this as condition, ignorance arises.'
translations.an10.61:2: "I say, bhikkhus, that ignorance is conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: 'The five hindrances.' I say, bhikkhus, that the five hindrances are conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: 'The three bad courses of action.' I say, bhikkhus, that the three bad courses of action are conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for the three bad courses of action? It should be said: 'Lack of sense restraint.' I say, bhikkhus, that lack of sense restraint is conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for lack of sense restraint? It should be said: 'Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension.' I say, bhikkhus, that lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension? It should be said: 'Improper attention.' I say, bhikkhus, that improper attention is conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for improper attention? It should be said: 'Lack of faith.' I say, bhikkhus, that lack of faith is conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for lack of faith? It should be said: 'Not hearing the true Dhamma.' I say, bhikkhus, that not hearing the true Dhamma is conditioned, not unconditioned. And what is the nutriment for not hearing the true Dhamma? It should be said: 'Association with bad persons.'
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, bhikkhus, association with bad persons fully nourishes not hearing the true Dhamma; not hearing the true Dhamma fully nourishes lack of faith; lack of faith fully nourishes improper attention; improper attention fully nourishes lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension; lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension fully nourishes lack of sense restraint; lack of sense restraint fully nourishes the three bad courses of action; the three bad courses of action fully nourish the five hindrances; the five hindrances fully nourish ignorance. Thus, bhikkhus, is the nutriment for this ignorance, thus is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, bhikkhus, when heavy rains fall on the mountain peaks, the water flows downhill, filling the clefts, gullies, and creeks; these, when full, fill the small pools; the small pools, when full, fill the large pools; the large pools, when full, fill the small rivers; the small rivers, when full, fill the great rivers; the great rivers, when full, fill the great ocean. Thus, bhikkhus, is the nutriment for the great ocean, thus is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, bhikkhus, association with good persons fully nourishes hearing the true Dhamma; hearing the true Dhamma fully nourishes faith; faith fully nourishes proper attention; proper attention fully nourishes mindfulness and clear comprehension; mindfulness and clear comprehension fully nourish sense restraint; sense restraint fully nourishes the three good courses of action; the three good courses of action fully nourish the four establishments of mindfulness; the four establishments of mindfulness fully nourish the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment fully nourish knowledge and liberation. Thus, bhikkhus, is the nutriment for this knowledge and liberation, thus is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous and amiable talk, he sat down to one side. As he sat to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Could it be, friend Sāriputta, that a monk might attain such a state of concentration in which he is not percipient of earth as earth, not percipient of water as water, not percipient of fire as fire, not percipient of air as air, not percipient of the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, not percipient of the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness, not percipient of the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, not percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not percipient of this world as this world, not percipient of the other world as the other world; yet still he is percipient?”
translations.an10.7:4: “How, friend Sāriputta, could a monk attain such a state of concentration in which he is not percipient of earth as earth … yet still he is percipient?” “Once, friend Ānanda, I was dwelling right here in Sāvatthī, in the Blind Men’s Grove. At that time I attained such a concentration in which I was not percipient of earth as earth, not percipient of water as water, not percipient of fire as fire, not percipient of air as air, not percipient of the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, not percipient of the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness, not percipient of the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, not percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not percipient of this world as this world, not percipient of the other world as the other world; yet still I was percipient.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Monks, endowed with three qualities, one who has not abandoned the three defilements is cast down into hell as if thrown. What three? He is immoral, and the defilement of immorality in him is not abandoned; he is envious, and the defilement of envy in him is not abandoned; he is miserly, and the defilement of miserliness in him is not abandoned. Monks, endowed with these three qualities, one who has not abandoned these three defilements is cast down into hell as if thrown.”
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, monks, in any region where a monk rightly knows, ‘This is suffering,’ rightly knows, ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ rightly knows, ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ rightly knows, ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ This, monks, is the second thing that is worthy of reverence for a monk for life.”
translations.an3.15:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in Benares, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an3.15:2: “Once, monks, there was a king named Sacetana. Then King Sacetana addressed the chariot-maker: ‘In six months from now, chariot-maker, there will be a battle. Can you, chariot-maker, make for me a new set of wheels?’ ‘I can, your majesty,’ the chariot-maker replied to King Sacetana. Then, monks, the chariot-maker completed one wheel in six months with great effort. Then King Sacetana addressed the chariot-maker: ‘In six days from now, chariot-maker, there will be a battle. Is the new set of wheels completed?’ ‘This one wheel, your majesty, has been completed in six months with great effort.’ ‘Can you, chariot-maker, complete a second wheel within these six days?’ ‘I can, your majesty,’ said the chariot-maker. Then the chariot-maker completed the second wheel within six days, took the new set of wheels, and approached King Sacetana. Approaching, he said to the king: ‘Here, your majesty, is the new set of wheels, completed.’ ‘And what, chariot-maker, is the difference between this wheel you completed in six months with great effort and this wheel you completed in six days? I see no difference.’ ‘There is a difference, your majesty. Let the king observe the difference.’
translations.an3.15:3: Then, monks, the chariot-maker set in motion the wheel completed in six days. As it spun, it went as far as the momentum carried it, then wobbled and fell to the ground. But the wheel completed in six months with great effort, when set in motion, went as far as the momentum carried it, then stood firm as if on an axle.
translations.an3.15:5: It may be, monks, that you might think: ‘Surely, someone else was that chariot-maker at that time.’ But you should not regard it so. I myself was that chariot-maker at that time. Then, monks, I was skilled in the faults, diseases, and decay of wood. Now, however, I am the arahant, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, skilled in the faults, diseases, and decay of the body; skilled in the faults, diseases, and decay of speech; skilled in the faults, diseases, and decay of mind. Monks, whoever—monk or nun—has not abandoned bodily fault, bodily disease, bodily corruption; has not abandoned verbal fault, verbal disease, verbal corruption; has not abandoned mental fault, mental disease, mental corruption: such a one, monks, falls away from this Dhamma and discipline, just like the wheel completed in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: But whoever, monks—monk or nun—has abandoned bodily fault, bodily disease, bodily corruption; has abandoned verbal fault, verbal disease, verbal corruption; has abandoned mental fault, mental disease, mental corruption: such a one, monks, stands firm in this Dhamma and discipline, just like the wheel completed in six months with great effort.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, monks, the fool is fearful, the wise one is fearless. The fool is fraught with danger, the wise one is free from danger. The fool is fraught with trouble, the wise one is free from trouble. There is no danger from the wise, no danger from the wise, no trouble from the wise.
translations.an3.20:1: “Bhikkhus, a merchant endowed with three qualities quickly attains greatness and abundance in wealth. What are the three? Here, bhikkhus, a merchant is clear-sighted, capable, and well-supported. And how, bhikkhus, is a merchant clear-sighted? Here, bhikkhus, a merchant understands merchandise: ‘This merchandise is bought at such a price, sold at such a price; this will be the cost, this the profit.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a merchant is clear-sighted.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a merchant capable? Here, bhikkhus, a merchant is skilled in buying and selling merchandise. Thus, bhikkhus, a merchant is capable.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a merchant well-supported? Here, bhikkhus, householders or sons of householders who are wealthy, affluent, and of great fortune know of the merchant: ‘This venerable merchant is clear-sighted and capable, able to support his children and wife, and to provide for us in due season.’ They shower him with wealth: ‘Come, good merchant, earn wealth, support your children and wife, and provide for us in due season.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a merchant is well-supported. Bhikkhus, a merchant endowed with these three qualities quickly attains greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities quickly attains greatness and abundance in wholesome qualities. What are the three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is clear-sighted, capable, and well-supported. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu clear-sighted? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is clear-sighted.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu capable? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with aroused energy, striving to abandon unwholesome qualities and to acquire wholesome qualities; steadfast, vigorous, not neglecting the duty regarding wholesome qualities. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is capable.
translations.an3.22:1: “Bhikkhus, these three sick persons are found existing in the world. What three? Here, bhikkhus, one sick person, whether obtaining suitable food or not obtaining suitable food, whether obtaining suitable medicine or not obtaining suitable medicine, whether obtaining proper nursing or not obtaining proper nursing, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: But here, bhikkhus, one sick person, even while obtaining suitable food, not failing to obtain it, even while obtaining suitable medicine, not failing to obtain it, even while obtaining proper nursing, not failing to obtain it, recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Now, bhikkhus, regarding that sick person who, even while obtaining suitable food, not failing to obtain it, even while obtaining suitable medicine, not failing to obtain it, even while obtaining proper nursing, not failing to obtain it, recovers from that illness—on account of this sick person, bhikkhus, the allowance of food for the sick has been permitted, the allowance of medicine for the sick has been permitted, the allowance of a nurse for the sick has been permitted. And other sick persons, bhikkhus, should be nursed on account of this sick person. These are the three sick persons, bhikkhus, found existing in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: So too, bhikkhus, these three persons are found existing in the world, comparable to sick persons. What three? Here, bhikkhus, one person, whether seeing the Tathāgata or not seeing the Tathāgata, whether hearing the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata or not hearing the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, does not enter the right course in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.22:6: But here, bhikkhus, one person, whether seeing the Tathāgata or not seeing the Tathāgata, whether hearing the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata or not hearing the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, enters the right course in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.24:1: “Bhikkhus, these three persons are greatly beneficial to a person. What three? Bhikkhus, the person by relying on whom a person goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dhamma, goes for refuge to the Saṅgha—this person, bhikkhus, is greatly beneficial to that person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, the person by relying on whom a person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—this person, bhikkhus, is greatly beneficial to that person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, the person by relying on whom a person, with the destruction of the taints, attains taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself in this very life, and dwells in it—this person, bhikkhus, is greatly beneficial to that person. These, bhikkhus, are the three persons who are greatly beneficial to a person.
translations.an3.2:1: “Kamma is the mark of a fool, kamma is the mark of a wise person, wisdom is known by its fruit. Bhikkhus, a fool is to be known by three qualities. What three? By bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Bhikkhus, a fool is to be known by these three qualities.
translations.an3.2:2: Bhikkhus, a wise person is to be known by three qualities. What three? By good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Bhikkhus, a wise person is to be known by these three qualities.
translations.an3.30:4: A man of crooked wisdom, dull, without discernment; even though he goes frequently, to the bhikkhus’ presence.
translations.an3.30:5: He is like the beginning, middle, and end of a talk; unable to grasp it, for wisdom is not present in him.
translations.an3.30:6: A man of upright wisdom is said to be better than that; even though he goes frequently, to the bhikkhus’ presence.
translations.an3.30:8: A man of broad wisdom is said to be better than these; even though he goes frequently, to the bhikkhus’ presence.
translations.an3.32:4: “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu has this thought: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, fading away, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Thus, Ānanda, there may be the attainment of such a concentration for a bhikkhu that in this body endowed with consciousness, the underlying tendencies of ‘I am’ and ‘mine’ do not exist, nor do they exist externally in regard to all signs; and that with which, when dwelling having attained freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom, the underlying tendencies of ‘I am’ and ‘mine’ are absent, that very freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom he would dwell in.”
translations.an3.33:1: Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Even if I were to teach the Dhamma briefly, Sāriputta, or in detail, or both briefly and in detail, those who understand the Dhamma are hard to find.” “Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma briefly, in detail, or both briefly and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
translations.an3.33:2: “Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train thus: ‘In this body endowed with consciousness, the underlying tendencies of “I am” and “mine” will not be present; externally, in regard to all signs, the underlying tendencies of “I am” and “mine” will not be present; and with which, when dwelling having attained freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom, the underlying tendencies of “I am” and “mine” are absent, that very freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom I will dwell in.’ Thus, Sāriputta, should you train.”
translations.an3.33:3: “When, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu’s underlying tendencies of ‘I am’ and ‘mine’ are not present in this body endowed with consciousness, nor externally in regard to all signs, and when dwelling having attained freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom, the underlying tendencies of ‘I am’ and ‘mine’ are absent, and he dwells having attained that very freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom—such a bhikkhu is called one who has cut craving, untangled the fetter, and rightly ended suffering through the full understanding of conceit. And this, Sāriputta, is what was spoken of in the Pārāyana, in the Udaya Question:”
translations.an3.33:4: “The abandoning of perceptions of sensual desire, and of both sorrow and joy; The dispelling of dullness, and the removal of restlessness.”
translations.an3.34:1: “These three, bhikkhus, are the conditions for the arising of kamma. What three? Greed is a condition for the arising of kamma, hatred is a condition for the arising of kamma, delusion is a condition for the arising of kamma.”
translations.an3.34:10: “Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is produced free from delusion, born of non-delusion, having non-delusion as its source and origin, when delusion is abandoned, such kamma is completely eradicated, rooted out, made like a palm stump, annihilated, so that it cannot arise in the future.”
translations.an3.34:11: “Just as, bhikkhus, seeds that are unbroken, unrotten, unspoiled by wind and sun, fertile and well-stored—should a person burn them with fire, reduce them to ashes, and then scatter them in a strong wind or cast them into a swift-flowing stream—so too, bhikkhus, those seeds would be rooted out, made like a palm stump, annihilated, so that they cannot arise in the future. In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is produced free from greed, born of non-greed, having non-greed as its source and origin, when greed is abandoned, such kamma is completely eradicated, rooted out, made like a palm stump, annihilated, so that it cannot arise in the future.”
translations.an3.34:13: “Whatever kamma is done, whether little or much, born of greed, hatred, or delusion, when these are abandoned—there it is to be experienced, no other place exists.”
translations.an3.34:2: “Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is produced through greed, born of greed, having greed as its source and origin, wherever a being is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there the result of that kamma is experienced, either in this very life, or in a subsequent rebirth, or in some later existence.”
translations.an3.34:5: “Just as, bhikkhus, seeds that are unbroken, unrotten, unspoiled by wind and sun, fertile and well-stored, planted in well-prepared, fertile soil, and the rain-god properly sends down rain—so too, bhikkhus, those seeds would grow, increase, and expand. In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is produced through greed, born of greed, having greed as its source and origin, wherever a being is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there the result of that kamma is experienced, either in this very life, or in a subsequent rebirth, or in some later existence.”
translations.an3.34:6: “Whatever kamma is produced through hatred… Whatever kamma is produced through delusion, born of delusion, having delusion as its source and origin, wherever a being is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there the result of that kamma is experienced, either in this very life, or in a subsequent rebirth, or in some later existence. These, bhikkhus, are the three conditions for the arising of kamma.”
translations.an3.34:9: “Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is produced free from hatred, born of non-hatred, having non-hatred as its source and origin, when hatred is abandoned, such kamma is completely eradicated, rooted out, made like a palm stump, annihilated, so that it cannot arise in the future.”
translations.an3.35:3: “Well then, young man, I will question you on this matter. Answer as it seems fit to you. What do you think, young man? Suppose a householder or householder’s son has a well-built, plastered, windproof, well-furnished, and well-screened upper chamber, with a couch covered with a spread of fine linen, woolen cloth, and a canopy, with red cushions at both ends, and a lamp burning with sesame oil; and four charming wives wait upon him. What do you think, young man? Would he sleep happily or not? What is your opinion on this?” “He would sleep happily, sir. Among those who experience happiness in the world, he would be one of them.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, young man? Would there arise in that householder or householder’s son passionate distress—physical or mental—by which he, tormented by that passionate distress, would lie in suffering?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.an3.35:8: Always he lies in happiness, the Brahmin who is fully extinguished; who clings not to sensual pleasures, cooled and without clinging.
translations.an3.39:10: While I dwelt thus, having understood the Dhamma without clinging; regarding health, youth, and life, and the conceits connected with them.
translations.an3.39:2: I had, monks, three palaces: one for the cold season, one for the hot season, and one for the rainy season. And, monks, during the four months of the rainy season I was entertained in the rainy-season palace by musicians without leaving the palace. Just as, monks, in the households of others a small portion of food is given to a hired laborer or slave, so too, monks, in my father’s household a portion of salted meat was given to a hired laborer or slave.
translations.an3.39:3: Then, monks, endowed with such a state of mastery and such refinement, it occurred to me: ‘An untaught ordinary person, being himself subject to old age, not beyond old age, seeing another who is aged, is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking his own fact: “I myself am subject to old age, not beyond old age.” But if I, being myself subject to old age, not beyond old age, seeing another who is aged, were to be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.’ As I reflected thus, monks, the conceit of youth entirely abandoned in me.
translations.an3.39:4: ‘An untaught ordinary person, being himself subject to illness, not beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking his own fact: “I myself am subject to illness, not beyond illness.” But if I, being myself subject to illness, not beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, were to be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.’ As I reflected thus, monks, the conceit of health entirely abandoned in me.
translations.an3.39:5: ‘An untaught ordinary person, being himself subject to death, not beyond death, seeing another who is dead, is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking his own fact: “I myself am subject to death, not beyond death.” But if I, being myself subject to death, not beyond death, seeing another who is dead, were to be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.’ As I reflected thus, monks, the conceit of life entirely abandoned in me.
translations.an3.39:7: A monk intoxicated with youth, monks, rejects the training and reverts to a lower life. A monk intoxicated with health, monks, … or a monk intoxicated with life, monks, rejects the training and reverts to a lower life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to old age, and also subject to death; as is natural, the ordinary people are disgusted.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted with living beings who are such by nature, that would not be fitting for me, who lives in such a way.
translations.an3.40:1: “There are, monks, three kinds of mastery. What three? Mastery over self, mastery over the world, and mastery over the Dhamma. And what, monks, is mastery over self? Here, monks, a monk gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘I have not gone forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Nor for the sake of almsfood, nor for lodgings, nor for the sake of this or that state of becoming. Indeed, I am overwhelmed by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am overwhelmed by suffering and burdened by suffering. May there be an end to this entire mass of suffering!’ And if I, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of such pleasures, were to seek after such pleasures again, or even baser ones, that would not be fitting for me. He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused and unrelaxed, mindfulness established and unmuddled, body tranquil and undisturbed, mind concentrated and unified.’ Having made himself his own master, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and keeps himself pure. This, monks, is called mastery over self.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, monks, is mastery over the Dhamma? Here, monks, a monk gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘I have not gone forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Nor for the sake of almsfood, nor for lodgings, nor for the sake of this or that state of becoming. Indeed, I am overwhelmed by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am overwhelmed by suffering and burdened by suffering. May there be an end to this entire mass of suffering! The Dhamma has been well proclaimed by the Blessed One: visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, effective, to be personally experienced by the wise. And there are my fellow practitioners who dwell knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth into this well-proclaimed Dhamma and discipline, were to dwell slothful and heedless, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused and unrelaxed, mindfulness established and unmuddled, body tranquil and undisturbed, mind concentrated and unified.’ Having made the Dhamma his master, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and keeps himself pure. This, monks, is called mastery over the Dhamma. These, monks, are the three kinds of mastery.”
translations.an3.40:4: There is no hidden place in the world for one who commits evil; you yourself, O man, know—whether truth or falsehood.
translations.an3.40:5: How excellent indeed, O Sakka, is the witness: you esteem yourself highly, yet conceal the evil within yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: The devas and the Tathāgatas see the fool behaving wrongly in the world; therefore, one who is master of himself, master of the world, wise and meditative, master of the Dhamma and one who follows the Dhamma, does not fall away—the truthful, energetic sage.
translations.an3.48:1: “Monks, great sal trees grow in three ways relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains. What are the three? They grow through branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow through bark and outer skin; they grow through heartwood. Monks, great sal trees relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, grow in these three ways.
translations.an3.48:2: In the same way, monks, the inner person grows in three ways relying on a faithful householder. What are the three? They grow through faith, through virtue, and through wisdom. Monks, the inner person relying on a faithful householder grows in these three ways.
translations.an3.48:3: Just as a rocky mountain in the wilderness, In a sacred grove; Trees depending on it, Grow, the forest trees.
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins, aged, elderly, very old, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, about a hundred and twenty years old by birth, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One. After the exchange of friendly greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Gotama, we are brahmins, aged, elderly, very old, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, about a hundred and twenty years old by birth; we have done no good, performed no skillful deeds, achieved no protection from fear. May the Venerable Gotama instruct us, may he advise us, so that it may be for our welfare and happiness for a long time.”
translations.an3.51:2: “Indeed, brahmins, you are aged, elderly, very old, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, about a hundred and twenty years old by birth; you have done no good, performed no skillful deeds, achieved no protection from fear. This world, brahmins, is drawn towards old age, illness, and death. When this world, brahmins, is drawn towards old age, illness, and death, then bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and mental restraint here become the shelter, refuge, island, support, and stronghold for that deceased one.
translations.an3.51:3: Life is drawn towards old age, short-lived; For one drawn to old age, there is no shelter. Seeing this danger in death, One should do meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
translations.an3.52:4: Indeed, the world is aflame with old age and death; Extinguish it with giving; what is given becomes well extinguished.
translations.an3.57:2: “Whoever, Vaccha, says thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama says: “Only my gift should be given … (repeat) … gifts given to others’ disciples bear great fruit”’—they do not speak my words; they wrongly attribute to me what is false. Whoever, Vaccha, discourages another from giving a gift, becomes an obstacle and hindrance in three ways. Which three? They become a hindrance to the merit of the donor, a hindrance to the gain of the recipients, and their own self is previously damaged and harmed. Whoever, Vaccha, discourages another from giving a gift, becomes an obstacle and hindrance in these three ways.
translations.an3.5:1: “A fool, monks, is to be known by three qualities. What three? He asks questions inappropriately, he answers questions inappropriately, and when another answers a question properly, he does not approve it, even if it is clearly explained with detailed words in a circle of people. Monks, one endowed with these three qualities is to be known as a fool.
translations.an3.60:1: Then Sangarava the brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After the exchange of friendly greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Sangarava the brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Gotama, we brahmins are known as such. We perform sacrifices and have sacrifices performed. Now, Venerable Gotama, those who sacrifice and those who have sacrifices performed—all of them follow a path of merit with many aspects, namely, the sacrificial way. But whoever, Venerable Gotama, from any family, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, trains only himself, calms only himself, and fully extinguishes only himself—surely he follows a path of merit with a single aspect, namely, the way of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:10: But here, brahmin, one neither perceives by means of a sign, nor upon hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities does he perceive: ‘Such is your mind, so is your mind, thus is your heart.’ Even if he perceives often, it remains just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: But here, brahmin, one neither perceives by means of a sign, nor upon hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities does he perceive, nor upon hearing the sound of thoughts and mental processes arising from thinking and pondering does he perceive: ‘Such is your mind, so is your mind, thus is your heart.’ Even if he perceives often, it remains just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: But here, brahmin, one neither perceives by means of a sign, nor upon hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities does he perceive, nor upon hearing the sound of thoughts and mental processes arising from thinking and pondering does he perceive, but having attained a concentration that is without thought and examination, he directly knows with his mind the mind of another: ‘This one’s mental formations are directed thus; immediately after this, this thought will arise in that mind.’ Even if he perceives often, it remains just so, not otherwise. This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, one instructs thus: ‘Think in this way, do not think in that way; apply your mind in this way, do not apply your mind in that way; abandon this, and abide having attained that.’ This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle seems most excellent and superior to you?”
translations.an3.60:14: “Now, Venerable Gotama, that miracle by which one experiences various kinds of psychic powers … (repeat) … even as far as the Brahma world, and wields bodily control—this miracle, Venerable Gotama, merely produces an effect, merely gives an experience; whatever effect it produces, that is all it is. This miracle, Venerable Gotama, seems to me like an illusion or a magical appearance.”
translations.an3.60:16: And that, friend Gotama, is the miracle of instruction, when one teaches thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; apply your mind in this way, do not apply it in that way; abandon this, and dwell having attained that.' This miracle, friend Gotama, is pleasing to me, and it is more excellent and sublime than those three miracles.
translations.an3.60:17: Amazing, friend Gotama! Astonishing, friend Gotama! This has been well said by the Blessed One. We accept the Blessed One as endowed with these three miracles. For indeed, the Blessed One personally experiences various kinds of psychic powers: ... even as far as the Brahmā world, he wields mastery with the body. And indeed, the Blessed One, with mind knowing the mind of one who has attained the concentration without thought or examination, understands: 'Just as this person's mental formations are directed, so will this mind immediately give rise to that particular thought.' And indeed, the Blessed One instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; apply your mind in this way, do not apply it in that way; abandon this, and dwell having attained that.'
translations.an3.60:18: Indeed, brahmin, what I have said is spoken with full commitment; yet I will explain further. For I, brahmin, personally experience various kinds of psychic powers: ... even as far as the Brahmā world, I wield mastery with the body. And I, brahmin, with mind knowing the mind of one who has attained the concentration without thought or examination, understand: 'Just as this person's mental formations are directed, so will this mind immediately give rise to that particular thought.' And I, brahmin, instruct thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; apply your mind in this way, do not apply it in that way; abandon this, and dwell having attained that.'
translations.an3.60:19: But is there, friend Gotama, another single monk besides the Blessed One who possesses these three miracles?
translations.an3.60:2: Then, brahmin, I will ask you about this matter. Answer as it seems fitting to you. What do you think, brahmin: here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed. He declares: 'This is the path, this is the practice; practicing accordingly, I myself realized and attained the supreme goal of the holy life, and made it known. Come, you too practice in this way; practicing accordingly, you too will realize and attain the supreme goal of the holy life, and dwell having attained it.' When this teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly, then indeed there are hundreds, thousands, even hundreds of thousands.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin: in such a case, is this path of merit consisting of going forth a single-body path or a many-bodied path?
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: 'Of these two paths of yours, brahmin, which path seems to you easier to undertake, requiring less effort, and more fruitful and beneficial?' When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Just as the Blessed One Gotama, so too the Venerable Ānanda. These are worthy of veneration for me, these are worthy of praise.'
translations.an3.60:5: A second time, Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: 'But I am not asking you, brahmin: Who are worthy of veneration for you, who are worthy of praise? Rather, I am asking you this: Of these two paths of yours, brahmin, which path seems to you easier to undertake, requiring less effort, and more fruitful and beneficial?' A second time, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Just as the Blessed One Gotama, so too the Venerable Ānanda. These are worthy of veneration for me, these are worthy of praise.'
translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'Even when questioned a third time by Ānanda with a proper question, the brahmin Saṅgārava flatters but does not answer. Why don't I intervene?' Then the Blessed One said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: 'Was there, brahmin, some conversation arising among the royal ministers gathered and assembled in the royal palace?' 'Indeed there was, friend Gotama. This conversation arose among the royal ministers gathered and assembled in the royal palace: “Previously, there were fewer monks but more supramundane psychic miracles displayed; now, however, there are more monks but fewer supramundane psychic miracles displayed.” This, friend Gotama, was the conversation that arose among the royal ministers gathered and assembled in the royal palace.'
translations.an3.60:8: There are, brahmin, these three miracles. What three? The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of instruction, and the miracle of teaching. And what, brahmin, is the miracle of psychic power?
