Here, brahmin, someone personally experiences various kinds of psychic powers: 'Having been one, I become many; having been many, I become one; I appear and vanish; I go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains, as though through space; I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; I walk on water without sinking as though on dry land; I fly cross-legged through the air like a bird; with my hand I touch and stroke the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; and I exercise bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world.' This, brahmin, is called the miracle of psychic power.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, a certain one instructs with a sign: 'Thus is your mind, so is your mind, such is your mind.' If he instructs many times, it remains just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: These are the four noble truths, monks, that I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins. Thus it was said. But in reference to what was this said? Dependent on the six elements, there is descent of the embryo; with descent, name-and-form; dependent on name-and-form, the six sense bases; dependent on the six sense bases, contact; dependent on contact, feeling. And, monks, I declare this: what is felt is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, (…) death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Thus arises this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus ceases this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: Previously, monks, there is no desire or effort to return to what is essential, no thought of 'this should be done, this should not be done.' When right and wrong actions are not truly discerned, and one dwells with muddled mindfulness and lack of restraint, there is no self-consistent ascetic doctrine. This, monks, is my first consistent criterion among those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and doctrines.
translations.an3.61:8: These three, monks, are the fords that, when properly followed, pursued, and practiced by the wise, lead even beyond and come to rest in inaction.
translations.an3.61:9: But this, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins? These six elements, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins. These six bases of contact, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins. These eighteen mental investigations, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins. These four noble truths, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—unshakable, unblemished, irreproachable, unchallenged by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: "These three, monks, are the fears of mother and child spoken of by the uninstructed worldling. What three? There comes a time, monks, when a great fire blaze arises. When a great fire blaze arises, villages, towns, and cities are burned. While villages, towns, and cities are burning, there the mother does not find her child, and the child does not find his mother. This, monks, is the first fear of mother and child spoken of by the uninstructed worldling.
translations.an3.62:2: Again, monks, there comes a time when a great cloud arises. When a great cloud arises, a great flood occurs. When a great flood occurs, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. While villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there the mother does not find her child, and the child does not find his mother. This, monks, is the second fear of mother and child spoken of by the uninstructed worldling.
translations.an3.62:3: Again, monks, there comes a time when there is fear, unrest in the wilderness, and people with weapons roam the countryside. When there is fear and unrest in the wilderness, and people with weapons roam the countryside, there the mother does not find her child, and the child does not find his mother. This, monks, is the third fear of mother and child spoken of by the uninstructed worldling. These three, monks, are the fears of mother and child spoken of by the uninstructed worldling.
translations.an3.62:4: Indeed, these three, bhikkhus, are the only fears that an unlearned worldling speaks of as fears without mother and child. What three? There comes a time, bhikkhus, when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire has broken out, bhikkhus, villages are burned, towns are burned, cities are burned. While villages are being burned, towns are being burned, cities are being burned, there comes a time when a mother might again obtain her child, or a child might again obtain her mother. This, bhikkhus, is the first fear that an unlearned worldling speaks of as a fear without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:5: Again, bhikkhus, there comes a time when a great cloud arises. When a great cloud has arisen, bhikkhus, a great flood occurs. When a great flood has occurred, bhikkhus, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. While villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there comes a time when a mother might again obtain her child, or a child might again obtain her mother. This, bhikkhus, is the second fear that an unlearned worldling speaks of as a fear without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:6: Again, bhikkhus, there comes a time when there is danger, a state of unrest in the wilderness, and people mounted on chariots wander about. When there is danger, bhikkhus, with unrest in the wilderness and people mounted on chariots wandering about, there comes a time when a mother might again obtain her child, or a child might again obtain her mother. This, bhikkhus, is the third fear that an unlearned worldling speaks of as a fear without mother and child. These three, bhikkhus, are the only fears that an unlearned worldling speaks of as fears without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:7: These three, bhikkhus, are fears without mother and child. What three? The fear of aging, the fear of illness, the fear of death. A mother does not obtain her son who is aging and say thus: 'I am aging, may my son not age'; nor does a son obtain his mother who is aging and say thus: 'I am aging, may my mother not age'.
translations.an3.62:8: A mother does not obtain her son who is ill and say thus: 'I am ill, may my son not be ill'; nor does a son obtain his mother who is ill and say thus: 'I am ill, may my mother not be ill'.
translations.an3.62:9: A mother does not obtain her son who is dying and say thus: 'I am dying, may my son not die'; nor does a son obtain his mother who is dying and say thus: 'I am dying, may my mother not die'. These three, bhikkhus, are fears without mother and child.
translations.an3.63:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering among the Kosalans with a large community of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Venāgapura. The brahmins and householders of Venāgapura heard: 'Indeed, the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan, having gone forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura. The good repute of Master Gotama has spread thus: "He is indeed the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, the Fortunate One, knower of the world, the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Awakened One, the Blessed One." He makes known this world with its devas, its Māras, its Brahmas, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. It is indeed good to see such arahants.'
translations.an3.63:11: "How amazing, Master Gotama, how extraordinary, Master Gotama! Who else but the Blessed One could obtain such a lofty and great resting place so effortlessly, without difficulty, without strain?"
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmins and householders of Venāgapura approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after a polite and friendly conversation, sat down at one side; some raised their hands in salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down at one side; some sat down at one side in silence. Then Vacchagotta, the Venāgapura brahmin, sitting at one side, said to the Blessed One:
translations.an3.63:5: "There are three, brahmin, lofty and great resting places, which I now obtain effortlessly, without difficulty, without strain. What three? The divine lofty and great resting place, the brahmic lofty and great resting place, the noble lofty and great resting place. These three, brahmin, are the lofty and great resting places, which I now obtain effortlessly, without difficulty, without strain."
translations.an4.10:10: Beings wander on in saṁsāra, going in birth and death; those who fully understand sensual pleasures and completely abandon the yoke of becoming.
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by the yoke of sensual desire, and by the yoke of becoming on both sides; bound by the yoke of views, preceded by ignorance.
translations.an4.18:1: "These four, bhikkhus, are ways of not going to a bad destination. What four? One does not go by way of desire, one does not go by way of aversion, one does not go by way of delusion, one does not go by way of fear. These four, bhikkhus, are ways of not going to a bad destination."
translations.an4.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians in Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.1:4: "Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation; these qualities, well-understood by the renowned Gotama."
translations.an4.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Kālakārāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said:
translations.an4.24:2: "Whatever, bhikkhus, has been seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, or mentally explored by the world with its devas, its Māras, its Brahmas, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans—this I know."
translations.an4.24:5: If, monks … then I would say that this too is just such as that.
translations.an4.24:7: Thus, monks, the Tathāgata sees what is to be seen, but does not conceive 'seer'; he does not conceive 'unseen', does not conceive 'to be seen', does not conceive 'the seer'. Having heard what is to be heard, he does not conceive 'heard', does not conceive 'unheard', does not conceive 'to be heard', does not conceive 'the hearer'. Having cognized what is to be cognized, he does not conceive 'cognized', does not conceive 'uncognized', does not conceive 'to be cognized', does not conceive 'the cognizer'. Thus, monks, the Tathāgata is just such in regard to things seen, heard, cognized, and thought. 'And there is no other such one, higher or better than this,' I say.
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or cognized, truly known by others— one who is such, firmly bound in such ways, harms no other, whether truth or falsehood.
translations.an4.28:1: These four, monks, are noble lineages—noble, excellent, ancient, pure, uncorrupted, never before corrupted—uncontaminated by ascetics, brahmins, or the wise. What four? Here, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, praises contentment with any robe, and does not resort to improper means for the sake of a robe; when he does not obtain a robe, he is not distressed, and when he obtains one, he uses it without attachment, without clinging, without infatuation, clearly seeing the danger and wisely seeking release. And by means of this contentment with any robe, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Whoever among them is skilled, diligent, fully aware, and mindful—such a monk, monks, is said to stand in the ancient noble lineage.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, monks, a monk delights in development, takes pleasure in development; he delights in abandoning, takes pleasure in abandoning. And by means of this delight and pleasure in development and in abandoning, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Whoever among them is skilled, diligent, fully aware, and mindful—such a monk, monks, is said to stand in the ancient noble lineage. These four, monks, are noble lineages—noble, excellent, ancient, pure, uncorrupted, never before corrupted—uncontaminated by ascetics, brahmins, or the wise.
translations.an4.28:5: And, monks, a monk endowed with these four noble lineages, even if he dwells in the eastern direction, he overcomes discontent, and discontent does not overcome him; even if he dwells in the western direction, he overcomes discontent, and discontent does not overcome him; even if he dwells in the northern direction, he overcomes discontent, and discontent does not overcome him; even if he dwells in the southern direction, he overcomes discontent, and discontent does not overcome him. Why is that? Because, monks, the wise man is victorious over discontent.
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent does not overcome the wise, discontent is not overcome by the wise; the wise alone overcome discontent, for the wise are victorious over discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: These four, monks, are wheels, by possessing which gods and humans are said to have the fourfold wheel, and by possessing which gods and humans quickly attain greatness and abundance in wealth. What four? Dwelling in a suitable place, association with good persons, one's own proper aspiration, and meritorious deeds done previously. These four, monks, are wheels, by possessing which gods and humans are said to have the fourfold wheel, and by possessing which gods and humans quickly attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an4.32:1: These four, monks, are means of embracing. What four? Giving, kindly speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. These four, monks, are the means of embracing.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kindly speech, beneficial conduct here, and impartiality in accordance with Dhamma, wherever appropriate—these are the bonds in the world, like the linchpin of a chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If these bonds did not exist, not even a mother would receive honor and reverence from her child; nor would a father receive honor and reverence from his child.
translations.an4.33:1: The lion, monks, the king of beasts, emerges from his lair in the evening. Having emerged, he yawns. Having yawned, he surveys the four directions all around. Having surveyed the four directions, he roars three times. Having roared three times, he sets out for his pasture. And those, monks, the animals of the earth who hear the sound of the roaring of the lion, the king of beasts, for the most part experience fear, dread, and terror. They enter their holes, enter their burrows, enter the forest, and birds take to the sky. Even those royal elephants, monks, bound with strong iron chains in villages, towns, and royal cities, break through those bonds, leap over them, and flee in fear, defecating as they go, wherever they can. So mighty, monks, is the lion, the king of beasts, among the animals of the earth—so powerful, so majestic.
translations.an4.33:2: Even so, monks, when the Tathāgata arises in the world, the perfected one, the fully enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, the fortunate one, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed tamer of persons, the teacher of gods and humans, the awakened one, the blessed one, he teaches the Dhamma: 'This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' And those, monks, the long-lived, beautiful, blissful devas dwelling in high heavens for a long time, upon hearing the Tathāgata's teaching of Dhamma, for the most part experience fear, dread, and terror: 'Indeed, we who thought ourselves permanent are impermanent, friends; we who thought ourselves stable are unstable, friends; we who thought ourselves eternal are not eternal, friends. Indeed, we are impermanent, unstable, inconstant, bound within the cycle of existence.' So mighty, monks, is the Tathāgata in the world with its devas—so powerful, so majestic.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, endowed with direct knowledge, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, the unmatched teacher in the world with its devas.
translations.an4.33:4: The self, its cessation, and the origin of self; and the noble eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “These four, bhikkhus, are supreme devotions. What four? As far as beings go, whether footless or with two feet, four feet, or many feet, with form or formless, percipient or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient, the Tathāgata is declared supreme among them—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Those, bhikkhus, who have devotion towards the Buddha, have devotion towards the supreme. And for those devoted to the supreme, the supreme fruit arises.
translations.an4.34:2: As far as conditioned phenomena go, the noble eightfold path is declared supreme among them. Those, bhikkhus, who have devotion towards the noble eightfold path, have devotion towards the supreme. And for those devoted to the supreme, the supreme fruit arises.
translations.an4.34:3: As far as phenomena go, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared supreme among them—namely, the destruction of lust, the overcoming of thirst, the removal of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle, the cessation of craving: dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those, bhikkhus, who have devotion towards the Dhamma of dispassion, have devotion towards the supreme. And for those devoted to the supreme, the supreme fruit arises.
translations.an4.34:4: As far as communities or groups go, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared supreme among them—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals; this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those, bhikkhus, who have devotion towards the Saṅgha, have devotion towards the supreme. And for those devoted to the supreme, the supreme fruit arises. These, bhikkhus, are the four supreme devotions.”
translations.an4.34:5: Indeed, for those devoted to the supreme, who clearly understand the supreme Dhamma; for those devoted to the supreme Buddha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:6: For those devoted to the supreme Dhamma, happiness in dispassion and peace; for those devoted to the supreme Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:7: When a gift is given to the supreme, supreme merit increases; supreme is life, beauty, fame, glory, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.35:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. Then Vassakāra the Brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; and having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Vassakāra the Brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “We, Master Gotama, recognize a great wise person, a great being, endowed with four qualities. What four? Here, Master Gotama, he is learned, knowing the meaning of what has been heard and repeatedly heard: ‘This is the meaning of this statement, this is the meaning of that statement.’ And he is mindful, remembering and not forgetting things done long ago and said long ago. In whatever household duties arise, he is skilled, diligent, endowed with inquiry and analysis, capable and competent to act and arrange. These four qualities, Master Gotama, are the ones with which we recognize a great wise person, a great being. If what I say is acceptable, may Master Gotama approve; if not, may Master Gotama reject it.”
translations.an4.35:6: Who knows the liberation from the bonds of death for all beings; who teaches the way of Dhamma for the welfare of gods and humans; whom, having seen or heard, many people are pleased with.
translations.an4.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭha and Setavya. The Brahmin Doṇa was also traveling along the same road between Ukkaṭṭha and Setavya. Doṇa the Brahmin saw the wheels of a thousand-spoked Dhamma chariot, with hubs and rims, fully formed, on the feet of the Blessed One; and seeing this, he thought: “Indeed, this is astonishing, truly wonderful! These cannot be the feet of a mere human being.” Then the Blessed One, having left the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree, arranging his cross-legged posture, straightening his body, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then Doṇa the Brahmin, following the footprints, saw the Blessed One seated at the foot of a tree—serene, inspiring serenity, with tranquil faculties, a tranquil mind, having attained the highest taming and calm, tamed, guarded, with faculties restrained, like a noble elephant. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One and said to him:
translations.an4.36:2: “Will you be a god, sir?” “I am not, brahmin, going to be a god.” “Will you be a heavenly musician, sir?” “I am not, brahmin, going to be a heavenly musician.” “Will you be a demon, sir?” “I am not, brahmin, going to be a demon.” “Will you be a human, sir?” “I am not, brahmin, going to be a human.”
translations.an4.36:4: “The defilements, brahmin, because of which I might become a god, have been abandoned by me—uprooted, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and no longer subject to future arising. The defilements, brahmin, because of which I might become a heavenly musician … a demon … a human, have been abandoned by me—uprooted, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and no longer subject to future arising. Just as, brahmin, a blue, red, or white lotus, born in the water, growing in the water, rises above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; so too, brahmin, though born in the world, grown in the world, I dwell unsoiled by the world. Brahmin, regard me as the Buddha.”
translations.an4.37:1: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with four qualities is incapable of decline, being right at the threshold of Nibbāna. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue, guarded in the sense doors, moderate in eating, and devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous, living restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and way of life, seeing danger in the slightest faults, training himself in the training rules. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue.
translations.an4.37:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who guards the sense doors? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its sign or features. Whatever unwholesome, evil, unskillful states such as covetousness and displeasure would arise in one who dwells with the faculty of the eye unguarded, for the sake of restraining them he practices; he guards the faculty of the eye; he undertakes the restraint of the faculty of the eye. Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible with the body … having cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its sign or features. Whatever unwholesome, evil, unskillful states such as covetousness and displeasure would arise in one who dwells with the faculty of the mind unguarded, for the sake of restraining them he practices; he guards the faculty of the mind; he undertakes the restraint of the faculty of the mind. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who guards the sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu moderate in eating? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reflects wisely upon the alms food he consumes: 'Not for fun, not for indulgence, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the support and maintenance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I shall be healthy, blameless, and live in comfort.' Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness? Here, bhikkhus, by day, while walking back and forth or sitting, he purifies his mind from hindering states. During the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth or sitting, he purifies his mind from hindering states. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down in the lion’s posture, on his right side, placing one foot on top of the other, mindful and fully aware, with the thought of rising in mind. During the last watch of the night, having risen, while walking back and forth or sitting, he purifies his mind from hindering states. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness. A bhikkhu endowed with these four qualities is incapable of decline, being close to nibbāna.
translations.an4.37:6: Established in virtue is the bhikkhu, restrained in the sense faculties; moderate in food, devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Dwelling thus, diligent, day and night untiring, he cultivates wholesome states for the attainment of peace and security.
translations.an4.38:1: A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who has destroyed speculative views, one at peace, one with tranquillized bodily formations, one who has attained cessation. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has destroyed speculative views? Here, bhikkhus, all the various speculative views held by various ascetics and brahmins—such as the view that the world is eternal, or the world is not eternal, the world is finite, or the world is infinite, the soul and the body are the same, or the soul is one thing and the body another, the Tathāgata exists after death, or the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—all these are pierced through, destroyed, vomited up, rejected, abandoned, and relinquished. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has destroyed speculative views.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has attained cessation? Here, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu’s conceit 'I am' is abandoned, its root destroyed, like a palm stump, eradicated, not subject to future arising. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has attained cessation. A bhikkhu who has destroyed speculative views, is at peace, has tranquillized bodily formations, and has attained cessation is thus called.
translations.an4.38:5: Desire for sense pleasures, desire for existence, desire for the holy life, along with views and attachments to fixed standpoints.
translations.an4.38:6: For one dispassionate towards all lust, liberated by the destruction of craving, all searchings are relinquished, all attachments to fixed standpoints uprooted.
translations.an4.52:1: These four, bhikkhus, are accumulations of merit, accumulations of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' This, bhikkhus, is the first accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally experienced by the wise.' This, bhikkhus, is the second accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples who have practiced well, practiced straight-forwardly, practiced correctly, practiced properly—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' This, bhikkhus, is the third accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with noble, unbroken, unblemished, unblotched, unclouded, uncorrupted, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven. These four, bhikkhus, are accumulations of merit, accumulations of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven.
translations.an4.52:5: Whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable, well established; whose virtue is excellent, praised, and noble.
translations.an4.52:6: One has confidence in the Sangha, and their view is upright; they are called blameless, and their life is fruitful.
translations.an4.53:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañja. Several householder men and women were also traveling along the same road. Then the Blessed One left the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The householders saw the Blessed One seated at the foot of a tree. Seeing him, they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. When they were seated, the Blessed One said to them:
translations.an4.53:10: Both faithful and wise, restrained and living righteously; they become companions, speaking affectionately to each other.
translations.an4.53:11: Prosperity increases greatly, ease arises; their enemies are distressed, both being of equal virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: "These four, householder, are types of cohabitation. What four? A corpse cohabits with a corpse, a corpse with a goddess, a god with a corpse, and a god with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householder, does a corpse cohabit with a corpse? Here, householder, the husband is a killer of living beings, one who takes what is not given, one who engages in wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, a speaker of false speech, one who indulges in intoxicants causing negligence; of bad conduct, of evil ways, with mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, living in the house, abusive and insulting to ascetics and brahmins; and the wife is also a killer of living beings, one who takes what is not given, one who engages in wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, a speaker of false speech, one who indulges in intoxicants causing negligence; of bad conduct, of evil ways, with mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, living in the house, abusive and insulting to ascetics and brahmins. Thus, householder, a corpse cohabits with a corpse.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is immoral, mean, and abusive; the wife is virtuous, wise, and free from stinginess; she, as a goddess, cohabits with a corpse as her husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, wise, and free from stinginess; the wife is immoral, mean, and abusive; she, as a corpse, cohabits with a god as her husband.
translations.an4.5:1: "These four persons, bhikkhus, exist in the world. What four? The person who follows the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the person who stands firm, and the person who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land—a brahmin. And who, bhikkhus, is the person who follows the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who follows the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And who, bhikkhus, is the person who goes against the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures, does not perform evil deeds, yet even with suffering, even with mental unhappiness, with tears streaming and weeping, he fulfills and practices a complete and pure spiritual life. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And who, bhikkhus, is the person who stands firm? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, through the destruction of the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously, there he attains final Nibbāna, not returning from that world. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who stands firm.
translations.an4.5:4: And who, bhikkhus, is the person who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land—a brahmin? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, with the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land—a brahmin. These, bhikkhus, are the four persons existing in the world.
translations.an4.5:5: Those who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, who are not free from lust, indulging in pleasures here; they go again and again through birth and old age, bound by craving, followers of the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore, the wise person, established here with mindfulness, not indulging in sensual pleasures and evil deeds, should abandon sensual pleasures even with suffering; such a person is called one who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: One who has abandoned the five defilements, a complete trainee, one whose nature is unshakeable; whose mind is tamed, senses restrained—such a man is called one who stands firm.
translations.an4.62:2: "Four kinds of happiness, householder, are to be gained by a householder enjoying sensual pleasures, at the right time, from time to time. What four? The happiness of having, the happiness of using, the happiness of being free from debt, and the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of having? Here, householder, a householder's wealth is acquired by energetic effort, amassed by strength, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and lawfully acquired. He reflects: 'I possess wealth acquired by energetic effort, amassed by strength, earned by the sweat of my brow, righteous and lawfully acquired.' He gains happiness and joy. This is called, householder, the happiness of having.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of being free from debt? Here, householder, a householder owes nothing, not even a small amount, to anyone. He reflects: 'I owe nothing to anyone, not even a small amount.' He gains happiness and joy. This is called, householder, the happiness of being free from debt.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily conduct, blameless verbal conduct, and blameless mental conduct. He reflects: 'I am endowed with blameless bodily conduct, blameless verbal conduct, and blameless mental conduct.' He gains happiness and joy. This is called, householder, the happiness of blamelessness. These four, householder, are the kinds of happiness to be gained by a householder enjoying sensual pleasures, at the right time, from time to time.
translations.an4.62:7: Having understood the happiness of being free from debt, and then the higher happiness of having, a mortal should enjoy the happiness of wealth, and then wisdom will see clearly.
translations.an5.23:1: “Bhikkhus, these five are impurities of gold, by which gold, when tainted, is neither malleable, nor workable, nor radiant, but brittle and unfit for proper use. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver—these, bhikkhus, are the five impurities of gold, by which gold, when tainted, is neither malleable, nor workable, nor radiant, but brittle and unfit for proper use. But when, bhikkhus, gold is freed from these five impurities, it becomes malleable, workable, radiant, not brittle, and fit for proper use. And whatever form it is to be shaped into—whether a ring, an earring, a necklace, or a gold chain—it serves that purpose well.
translations.an5.23:2: In the same way, bhikkhus, these five are impurities of the mind, by which the mind, when tainted, is neither malleable, nor workable, nor radiant, but brittle and unfit for proper concentration leading to the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—these, bhikkhus, are the five impurities of the mind, by which the mind, when tainted, is neither malleable, nor workable, nor radiant, but brittle and unfit for proper concentration leading to the destruction of the taints. But when, bhikkhus, the mind is freed from these five impurities, it becomes malleable, workable, radiant, not brittle, and properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. And whatever quality the mind directs itself to for realization through direct knowledge, there it achieves the capability of direct experience, in each and every case.
translations.an5.23:3: If one wishes: ‘May I experience various kinds of supernormal powers: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains, as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though on dry land; may I fly cross-legged through the air like a bird; may I with my hand touch and stroke the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; may I even reach the Brahmā world with this body’—in each and every case, one achieves the capability of direct experience.
translations.an5.23:4: If one wishes: ‘May I hear, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near’—in each and every case, one achieves the capability of direct experience.
translations.an5.23:5: If one wishes: ‘May I know the minds of other beings, of other persons, with my mind—knowing a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate, a mind without hate as a mind without hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind; a lofty mind as a lofty mind, a mind not lofty as a mind not lofty; a superior mind as a superior mind, an incomparable mind as an incomparable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind’—in each and every case, one achieves the capability of direct experience.
translations.an5.25:1: “Bhikkhus, with five factors, right view is supported, and there is the fruit of mind-liberation and the benefits of mind-liberation; there is the fruit of wisdom-liberation and the benefits of wisdom-liberation.
translations.an5.26:1: “Bhikkhus, these are the five grounds of liberation where, for a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, either the unliberated mind is liberated, or the taints not yet destroyed come to destruction, or the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, it may be that neither the Teacher teaches the Dhamma, nor a respected senior fellow monastic, but the bhikkhu himself thoroughly teaches the Dhamma to others as he has heard and learned. As, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu thoroughly teaches the Dhamma to others as he has heard and learned, so in that Dhamma he experiences meaning and realizes the Dhamma. From experiencing meaning and realizing the Dhamma, joy arises. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. With a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This, bhikkhus, is the second ground of liberation where, for a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, either the unliberated mind is liberated, or the taints not yet destroyed come to destruction, or the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, it may be that neither the Teacher teaches the Dhamma, nor a respected senior fellow monastic, nor does he thoroughly teach the Dhamma to others, but he himself thoroughly recites the Dhamma as he has heard and learned. As, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu thoroughly recites the Dhamma as he has heard and learned, so in that Dhamma he experiences meaning and realizes the Dhamma. From experiencing meaning and realizing the Dhamma, joy arises. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. With a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This, bhikkhus, is the third ground of liberation where, for a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, either the unliberated mind is liberated, or the taints not yet destroyed come to destruction, or the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk is not taught the Dhamma by the Teacher or by some respected fellow practitioner, nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others according to what he has heard and learned, nor does he recite in detail the Dhamma according to what he has heard and learned, nor does he mentally examine and reflect upon the Dhamma according to what he has heard and learned. Yet, he has clearly grasped, clearly attended to, firmly established, and thoroughly comprehended with wisdom some object of concentration. As, monks, that monk clearly grasps, clearly attends to, firmly establishes, and thoroughly comprehends with wisdom some object of concentration, so he experiences meaning and experiences Dhamma in that state. For one who experiences meaning and experiences Dhamma, joy arises. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. With a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the fifth basis of liberation: when a heedful, ardent, and resolute monk dwells thus, either his mind is liberated, or if there is still some underlying taints, they are completely destroyed, or if he has not yet attained the supreme security from bondage, he reaches it.
translations.an5.27:1: "Monks, develop concentration that is boundless, wise, and mindful. When monks develop concentration that is boundless, wise, and mindful, five kinds of knowledge arise in them personally. What five? The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is pleasant in the present and will have a pleasant result in the future.' The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is noble and unworldly.' The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is not frequented by ordinary people.' The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained through tranquility and unification, not attained by forceful suppression.' The knowledge arises personally: 'I enter into this concentration mindfully, and I emerge from it mindfully.'"
translations.an5.28:1: "I will teach you the development of the noble fivefold right concentration. Listen, pay close attention, I will speak."
translations.an5.28:10: Just as, monks, a well-harnessed chariot stands ready at a crossroads on level ground, and a skilled charioteer, taking the reins in his left hand and the whip in his right, could drive it wherever he wishes, forward or back—so too, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, wherever he directs his mind toward the realization of any knowledge, he can attain the capability of realization at each and every basis.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: 'May I know beings according to their kamma, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human'—he can attain the capability of realization at each and every basis.
translations.an5.28:7: Thus, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, wherever he directs his mind toward the realization of any knowledge, he can attain the capability of realization at each and every basis.
translations.an5.28:8: Just as, monks, a water jug placed on a stand, full to the brim, could be drawn from by a strong man from any side, and water would come forth—"'Yes, sir.'"—"So too, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, wherever he directs his mind toward the realization of any knowledge, he can attain the capability of realization at each and every basis."
translations.an5.28:9: Just as, monks, a pond with level banks, full to the brim, could have its water drawn from any side by a strong man if the bank were opened, and water would come forth—"'Yes, sir.'"—"So too, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, wherever he directs his mind toward the realization of any knowledge, he can attain the capability of realization at each and every basis."
translations.an5.2:1: "These five, monks, are the powers of a learner. What five? The power of faith, the power of conscience, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, the power of wisdom."
translations.an5.2:2: And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple is faithful; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.' This is called, monks, the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, monks, is the power of conscience? Here, monks, a noble disciple has conscience; he feels shame at bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, and feels shame at the acquisition of evil, unwholesome qualities. This is called, monks, the power of conscience.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, monks, is the power of moral dread? Here, monks, a noble disciple has moral dread; he fears bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, and fears the acquisition of evil, unwholesome qualities. This is called, monks, the power of moral dread.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the acquisition of wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in effort, not shirking his responsibility regarding wholesome qualities. This is called, monks, the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise, endowed with wisdom leading to arising and passing away, noble, penetrating, leading rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called, monks, the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of a learner.
translations.an5.30:1: Thus have I heard — on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large community of monks, and arrived at a Brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala. There the Blessed One stayed in the Icchānaṅgala woodland. Then the Brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: 'Indeed, the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan, who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala; he is staying in the Icchānaṅgala woodland. The good repute of Master Gotama has spread thus: “He is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, the Fortunate One, knower of the world, the unsurpassed trainer of persons, the teacher of gods and humans, the Awakened One, the Blessed One.” He makes known this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmas, this generation with its ascetics and Brahmins, its gods and humans, having realized it by his own direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. It is indeed good to see such Arahants.”' Then the Brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala, after night had passed, took abundant solid and soft food and went to the Icchānaṅgala woodland; arriving there, they stood outside the gatehouse making a loud and great noise.
translations.an5.30:3: "Please, sir, let the Blessed One accept; let the Sugata accept. Now is the time for the Blessed One to accept. Wherever now the Blessed One will go, the Brahmins and householders, both villagers and townsmen, will follow in that direction. Just as, sir, when heavy rain falls from the sky, the waters flow down along their course; so too, sir, wherever now the Blessed One will go, the Brahmins and householders, both villagers and townsmen, will follow in that direction. Why is that? Because of the Blessed One's virtue and wisdom."
translations.an5.31:1: On one occasion ... at the Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, went to the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Princess Sumanā said to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: Just so, one endowed with virtue, a faithful man; In the world, all the stingy ones are outshone by generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud, thundering, lightning flashing, Fills lowlands and plains, drenching the earth;
translations.an5.31:12: So the disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with vision, Surpasses stinginess in five ways, the wise one.
translations.an5.31:2: "Suppose, sir, two disciples of the Blessed One with equal faith, equal virtue, equal wisdom—one is a giver, the other not a giver. After the breakup of the body, after death, both are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world. But, sir, would there be a distinction, a difference between them as devas?"
translations.an5.31:3: "There would be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said: "The one who is a giver, being reborn as a deva, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: with divine life span, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine sovereignty. The one who is a giver, being reborn as a deva, surpasses the non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:4: "But if, sir, they pass away from there and come to human existence, would there be, sir, a distinction, a difference between them as humans?" "There would be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said: "The one who is a giver, being reborn as a human, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: with human life span, human beauty, human happiness, human fame, and human sovereignty. The one who is a giver, being reborn as a human, surpasses the non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:5: "But if, sir, both go forth from the household life into homelessness, would there be, sir, a distinction, a difference between them as renunciants?" "There would be, Sumanā," the Blessed One said: "The one who is a giver, being a renunciant, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: he obtains abundant robes when asked, but little when not asked; he obtains abundant almsfood when asked, but little when not asked; he obtains abundant lodging when asked, but little when not asked; he obtains abundant medicines and requisites for the sick when asked, but little when not asked. And those fellow monastics with whom he dwells conduct themselves toward him mostly with pleasant bodily actions, rarely with unpleasant; mostly with pleasant verbal actions, rarely with unpleasant; mostly with pleasant mental actions, rarely with unpleasant; and they mostly offer him pleasant gifts, rarely unpleasant. The one who is a giver, being a renunciant, surpasses the non-giver in these five respects."
translations.an5.31:6: "But if, sir, both attain arahantship, would there be, sir, a distinction, a difference between them as arahants?" "Here, Sumanā, I declare no difference whatsoever, that is, in liberation by liberation."
translations.an5.31:9: Just as the pure moon, Moving through the realm of space, Outshines all the host of stars In radiance;
translations.an5.34:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then General Sīha went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, General Sīha said to the Blessed One: "Can the Blessed One, sir, point out a visible fruit of giving?"
translations.an5.34:2: "It is possible, Sīha," the Blessed One said: "The giver, the donor, is dear and agreeable to many people. That the giver, the donor, is dear and agreeable to many people—this too is a visible fruit of giving.
translations.an5.34:8: The giver is loved, many honor him; He gains fame and his glory increases; Unashamed, he moves among assemblies; The generous, un-stingy man is confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore the wise give gifts, Having abandoned the stain of stinginess, happy; They remain established for a long time in the heavens, Sharing companionship with the gods, they delight.
translations.an5.36:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these five timely gifts. What are the five? Giving a gift to a visitor; giving a gift to one who is departing; giving a gift to the sick; giving a gift in times of famine; and placing newly harvested grains and fresh fruits first into the hands of the virtuous. These, bhikkhus, are the five timely gifts.”
translations.an5.36:2: The wise, understanding and free from stinginess, give at the right time, to noble ones who are upright and pure.
translations.an5.36:3: Their mind becomes serene, and the gift becomes abundant. Those who rejoice in it or assist in the act, do not lack merit; they too become sharers in the merit.
translations.an5.37:1: “Bhikkhus, when giving food, the donor gives the recipients five things. What are the five? He gives life, beauty, happiness, strength, and wisdom. By giving life, he becomes a sharer in life, whether divine or human; by giving beauty, he becomes a sharer in beauty, whether divine or human; by giving happiness, he becomes a sharer in happiness, whether divine or human; by giving strength, he becomes a sharer in strength, whether divine or human; by giving wisdom, he becomes a sharer in wisdom, whether divine or human. Bhikkhus, when giving food, the donor gives the recipients these five things.”
translations.an5.37:2: He who gives life gives strength, beauty, and wisdom; the wise giver of happiness himself attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Just as, bhikkhus, a great banyan tree standing at a crossroads on good soil becomes a shelter for birds all around, so too, bhikkhus, a faithful householder becomes a refuge for many—bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male and female lay followers.
translations.an5.38:3: Covered with branches, leaves, and fruits, tall like a great tree, rooted firmly, it stands as a support for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: Birds delight in its pleasant dwelling, seeking its shade and fruit; they go for shade where shade is needed, and for fruit, they become fruit-eaters.
translations.an5.38:5: In the same way, a virtuous, faithful person, firm in conduct, intent on what is beneficial, steady, unwavering, gentle.
translations.an5.38:6: Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, without taints; such a person is a field of merit for the world, and beings seek one such as him.
translations.an5.41:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Anāthapiṇḍika the householder: “Householder, there are these five legitimate uses of wealth. What are the five? Here, householder, a noble disciple enjoys wealth acquired by energetic effort, gathered by strength of arm, earned by the sweat of one’s brow, rightly acquired. He makes himself happy and satisfied, and shares it with others, using wealth rightly to bring happiness. He makes his mother and father happy and satisfied, rightly providing them with happiness. He makes his children, wife, servants, and workers happy and satisfied, rightly providing them with happiness. This is the first legitimate use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, having acquired wealth by energetic effort, gathered by strength of arm, earned by the sweat of one’s brow, rightly acquired, performs the fivefold offering: the offering to relatives, the offering to guests, the offering to ancestors, the offering to rulers, and the offering to deities. This is the fourth legitimate use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, having acquired wealth by energetic effort, gathered by strength of arm, earned by the sweat of one’s brow, rightly acquired, makes offerings to those ascetics and brahmins who abstain from intoxication and heedlessness, who are patient and gentle, who dwell in tranquility, who subdue themselves, calm themselves, and lead themselves to final Nibbāna. He establishes offerings to such ascetics and brahmins—elevated, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, ripening in heaven. This is the fifth legitimate use of wealth. These, householder, are the five legitimate uses of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: Now, householder, if a noble disciple, while using these five legitimate uses of wealth, sees his wealth decrease, he reflects thus: ‘The legitimate uses of wealth that I have used—those have been used, and my wealth has decreased.’ He feels no remorse. But if, while using these five legitimate uses of wealth, his wealth increases, he reflects thus: ‘The legitimate uses of wealth that I have used—those have been used, and my wealth has increased.’ He feels no remorse in either case.
translations.an5.41:7: My wealth has been enjoyed, my debts have been paid, hardships have been overcome; elevated offerings have been given, and the fivefold offering has been performed; virtuous ones have been supported, those who are restrained and live the holy life.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever purpose wealth was needed for, the wise householder desired; that purpose has been fulfilled for me—what was done brings no regret.
translations.an5.43:1: Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.43:4: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple to wish for life, to pray for life, to delight in life, or to seek life as a goal. Rather, householder, a noble disciple who wishes for life should practice the path that leads to life. When one practices the path leading to life, it results in the attainment of life. Thus he becomes a sharer in life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple to wish for beauty, to pray for beauty, to delight in beauty, or to seek beauty as a goal. Rather, householder, a noble disciple who wishes for beauty should practice the path that leads to beauty. When one practices the path leading to beauty, it results in the attainment of beauty. Thus he becomes a sharer in beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: It is not fitting, householder, for a noble disciple to wish for happiness, to pray for happiness, to delight in happiness, or to seek happiness as a goal. Rather, householder, a noble disciple who wishes for happiness should practice the path that leads to happiness. When one practices the path leading to happiness, it results in the attainment of happiness. Thus he becomes a sharer in happiness, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:7: No, householder, a noble disciple who is an arahant does not desire fame, nor does he delight in seeking fame or in fame itself. A noble disciple who desires fame should follow a path conducive to fame. When one follows such a path conducive to fame, attainment of fame comes about. He gains divine or human fame.
translations.an5.43:9: Life, beauty, fame, and renown, heaven, high birth; successive rebirths desired by one who yearns, abundant and ever-renewed.
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallikā had passed away. Then a certain man approached King Pasenadi of Kosala and reported to him: 'Queen Mallikā, sire, has passed away.' When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala, sorrowful and dejected, with drooping shoulders, downcast, silent, sat with no response.
translations.an5.51:3: Indeed, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstacles that overwhelm the mind and weaken wisdom, cannot know his own good, the good of others, or the good of both, nor can he realize the supreme human state, the noble knowledge and vision of distinction. Just as, bhikkhus, a mountain stream that travels far, swift-flowing and carrying away debris, if a person were to open its banks on both sides, then that middle current of the river would be scattered, blocked, and disrupted—neither far-reaching, swift, nor carrying away debris—so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstacles that overwhelm the mind and weaken wisdom, cannot know his own good, the good of others, or the good of both, nor can he realize the supreme human state, the noble knowledge and vision of distinction.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain bhikkhu approached his own preceptor and said to him: 'Sir, now my body feels soft and pleasant, the directions do not appear to me, the Dhammas do not become clear, my mind is overcome by dullness and drowsiness, I practice the holy life without joy, and I have doubt regarding the Dhammas.'
translations.an5.56:3: 'It is just so, bhikkhu, when one dwells with faculties unguarded, without moderation in eating, not devoted to wakefulness, not contemplating wholesome qualities, and not persistently practicing the development of the factors of enlightenment both in the early and late parts of the night: then the body feels soft and pleasant, the directions do not appear, Dhammas do not become clear, the mind is overcome by dullness and drowsiness, one practices the holy life without joy, and doubt arises regarding the Dhammas. Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train thus: 'I will be one with guarded faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, one who contemplates wholesome qualities, and persistently devoted to developing the factors of enlightenment both in the early and late parts of the night.' This is how you should train.'
translations.an5.56:4: Then that bhikkhu, having been advised by the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed. Then that bhikkhu, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—having realized for himself with direct knowledge, even in this very life—the supreme goal of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, attained and abided in it. He knew: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state.' And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: 'It is not only for me that separation and loss from all dear and pleasing things occurs, but for as far as beings go in birth, passing away, death, and rebirth, all beings experience separation and loss from dear and pleasing things.' When he frequently reflects on this, the path arises in him. He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path. As he cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path, all fetters are completely abandoned, and underlying tendencies are eradicated.
translations.an5.57:11: 'It is not only I who am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, have my actions as my refuge; whatever action I do, good or bad, of that I will be the heir. But for as far as beings go in birth, passing away, death, and rebirth, all beings are owners of their actions, heirs to their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, have their actions as their refuge; whatever actions they do, good or bad, of that they will be the heirs.' When he frequently reflects on this, the path arises in him. He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path. As he cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path, all fetters are completely abandoned, and underlying tendencies are eradicated.
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all intoxication, I have seen renunciation as safe; for this I had the effort, contemplating Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple reflects thus: 'It is not only I who am subject to aging, not beyond aging; but for as far as beings go in birth, passing away, death, and rebirth, all beings are subject to aging, not beyond aging.' When he frequently reflects on this, the path arises in him. He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path. As he cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path, all fetters are completely abandoned, and underlying tendencies are eradicated.
translations.an5.57:8: 'It is not only I who am subject to illness, not beyond illness; but for as far as beings go in birth, passing away, death, and rebirth, all beings are subject to illness, not beyond illness.' When he frequently reflects on this, the path arises in him. He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path. As he cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that path, all fetters are completely abandoned, and underlying tendencies are eradicated.
translations.an8.13:1: “Bhikkhus, a fine royal warhorse endowed with eight qualities is worthy of a king, fit for a king, reckoned as a royal asset. What are the eight? Here, bhikkhus, a fine royal warhorse is well-born on both sides—by mother and by father. He is born in a direction where other fine royal warhorses are born. Whatever food is given to him—wet or dry—he consumes it carefully, without scattering it. He is disgusted with defecating or urinating, or lying down or rolling over. He is gentle in going, and does not agitate other horses. Whatever feigned moves, tricks, dodges, or tricks he has, he reveals them exactly as they are to the charioteer. His charioteer makes an effort to overcome them. He is willing to go: ‘Let other horses pull or not, I will pull here,’ he generates the thought. And when going, he goes straight along the path. He is steadfast, determined to endure even to the end of life and death. Bhikkhus, a fine royal warhorse endowed with these eight qualities is worthy of a king, fit for a king, reckoned as a royal asset.”
translations.an8.14:1: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you eight horse-characteristics and eight horse-defects, eight person-characteristics and eight person-defects. Listen to this, attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.14:2: “And what, bhikkhus, are the eight horse-characteristics and eight horse-defects? Here, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, moves backward, turning the chariot around from behind. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the first horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:3: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, leaps backward, kicks, breaks the yoke. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the second horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:4: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, lifts the sharp point from the pole and only tramples the pole itself. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the third horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:5: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, takes the wrong path, making the chariot unsteady. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:6: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, leaps forward, taking hold with its front body, with its front feet. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:7: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, disregarding the charioteer, disregarding the goad and whip, biting through the bit, goes wherever it wishes. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:8: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, neither advances nor retreats, but stands rooted in place like a post. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:9: Again, bhikkhus, a certain horse, when told ‘Go forward!’, struck and urged by the charioteer, draws in its front feet and draws in its hind feet, and right there sits down on all four feet. Such too, bhikkhus, is a certain horse. This, bhikkhus, is the eighth horse-defect. These, bhikkhus, are the eight horse-characteristics and eight horse-defects.
translations.an8.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Veranja, at the foot of the Nālā-creeper. Then Pahārāda, the lord of the asuras, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One said to Pahārāda, the lord of the asuras:
translations.an8.22:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians at Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, remember Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma as endowed with eight wonderful and amazing qualities.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: But if, venerable sir, I were to pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare of me: ‘There is no fetter by which Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma would return to this world.’ This, venerable sir, is the eighth wonderful and amazing quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These, venerable sir, are the eight wonderful and amazing qualities found in me. Yet I do not know: ‘By which eight wonderful and amazing qualities was I declared so by the Blessed One?’
translations.an8.22:12: Then that bhikkhu, having taken almsfood at the residence of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after the meal, returning from his almsround, that bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:4: So I, sir, with a confident heart, attended on the Blessed One. The Blessed One gradually gave me a talk, just as follows—on giving, on virtue, on heaven; on the drawbacks, degradation, and corruption in sensual pleasures, and on the benefit in renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready—malleable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident—then he revealed to me the teaching specific to Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean, uncolored cloth would properly take dye, so right there on that seat, my mind was freed from impurities and became stainless—the Dhamma eye arose: ‘Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.’ So I, sir, being one who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, mastered the Dhamma, free from doubts, rid of uncertainty, possessing confidence, independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction—right there I went for refuge to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, and undertook the five training rules for lay followers. This, sir, is the second wonderful and amazing quality present in me.
translations.an8.23:1: On one occasion the Buddha was staying in Āḷavi at the Aggāḷava shrine. There the Buddha addressed the monks: 'Monks, remember Hatthaka Āḷavaka as endowed with seven wonderful and amazing qualities. What are the seven? For Hatthaka Āḷavaka is faithful, monks; virtuous, monks; conscientious, monks; fearful of wrongdoing, monks; learned, monks; generous, monks; wise, monks. These are the seven wonderful and amazing qualities with which Hatthaka Āḷavaka is endowed; remember him thus.' Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.22:3: 'I don’t know, sir, which eight wonderful and amazing qualities the Blessed One has declared in me. But, sir, I do have eight wonderful and amazing qualities; listen and pay close attention; I will speak.' 'Very well, householder,' the monk then replied to Uggasena the householder of Hatthigāma. Then Uggasena the householder of Hatthigāma said: 'When, sir, I was attending on the Blessed One at Nāgavana and first saw him from afar, immediately upon seeing the Blessed One, my mind became confident and my intoxication was abandoned. This, sir, is the first wonderful and amazing quality present in me.'
translations.an8.22:6: Indeed, sir, there is wealth in my family. Yet this wealth is not distributed unequally among those who are virtuous and of good conduct. This, sir, is the fourth wonderful and amazing quality present in me.
translations.an8.22:8: Moreover, sir, when the Sangha is invited, deities come to me and report: ‘Householder, this bhikkhu is liberated in both ways, this bhikkhu is liberated by wisdom, this bhikkhu is a body-witness, this bhikkhu is one attained to view, this bhikkhu is liberated by faith, this bhikkhu is a follower of the Dhamma, this bhikkhu is a follower of faith, this bhikkhu is virtuous and of good conduct, this bhikkhu is immoral and of bad conduct.’ Yet, sir, when I attend on the Sangha, I do not generate a mind such as: ‘I will give little to this one, much to that one.’ Rather, sir, I give equally to all. This, sir, is the sixth wonderful and amazing quality present in me.
translations.an8.22:7: Moreover, sir, whomever bhikkhu I attend on, I attend on him carefully, not carelessly. If that venerable one teaches me Dhamma, I listen carefully, not carelessly. If that venerable one does not teach me Dhamma, I teach him Dhamma. This, sir, is the fifth wonderful and amazing quality present in me.
translations.an8.22:9: Moreover, sir, deities come to me and say: ‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed, householder, by the Blessed One.’ When this is said, I say to those deities: ‘Whether you say so, devas, or whether you do not say so, still the Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.’ Yet, sir, I do not recognize that from this cause my mind advances: ‘Those deities come to me, or I converse with deities.’ This, sir, is the seventh wonderful and amazing quality present in me.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and went to the residence of Uggasena the householder of Hatthigāma; having gone, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then Uggasena the householder of Hatthigāma went to that monk; having approached, he paid homage to the monk and sat down to one side. The monk then said to Uggasena the householder of Hatthigāma, seated to one side: 'Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight wonderful and amazing qualities.
