What, householder, are the eight wonderful and amazing qualities with which you are endowed, as declared by the Blessed One?'
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and went to the residence of Hatthaka Āḷavaka; having gone, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then Hatthaka Āḷavaka went to that monk; having approached, he paid homage to the monk and sat down to one side. The monk then said to Hatthaka Āḷavaka, seated to one side:
translations.an8.22:5: I had four maiden wives, sir. Then I went to them and said: ‘Sisters, I have undertaken the five training rules for lay followers. Whoever wishes may enjoy the wealth and make merit here, or go to her own family. But if someone desires a husband, to whom shall I give her?’ When this was said, the eldest wife said to me: ‘Give me to so-and-so, good sir.’ Then, sir, I summoned that man, took the wife by the left hand, took the firebrand by the right hand, and handed her over to that man. Yet, sir, while giving up a wife, I did not recognize any change in my mind. This, sir, is the third wonderful and amazing quality present in me.
translations.an8.2:11: Having heard the Dhamma from this venerable one, he fully comprehends it in two ways—through bodily realization and through mental realization. Indeed, this venerable one knows and sees.' This quality too leads to intimacy, respect, development, harmony, and unification.
translations.an8.2:15: This venerable one, having gone to the Saṅgha, does not engage in irrelevant talk or gossip. He speaks Dhamma himself, encourages others, or maintains noble silence without despising it. Indeed, this venerable one knows and sees.' This quality too leads to intimacy, respect, development, harmony, and unification.
translations.an8.23:3: 'Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to possess seven wonderful and extraordinary qualities. What seven? “He is faithful, bhikkhus; virtuous …; conscientious …; fearful of wrongdoing …; learned …; generous …; wise, bhikkhus, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī.” Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to possess these seven wonderful and extraordinary qualities.' 'Venerable sir, was there no householder there wearing white robes?' 'No, friend, there was no householder there wearing white robes.' 'Good, sir, that there was no householder there wearing white robes.'
translations.an8.23:4: Then that bhikkhu, having obtained almsfood at Hatthaka’s residence in Āḷavi, rose from his seat and departed. Later, after the meal, returning from his almsround, he went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated there, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and well cultivated. Whatever, sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness being developed and well cultivated, this too, sir, is the strength of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by relying on which the taint-free bhikkhu declares: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’
translations.an8.2:1: ‘Bhikkhus, these eight factors, eight conditions, lead to the attainment, growth, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells dependent on the Teacher or on some other respected spiritual companion, in whom keen shame and fear of wrongdoing, as well as affection and respect, are established. This, bhikkhus, is the first factor, the first condition, that leads to the attainment, growth, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life.
translations.an8.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavi, at the Aggāḷava shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavi, accompanied by five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Hatthaka of Āḷavi, seated there: ‘Great indeed, Hatthaka, is this assembly. But how, Hatthaka, do you hold together this large assembly?’ ‘Venerable sir, I hold together this great assembly by means of the four ways of embracing that were taught by the Blessed One. When I know: “This one should be embraced by generosity,” I embrace him with generosity; when I know: “This one should be embraced by kindly speech,” I embrace him with kindly speech; when I know: “This one should be embraced by beneficial conduct,” I embrace him with beneficial conduct; when I know: “This one should be embraced by impartiality,” I embrace him with impartiality. But, venerable sir, I do have wealth in my family. The poor are not considered worthy of being heard.’ ‘Well said, well said, Hatthaka. Indeed, Hatthaka, this is the proper way to hold together a great assembly. For all those in the past who held together a great assembly, they all did so by means of these four ways of embracing. And all those in the future who will hold together a great assembly, they all will do so by means of these four ways of embracing. And all those in the present who hold together a great assembly, they all do so by means of these four ways of embracing.’
translations.an8.26:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated there, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, to what extent is a lay follower considered a lay follower?’ ‘Jīvaka, when a lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent is he considered a lay follower.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four bases of spiritual power are developed and well cultivated … the five faculties are developed and well cultivated … the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and well cultivated … the noble eightfold path is developed and well cultivated. Whatever, sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the noble eightfold path being developed and well cultivated, this too, sir, is the strength of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by relying on which the taint-free bhikkhu declares: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’
translations.an8.26:2: ‘To what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower considered virtuous?’ ‘Jīvaka, when a lay follower abstains from killing living beings … abstains from taking what is not given … abstains from sexual misconduct … abstains from false speech … abstains from intoxicants that cause heedlessness, to that extent is a lay follower considered virtuous.’
translations.an8.26:3: ‘To what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower practicing for his own welfare, not for the welfare of others?’ ‘Jīvaka, when a lay follower himself is endowed with faith, but does not encourage others to attain faith … himself is virtuous, but does not encourage others to attain virtue … himself is generous, but does not encourage others to be generous … himself, with knowledge, understands the Dhamma and practices in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not encourage others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma— to that extent, Jīvaka, is a lay follower practicing for his own welfare, not for the welfare of others.’
translations.an8.2:2: Living relying on that teacher, he from time to time approaches a certain respected fellow practitioner in whom he has strong moral shame and fear, as well as affection and reverence, and he questions and interrogates him: 'Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones clarify what is unclear, reveal what is concealed, and remove his doubts regarding various doubtful and problematic matters. This, bhikkhus, is the second reason, the second condition, whereby the noble wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, not yet obtained, is obtained; and that which is obtained grows, expands, is developed, and brought to fulfillment.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous, living restrained by the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger even in minor faults, and undertaking the training rules, he trains in them. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth reason, the fourth condition, whereby the noble wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, not yet obtained, is obtained; and that which is obtained grows, expands, is developed, and brought to fulfillment.
translations.an8.2:5: He is learned, retaining what he has heard, accumulating what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has learned in abundance, stored in his memory, recited verbally, mentally examined, and clearly comprehended with right view. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth reason, the fifth condition, whereby the noble wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, not yet obtained, is obtained; and that which is obtained grows, expands, is developed, and brought to fulfillment.
translations.an8.2:6: He dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and acquiring wholesome qualities; steadfast, strong in effort, not neglecting the duty regarding wholesome states. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth reason, the sixth condition, whereby the noble wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, not yet obtained, is obtained; and that which is obtained grows, expands, is developed, and brought to fulfillment.
translations.an8.2:7: When in the Sangha, he does not engage in irrelevant talk or idle chatter. He either speaks Dhamma himself, urges others on, or does not disdain noble silence. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh reason, the seventh condition, whereby the noble wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, not yet obtained, is obtained; and that which is obtained grows, expands, is developed, and brought to fulfillment.
translations.an8.2:8: He dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: 'Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception... such are mental formations... such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.' This, bhikkhus, is the eighth reason, the eighth condition, whereby the noble wisdom pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, not yet obtained, is obtained; and that which is obtained grows, expands, is developed, and brought to fulfillment.
translations.an8.2:9: His fellow practitioners honor him thus: 'This venerable one indeed lives relying on the Teacher or on a certain respected fellow practitioner, in whom he has strong moral shame and fear, as well as affection and reverence. Surely this venerable one knows and sees.' This quality too contributes to affection, respect, development, harmony, and unification.
translations.an8.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṁsumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Cetis at the Eastern Banyan Grove. Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was living in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: 'This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires; this Dhamma is for one content, not for one discontent; this Dhamma is for one secluded, not for one fond of company; this Dhamma is for one ardent, not for one lazy; this Dhamma is for one established in mindfulness, not for one unmindful; this Dhamma is for one concentrated, not for one unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for the wise, not for the foolish.'
translations.an8.30:10: When, Anuruddha, you reflect on these eight noble thoughts and attain easily, effortlessly, and without difficulty the acquisition of these four jhānas, which are sublime states of mind and pleasant abidings in the present life, then, Anuruddha, your dwelling at the root of a tree will be as delightful for you, while living content, joyful, untroubled, at ease, and progressing towards Nibbāna, as a householder’s or householder’s son’s roofed and plastered mansion, windproof, with secure gables, and closed windows.
translations.an8.30:11: When, Anuruddha, you reflect on these eight noble thoughts and attain easily, effortlessly, and without difficulty the acquisition of these four jhānas, which are sublime states of mind and pleasant abidings in the present life, then, Anuruddha, your bed of straw spread under a tree will be as delightful for you, while living content, joyful, untroubled, at ease, and progressing towards Nibbāna, as a householder’s or householder’s son’s couch, stuffed with cotton, spread with fine cloth, covered with a canopy, and having red bolsters at both ends.
translations.an8.30:12: When, Anuruddha, you reflect on these eight noble thoughts and attain easily, effortlessly, and without difficulty the acquisition of these four jhānas, which are sublime states of mind and pleasant abidings in the present life, then, Anuruddha, your medicine of putrid urine will be as delightful for you, while living content, joyful, untroubled, at ease, and progressing towards Nibbāna, as various delicacies for a householder or householder’s son—such as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and syrup. Therefore, Anuruddha, spend the rainy season retreat right here among the Cetis, at the Eastern Banyan Grove.' 'Yes, sir,' replied the Venerable Anuruddha to the Blessed One.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Anuruddha with this exhortation, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, disappeared from the Cetiya region of the western slope and reappeared in the deer park at Bhesakaḷāvana in the Bhaggas on the Susumāragiri. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Seated, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, I will teach you the eight thoughts of a great man; listen to that... And what, monks, are the eight thoughts of a great man? This, monks, is the quality of one of few wishes, not of one of many wishes; this, monks, is the quality of one content, not of one discontent; this, monks, is the quality of one fond of seclusion, not of one fond of company; this, monks, is the quality of one with aroused energy, not of one lazy; this, monks, is the quality of one with established mindfulness, not of one unmindful; this, monks, is the quality of one concentrated, not of one unconcentrated; this, monks, is the quality of one wise, not of one foolish; this, monks, is the quality of one who delights in non-proliferation, who enjoys non-proliferation, not of one who delights in proliferation, who enjoys proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, disappeared from the Bhaggas on the Susumāragiri in the deer park at Bhesakaḷāvana and reappeared in the Cetiya region of the western slope directly in front of the Venerable Anuruddha. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The Venerable Anuruddha paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Anuruddha, who was seated to one side:
translations.an8.30:22: Then the Venerable Anuruddha spent the next rainy season right there in the Cetiya region of the western slope. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, quickly realized—by himself, directly attaining and abiding in—the supreme goal of the holy life for which sons of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state'—he understood. And indeed, the Venerable Anuruddha became one of the arahants. Then the arahant Venerable Anuruddha, at that very moment, spoke these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: 'Knowing my thought, the unsurpassed Teacher in the world came to me with a mind-made body by means of psychic power.'
translations.an8.30:24: 'As I had the thought, so did he teach further; the Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:3: 'Well done, well done, Anuruddha! Indeed, you have rightly considered the thought of a great man: "This is the quality of one of few wishes, not of one of many wishes; this is the quality of one content, not of one discontent; this is the quality of one fond of seclusion, not of one fond of company; this is the quality of one with aroused energy, not of one lazy; this is the quality of one with established mindfulness, not of one unmindful; this is the quality of one concentrated, not of one unconcentrated; this is the quality of one wise, not of one foolish." Therefore, Anuruddha, now consider this eighth thought of a great man: "This is the quality of one who delights in non-proliferation, who enjoys non-proliferation, not of one who delights in proliferation, who enjoys proliferation."'
translations.an8.30:4: 'When, Anuruddha, you consider these eight thoughts of a great man, then you will dwell, as long as you wish, having attained the first jhāna—secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, with thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure.'
translations.an8.30:5: 'When, Anuruddha, you consider these eight thoughts of a great man, then you will dwell, as long as you wish, having attained the second jhāna—without thought and examination, with internal tranquility and unification of mind, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure.'
translations.an8.30:6: 'When, Anuruddha, you consider these eight thoughts of a great man, then you will dwell, as long as you wish, having abandoned rapture, equanimous, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing pleasure with the body, having attained the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: "One who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily."'
translations.an8.30:7: 'When, Anuruddha, you consider these eight thoughts of a great man, then you will dwell, as long as you wish, having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, having attained the fourth jhāna—neither-painful-nor-pleasant, with purity of mindfulness and equanimity.'
translations.an8.39:1: 'These eight, monks, are accumulations of merit, accumulations of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven. What eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple goes for refuge to the Buddha. This, monks, is the first accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillfulness, conducive to happiness, leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is desirable, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.'
translations.an8.39:2: 'Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple goes for refuge to the Dhamma. This, monks, is the second accumulation of merit... which leads to what is desirable, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.'
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, the noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Sangha. This, bhikkhus, is the third accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillful qualities, a source of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven. These five, bhikkhus, are great gifts, foremost, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not to be adulterated, unblamable by wise ascetics and brahmins. What are the five? Here, bhikkhus, the noble disciple, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life. The noble disciple, bhikkhus, who abstains from the destruction of life, gives fearlessness, non-hostility, and harmlessness to immeasurable beings. Having given fearlessness, non-hostility, and harmlessness to immeasurable beings, he becomes a sharer in immeasurable fearlessness, non-hostility, and harmlessness. This, bhikkhus, is the first great gift, foremost, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not to be adulterated, unblamable by wise ascetics and brahmins. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillful qualities, a source of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven.
translations.an8.39:7: Having abandoned intoxicating drinks and drugs that lead to carelessness, he abstains from intoxicating drinks and drugs that lead to carelessness. The noble disciple, bhikkhus, who abstains from intoxicating drinks and drugs that lead to carelessness, gives fearlessness, non-hostility, and harmlessness to immeasurable beings. Having given fearlessness, non-hostility, and harmlessness to immeasurable beings, he becomes a sharer in immeasurable fearlessness, non-hostility, and harmlessness. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth great gift, foremost, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not to be adulterated, unblamable by wise ascetics and brahmins. This, bhikkhus, is the eighth accumulation of merit, accumulation of skillful qualities, a source of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven.
translations.an8.40:1: Killing living beings, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of killing living beings, in the case of one reborn as a human, is shortness of life.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of taking what is not given, in the case of one reborn as a human, is loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of sexual misconduct, in the case of one reborn as a human, is rivalry and hostility.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of false speech, in the case of one reborn as a human, is being subject to false accusations.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of divisive speech, in the case of one reborn as a human, is the breaking of friendships.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of harsh speech, in the case of one reborn as a human, is unpleasing sounds.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the domain of hungry ghosts. The full result of idle chatter, in the case of one reborn as a human, is speech not being trusted.
translations.an8.6:2: For the unlearned ordinary person, bhikkhus, gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain arise. For the learned noble disciple, bhikkhus, gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain also arise. What then, bhikkhus, is the distinction, the difference, the distinction in function between the learned noble disciple and the unlearned ordinary person?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
translations.an8.6:4: With gain, his mind remains preoccupied; with loss, his mind remains preoccupied; with fame, his mind remains preoccupied; with disgrace, his mind remains preoccupied; with blame, his mind remains preoccupied; with praise, his mind remains preoccupied; with pleasure, his mind remains preoccupied; with pain, his mind remains preoccupied. He delights in arisen gain, resists loss; delights in arisen fame, resists disgrace; delights in arisen praise, resists blame; delights in arisen pleasure, resists pain. Being thus bound by delight and resistance, he is not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say he is not liberated from suffering.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain; these are impermanent conditions among humans, unstable, subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Having understood these, the mindful wise person observes the nature of change; desirable conditions do not disturb his mind, nor does he react with aversion to undesirable ones.
translations.mn108:2: At that time King Ajātasattu, the son of Vedehiputta, was fortifying Rājagaha, fearing the danger from King Pajjota.
translations.an8.7:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling on the Vulture's Peak in Rājagaha, shortly after Devadatta had departed. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta: 'It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to reflect from time to time on his own failings. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to reflect from time to time on the failings of others. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to reflect from time to time on his own attainments. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to reflect from time to time on the attainments of others. Overcome and overwhelmed in mind by eight bad qualities, Devadatta has become bound for perdition, for hell, for a long time, irredeemable.'
translations.an8.7:2: By which eight? Overcome and overwhelmed in mind by gain, bhikkhus, Devadatta has become bound for perdition, for hell, for a long time, irredeemable. By loss, bhikkhus... by fame, bhikkhus... by lack of fame, bhikkhus... by honor, bhikkhus... by lack of honor, bhikkhus... by bad desire, bhikkhus... by bad friendship, bhikkhus, overcome and overwhelmed in mind, Devadatta has become bound for perdition, for hell, for a long time, irredeemable. By these eight bad qualities, bhikkhus, overcome and overwhelmed in mind, Devadatta has become bound for perdition, for hell, for a long time, irredeemable.
translations.mn108:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion Venerable Ānanda was dwelling in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel's Feeding Place, shortly after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
translations.mn108:15: He is learned, a repository of what has been heard, one who accumulates what has been heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned in abundance, retained in memory, examined with the mind, and clearly seen with wisdom.
translations.mn108:18: He experiences various kinds of supernormal powers: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains, as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking, as though on dry land; he travels through the air cross-legged, like a bird on wing; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; and he exercises mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā world.
translations.an8.8:7: "It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous! How well said indeed by the Venerable Uttara: 'Whatever is well spoken, all that is the speech of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. From that, taking and taking, we also speak.' On one occasion, venerable sir Uttara, the Blessed One was dwelling on the Vulture's Peak in Rājagaha, shortly after Devadatta had departed. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta:
translations.mn108:13: "There are, brahmin, ten inspiring qualities declared by the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who knows and sees. Wherever these qualities are found, we now honor, revere, esteem, and venerate that place; honoring, revering, and esteeming it, we dwell dependent upon it. What are the ten?
translations.mn108:19: With the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, he hears both kinds of sounds: divine and human, those that are far as well as near.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, the ruler of the devas, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, disappeared from among the Tāvatiṁsa devas and appeared before Venerable Uttara in the hermitage on Mount Mahisavatthu in the Sankheyya forest. Then Sakka, the ruler of the devas, approached Venerable Uttara; having approached, he paid homage to him and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, the ruler of the devas, said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.7:3: It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen gain, having repeatedly overcome arisen loss, having repeatedly overcome arisen fame, having repeatedly overcome arisen lack of fame, having repeatedly overcome arisen honor, having repeatedly overcome arisen lack of honor, having repeatedly overcome arisen bad desire, having repeatedly overcome arisen bad friendship.
translations.an8.8:6: "Suppose, Lord of Devas, not far from a village or town there were a great heap of grain. Then a large crowd of people would come to carry away the grain—using baskets, winnowing fans, cloaks, or their hands. If someone were to approach that large crowd and ask: 'Where are you carrying this grain from?', how would that large crowd rightly answer when questioned?" "They would rightly answer, 'We are carrying it from that great heap of grain,' venerable sir." "So too, Lord of Devas, whatever is well spoken, all that is the speech of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. From that, taking and taking, we also speak."
translations.mn108:17: He gains easily, without difficulty or trouble, the attainment of the four jhānas—exalted mental states providing a pleasant abiding in this very life.
translations.an8.8:5: "Is it true, venerable sir, that Venerable Uttara taught the bhikkhus thus: 'Good, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect from time to time on his own failings; good, friends, a bhikkhu should reflect from time to time on the failings of others; on his own attainments; on the attainments of others'?" "Yes, Lord of Devas." "Is this Venerable Uttara's own original insight, or is it the words of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?" "Then, Lord of Devas, I will give you a simile. By means of a simile some wise men understand the meaning of what is said.
translations.mn108:14: Here, brahmin, a monk is virtuous, living restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and range of activity; seeing danger even in the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the training rules.
translations.mn108:20: They understand the minds of other beings and individuals, perceiving mind with mind. If the mind has lust, they know it as 'the mind has lust'; if the mind is free from lust, they know it as 'the mind is free from lust'; if the mind has hatred, they know it as 'the mind has hatred'; if the mind is free from hatred, they know it as 'the mind is free from hatred'; if the mind has delusion, they know it as 'the mind has delusion'; if the mind is free from delusion, they know it as 'the mind is free from delusion'; if the mind is restricted, they know it as 'the mind is restricted'; if the mind is scattered, they know it as 'the mind is scattered'; if the mind is sublime, they know it as 'the mind is sublime'; if the mind is not sublime, they know it as 'the mind is not sublime'; if the mind is superior, they know it as 'the mind is superior'; if the mind is unsurpassed, they know it as 'the mind is unsurpassed'; if the mind is concentrated, they know it as 'the mind is concentrated'; if the mind is unconcentrated, they know it as 'the mind is unconcentrated'; if the mind is liberated, they know it as 'the mind is liberated'; if the mind is unliberated, they know it as 'the mind is unliberated'.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, they dwell having realized with their own insight the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life. These, brahmin, are the ten inspiring qualities declared by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees. Wherever these qualities exist, we now honor, revere, esteem, and venerate that place; honoring and revering it, we dwell dependent upon it.
translations.mn108:25: Then the Brahmin minister Vassakāra said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Where, Master Ānanda, are you dwelling now?' 'In the Bamboo Grove, Brahmin, I am dwelling now,' replied Ānanda. 'Is the Bamboo Grove, Master Ānanda, delightful, quiet, free from noise, secluded, suitable for seclusion and for human habitation?' 'Indeed, Brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, free from noise, secluded, suitable for seclusion and for human habitation—just as it is protected by guardians like yourselves.' 'Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, free from noise, secluded, suitable for seclusion and for human habitation—just as it is suited for meditators like yourselves who are devoted to meditation. You are meditators, Master Ānanda, devoted to meditation. Once, Master Ānanda, the Blessed One was dwelling in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then I approached the Great Wood, the Hall with the Peaked Roof, where the Blessed One was. There the Blessed One spoke to me at length about meditation. The Blessed One was himself a meditator, devoted to meditation. And the Blessed One praised meditation in every way.'
translations.mn108:28: 'Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Blessed One honored meditation and praised it. Well then, Master Ānanda, we must be going; we have much to do and many duties.' 'As you think fit, Brahmin,' replied Ānanda. Then the Brahmin minister Vassakāra, having approved and agreed with the words of Venerable Ānanda, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then, in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to Venerable Ānanda: 'It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Why don't I go to the working grounds of the Brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, to see the Brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna?'
translations.mn108:4: Then Venerable Ānanda went to the working grounds of the Brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, to the Brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna. The Brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna saw Venerable Ānanda coming from afar and, on seeing him, said: 'Come, Master Ānanda. Welcome, Master Ānanda. It is a long time since Master Ānanda has taken the opportunity to come here. Please sit down, Master Ānanda; this seat is prepared.' Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. Then the Brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: 'Is there, Master Ānanda, even one bhikkhu endowed in every way with all those qualities with which the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, was endowed?' 'No, Brahmin, there is not even one bhikkhu endowed in every way with all those qualities with which the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, was endowed. For the Blessed One, Brahmin, is the originator of the path yet unarisen, the producer of the path yet unproduced, the declarer of the path yet undeclared; he is the knower of the path, the finder of the path, the expert in the path. And now his disciples dwell following the path, having become endowed with it afterwards.'
translations.mn108:7: 'Is there, Master Ānanda, even one bhikkhu appointed by the Blessed One: "After my passing, he will be your refuge," such that you now follow him?' 'No, Brahmin, there is not even one bhikkhu appointed by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one who knows and sees, saying: "After my passing, he will be your refuge," such that we now follow him.'
translations.mn108:9: 'If it is thus without a refuge, Master Ānanda, what is the reason for harmony?' 'We are not, Brahmin, without a refuge; we have a refuge, Brahmin—we have refuge in the Dhamma.'
translations.mn117:10: In this case, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as 'wrong intention,' and right intention as 'right intention'; this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong intention? Intention of sensual desire, intention of ill will, intention of cruelty—this, bhikkhus, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, bhikkhus, is right thought? Right thought, I say, bhikkhus, is twofold: there is right thought that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum; and there is right thought that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, bhikkhus, is right thought that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum? Thought of renunciation, thought of non-ill-will, thought of non-harming: this, bhikkhus, is right thought that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum.
translations.mn117:14: And what, bhikkhus, is right thought that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? That thought, thinking, intention, application, exertion, mental firmness, verbal formation of one who has noble mind, taintless mind, endowed with the noble path, developing the noble path: this, bhikkhus, is right thought that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: He makes effort for the abandoning of wrong thought and for the acquisition of right thought; his right effort comes into being. Mindfully he abandons wrong thought, mindfully he acquires right thought; his right mindfulness comes into being. Thus these three states—right view, right effort, and right mindfulness—run and circle around right thought.
translations.mn117:16: Here, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong speech as wrong speech, and right speech as right speech; that is his right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Right speech, I say, bhikkhus, is twofold: there is right speech that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum; and there is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum? Abstention from false speech, abstention from divisive speech, abstention from harsh speech, abstention from idle chatter: this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum.
translations.mn117:2: “I will teach you the noble right concentration with its supports and prerequisites. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? That revulsion, disengagement, turning away, and abstention from the four verbal misconducts in one who has noble mind, taintless mind, endowed with the noble path, developing the noble path: this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: Here, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong action as wrong action, and right action as right action; that is his right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Right action, I say, bhikkhus, is twofold: there is right action that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum; and there is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, bhikkhus, is right action that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum? Abstention from the destruction of life, abstention from taking what is not given, abstention from sexual misconduct: this, bhikkhus, is right action that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum.
translations.mn117:28: Here, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, and right livelihood as right livelihood; that is his right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood? Cheating, deceiving, fortune-telling, greed for gains with gains, seeking profit with profit: this, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Right livelihood, I say, bhikkhus, is twofold: there is right livelihood that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum; and there is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns a living by right livelihood: this, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is with taints, meritorious, ripening in the substratum.
translations.mn117:34: Here, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? With one of right view, right thought arises; with right thought, right speech arises; with right speech, right action arises; with right action, right livelihood arises; with right livelihood, right effort arises; with right effort, right mindfulness arises; with right mindfulness, right concentration arises; with right concentration, right knowledge arises; with right knowledge, right liberation arises. Thus, bhikkhus, the learner endowed with eight factors, the arahant endowed with ten factors. And even here, with right knowledge, many evil unwholesome states are completely abandoned and reach fulfillment through development.
translations.mn117:35: Here, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? With one of right view, wrong view is completely eradicated. And those many evil unwholesome states that arise dependent on wrong view are also eradicated in him. Dependent on right view, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development. With one of right thought, bhikkhus, wrong thought is completely eradicated... With one of right speech, bhikkhus, wrong speech is completely eradicated... With one of right action, bhikkhus, wrong action is completely eradicated... With one of right livelihood, bhikkhus, wrong livelihood is completely eradicated... With one of right effort, bhikkhus, wrong effort is completely eradicated... With one of right mindfulness, bhikkhus, wrong mindfulness is completely eradicated... With one of right concentration, bhikkhus, wrong concentration is completely eradicated... With one of right knowledge, bhikkhus, wrong knowledge is completely eradicated... With one of right liberation, bhikkhus, wrong liberation is completely eradicated. And those many evil unwholesome states that arise dependent on wrong liberation are also eradicated in him. Dependent on right liberation, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
translations.mn117:36: Thus, bhikkhus, twenty factors of the wholesome side, twenty factors of the unwholesome side—this great cycle of forty-four Dhamma principles has been set in motion, unexcelled in the world with its deities, Māras, Brahmas, and among humans including ascetics and brahmins, by any ascetic, brahmin, deity, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.
translations.mn117:4: Here, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong view as 'wrong view' and right view as 'right view'—that becomes one's right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong view? 'There is no result from giving, no result from sacrifice, no result from offerings; there is no fruit or result of good or bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who are well-gone, rightly practising, who having realized by their own direct knowledge proclaim this world and the next'—this, bhikkhus, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Bhikkhus, I say right view has two aspects: there is, bhikkhus, right view that is accompanied by taints, meritorious, ripening in results; and there is, bhikkhus, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is accompanied by taints, meritorious, ripening in results? 'There is result from giving, from sacrifice, from offerings; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is another world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who are well-gone, rightly practising, who having realized by their own direct knowledge proclaim this world and the next'—this, bhikkhus, is right view that is accompanied by taints, meritorious, ripening in results.
translations.mn117:8: And what, bhikkhus, is noble right view, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas, right view as a factor of the path, present in one who has noble, taintless mind, endowed with the noble path, developing the noble path—this is called, bhikkhus, noble right view, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: He exerts himself to abandon wrong view and to acquire right view; that becomes his right effort. Mindfully he abandons wrong view, mindfully he enters and remains in right view; that becomes his right mindfulness. Thus these three states follow and pursue right view, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, in the Migāramātā's Hall, together with many eminent elder bhikkhus who were accomplished with various higher knowledges—Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahākassapa, Venerable Mahākaccāyana, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, Venerable Mahākappina, Venerable Mahācunda, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, Venerable Ānanda, and with other eminent elder bhikkhus as well.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, fulfils the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfil the seven factors of enlightenment. The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfil knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, straightened his body, and established mindfulness in front of him, he is fully aware; he breathes in mindfully, he breathes out mindfully.
translations.mn118:18: When breathing in a long breath, he knows 'I breathe in a long breath'; when breathing out a long breath, he knows 'I breathe out a long breath'; when breathing in a short breath, he knows 'I breathe in a short breath'; when breathing out a short breath, he knows 'I breathe out a short breath'. He trains thus: 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out'. He trains thus: 'Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I will breathe out'.
translations.mn118:19: He trains thus: 'Experiencing rapture, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing rapture, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Tranquillizing the mental formation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Tranquillizing the mental formation, I will breathe out'.
translations.mn118:2: At that time, the elder bhikkhus were instructing and advising the new bhikkhus. Some elder bhikkhus advised and instructed ten bhikkhus, some twenty, some thirty, some even forty bhikkhus. And those new bhikkhus, being instructed and advised by the elder bhikkhus, gained profound successive distinction in understanding.
translations.mn118:20: He trains thus: 'Experiencing the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Experiencing the mind, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Gladdening the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Gladdening the mind, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Concentrating the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Concentrating the mind, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Liberating the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Liberating the mind, I will breathe out'.
translations.mn118:21: He trains thus: 'Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating fading away, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating fading away, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating cessation, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating cessation, I will breathe out'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in'; he trains thus: 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out'.
translations.mn118:23: How, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfils the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: Whenever, monks, a monk breathes in long, he knows, 'I breathe in long'; when he breathes out long, he knows, 'I breathe out long'; when he breathes in short, he knows, 'I breathe in short'; when he breathes out short, he knows, 'I breathe out short'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out calming the bodily formation'. At that time, monks, the monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. In this way, monks, I say that mindfulness of breathing is one of the contemplations of the body. Therefore, monks, the monk at that time should dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:25: Whenever, monks, a monk trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing pleasure'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing pleasure'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing the mental formation'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in calming the mental formation'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out calming the mental formation'. At that time, monks, the monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. In this way, monks, I say that careful attention to in-breathing and out-breathing is one of the contemplations of feelings. Therefore, monks, the monk at that time should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:26: Whenever, monks, a monk trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in gladdening the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out gladdening the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in concentrating the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out concentrating the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in liberating the mind'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out liberating the mind'. At that time, monks, the monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Monks, I do not say that mindfulness of breathing exists for one who is unmindful and lacks clear comprehension. Therefore, monks, the monk at that time should dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:27: Whenever, monks, a monk trains himself, 'I will breathe in contemplating impermanence'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out contemplating impermanence'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in contemplating fading away'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out contemplating fading away'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in contemplating cessation'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out contemplating cessation'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; he trains himself, 'I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment'. At that time, monks, the monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He sees the removal of those very covetousness and displeasure with wisdom, and carefully maintains equanimity. Therefore, monks, the monk at that time should dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:28: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: How, monks, do the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
translations.mn118:3: At that time, the Blessed One, on that full-moon observance day, the fifteenth, sat surrounded by the community of monks in the open air. Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent community of monks, addressed the monks:
translations.mn118:30: Whenever, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world, mindfulness is established in him at that time, unconfused. Whenever, monks, mindfulness is established in a monk unconfused, at that time the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused in him; the monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches fulfillment in him at that time.
translations.mn118:31: While dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that phenomenon with wisdom, examines it, and comes to thoroughly scrutinize it. Whenever, monks, a monk while dwelling thus mindful investigates that phenomenon with wisdom, examines it, and comes to thoroughly scrutinize it, at that time the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena is aroused in him; the monk develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, and the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena reaches fulfillment in him at that time.
translations.mn118:33: In one who is energetically striving, unworldly rapture arises. Whenever, monks, unworldly rapture arises in a monk who is energetically striving, at that time the enlightenment factor of rapture is aroused in him; the monk develops the enlightenment factor of rapture, and the enlightenment factor of rapture reaches fulfillment in him at that time.
translations.mn118:34: When rapture is present, the body becomes calm and the mind becomes calm. Whenever, monks, the body and mind of a monk become calm due to rapture, at that time the enlightenment factor of tranquility is aroused in him; the monk develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility, and the enlightenment factor of tranquility reaches fulfillment in him at that time.
translations.mn118:35: With a calmed body and happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Whenever, monks, the mind of a monk becomes concentrated due to a calmed body and happiness, at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration is aroused in him; the monk develops the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of concentration reaches fulfillment in him at that time.
translations.mn118:36: He carefully observes that mind which is thus well-concentrated. Whenever, monks, a monk carefully observes that mind which is thus well-concentrated, at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused in him; at that time the monk develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity; at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches fulfillment through development.
translations.mn118:4: "I have striven, monks, by this path; my mind is resolute in this path. Therefore, monks, exert yourselves all the more to attain what has not yet been attained, to achieve what has not yet been achieved, to realize what has not yet been realized. Right here in Sāvatthī, I will spend the four-month rains-retreat."
translations.mn118:40: Thus developed, thus frequently cultivated, monks, the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven enlightenment factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how, monks, do the seven enlightenment factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those elder monks instructed and advised the new monks all the more. Some elder monks instructed and advised five monks, some elder monks instructed and advised twenty monks, some elder monks instructed and advised thirty monks, some elder monks instructed and advised forty monks. And those new monks, being instructed and advised by the elder monks, clearly understood profound successive distinctions.
translations.mn118:9: There are, monks, monks in this Saṅgha who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the spiritual life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are rightly liberated through final knowledge—such monks too, monks, exist in this Saṅgha.
translations.mn11:13: In such a Dhamma-discipline that is poorly proclaimed, poorly taught, not leading to the goal, not leading to peace, not proclaimed by the rightly self-awakened Buddha, confidence in the Teacher is not said to be well-placed; confidence in the Dhamma is not said to be well-placed; fulfillment in virtue is not said to be well-placed; affection for fellow practitioners is not said to be well-placed. Why is that? Because, monks, it is such that in a Dhamma-discipline poorly proclaimed, poorly taught, not leading to the goal, not leading to peace, not proclaimed by the rightly self-awakened Buddha.
translations.mn11:14: But the Tathāgata, monks, the arahant, the rightly self-awakened Buddha, declaring the full understanding of all clinging, rightly teaches the full understanding of all clinging—he teaches the full understanding of sensual clinging, the full understanding of clinging to views, the full understanding of clinging to rules and vows, the full understanding of clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn11:15: In such a Dhamma-discipline that is well-proclaimed, well-taught, leading to the goal, leading to peace, proclaimed by the rightly self-awakened Buddha, confidence in the Teacher is said to be well-placed; confidence in the Dhamma is said to be well-placed; fulfillment in virtue is said to be well-placed; affection for fellow practitioners is said to be well-placed. Why is that? Because, monks, it is such that in a Dhamma-discipline well-proclaimed, well-taught, leading to the goal, leading to peace, proclaimed by the rightly self-awakened Buddha.
translations.mn11:2: "Here indeed, monks, is a recluse, here a second recluse, here a third recluse, here a fourth recluse; other recluses' teachings are empty and void of recluses." Thus, monks, proclaim the lion's roar rightly.
translations.mn11:6: There are these two views, monks—eternalism and annihilationism. Whoever, monks, whether ascetics or brahmins, who are attached to eternalism, have adopted eternalism, are absorbed in eternalism—they are opposed to annihilationism. Whoever, monks, whether ascetics or brahmins, who are attached to annihilationism, have adopted annihilationism, are absorbed in annihilationism—they are opposed to eternalism.
translations.mn11:7: Whoever, monks, whether ascetics or brahmins, do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these two views, they are lustful, hateful, deluded, craving, clinging, unwise, opposed and contradictory, dwelling in proliferation, delighting in proliferation; they are not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I say they are not freed from suffering.
translations.mn11:9: These four, monks, are the clingings. What four? Clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and vows, clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows rightly the appropriate from the inappropriate, and the inappropriate from the appropriate. And, Sāriputta, insofar as the Tathāgata knows rightly the appropriate from the inappropriate, and the inappropriate from the appropriate, this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata's power, by relying on which the Tathāgata claims the superior position, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the brahmin-wheel.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, with the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life. And, Sāriputta, insofar as the Tathāgata, with the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata's power, by relying on which the Tathāgata claims the superior position, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the brahmin-wheel.
translations.mn12:2: At that time, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi had recently departed from this Dhamma-discipline. He was saying among the people of Vesālī: 'The ascetic Gotama has no higher human states, no superhuman knowledge and vision. The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma through logical reasoning, through investigation, through his own ingenuity. And whoever attains the purpose for which the Dhamma is taught, attains it through reasoning rightly leading to the complete destruction of suffering.'
translations.mn12:20: These ten, Sāriputta, are the Tathāgata's powers, by which endowed the Tathāgata claims the superior position, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the brahmin-wheel.
translations.mn12:22: These four, Sāriputta, are the Tathāgata's confidences, by which endowed the Tathāgata claims the superior position, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the brahmin-wheel. What four?
translations.mn12:23: ‘These dhammas have not been fully awakened to by one who claims to be a Fully Enlightened Buddha.’ Sāriputta, I do not perceive any sign by which a ascetic or brahmin, deity, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this point. Not perceiving such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:24: ‘These taints have not been utterly destroyed by one who claims to be one whose taints are destroyed.’ Sāriputta, I do not perceive any sign by which an ascetic or brahmin, deity, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this point. Not perceiving such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:25: ‘These unwholesome dhammas, which are said to be obstacles, when practiced, do not lead to obstruction.’ Sāriputta, I do not perceive any sign by which an ascetic or brahmin, deity, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this point. Not perceiving such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:26: ‘The dhamma taught for the sake of which purpose does not lead the earnest person to the complete destruction of suffering.’ Sāriputta, I do not perceive any sign by which an ascetic or brahmin, deity, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this point. Not perceiving such a sign, Sāriputta, I dwell secure, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:32: There are these four, Sāriputta, modes of birth. What four? Egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and rebirth without gestation.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born? Beings who emerge from eggs—this is called, Sāriputta, egg-born. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born? Beings who emerge from a womb—this is called, Sāriputta, womb-born. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born? Beings born in rotten flesh, in rotting dough, in mold, in decaying sweat, or in a cesspit—this is called, Sāriputta, moisture-born. And what, Sāriputta, is rebirth without gestation? Deities, beings in hell, some humans, and some beings in lower realms—this is called, Sāriputta, rebirth without gestation. These, Sāriputta, are the four modes of birth.
translations.mn12:35: There are these five, Sāriputta, destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, humans, and deities.
translations.mn12:36: Sāriputta, I fully understand hell, the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell; and I fully understand how one who practices accordingly, after death, is reborn in hell. I fully understand the animal realm, the path leading to the animal realm, and the practice leading to the animal realm; and I fully understand how one who practices accordingly, after death, is reborn in the animal realm. I fully understand the realm of ghosts, the path leading to the realm of ghosts, and the practice leading to the realm of ghosts; and I fully understand how one who practices accordingly, after death, is reborn in the realm of ghosts. I fully understand humans, the path leading to the human world, and the practice leading to the human world; and I fully understand how one who practices accordingly, after death, is reborn among humans. I fully understand deities, the path leading to the world of deities, and the practice leading to the world of deities; and I fully understand how one who practices accordingly, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. I fully understand Nibbāna, the path leading to Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna; and I fully understand how one who practices accordingly, through the destruction of the taints, realizes the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, here and now, and dwells having realized it for themselves.
translations.mn12:4: This person, Sāriputta, is angry and foolish. Indeed, this statement was spoken out of anger. But, Sāriputta, when a foolish person intends to speak disparagingly, they actually speak in praise of the Tathāgata. Praise indeed, Sāriputta, is this statement about the Tathāgata: ‘The dhamma taught for the sake of which purpose leads the earnest person to the complete destruction of suffering.’
translations.mn12:43: Whoever, Sāriputta, knowing and seeing me thus, were to say: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no higher human qualities, no noble knowledge and vision; the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma merely through logical reasoning and personal opinion’—without abandoning that statement, without abandoning that mind, without relinquishing that view, such a person would be cast down into hell just as if thrown there. Just as, Sāriputta, a monk accomplished in virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain another goal in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, I declare this: without abandoning that statement, without abandoning that mind, without relinquishing that view, such a person would be cast down into hell just as if thrown there.
translations.mn12:44: But indeed, Sāriputta, I know that I practiced the fourfold complete holy life—indeed, I was an ascetic, a great ascetic; indeed, I was austere, a great austere; indeed, I was disgusted, a greatly disgusted one; indeed, I was secluded, a greatly secluded one.
translations.mn12:46: At that time, Sāriputta, this was my austerity—dust and dirt accumulated on my body for years, matted together. Just as, Sāriputta, a tinduka tree trunk accumulates dirt and moss over many years, so too, Sāriputta, dust and dirt accumulated on my body for years, matted together. Yet it did not occur to me: ‘Oh, that I might rub this dust and dirt off with my hands, or that others might rub it off me with their hands.’ Even such a thought did not arise in me. This, Sāriputta, was my austerity.
translations.mn12:47: At that time, Sāriputta, this was my disgust—while walking forward or back, mindfulness was established in me, and compassion arose even at the sight of a drop of water: ‘May I not harm tiny creatures.’ This, Sāriputta, was my disgust.
translations.mn12:49: So, Sāriputta, when I approached the cow pens where the herds of cattle stood without a herdsman, I ate only the dung of young calves, of tender calves, of milch cows. And as long as my own excrement and urine were not yet fully digested, I ate only my own excrement and urine. This, Sāriputta, was my great coarse diet.
translations.mn12:5: Indeed, Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have this sequence of Dhamma regarding me: 'Truly, the Blessed One is an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.'
translations.mn12:50: So, Sāriputta, I dwelt having entered a thicket of thorny plants. There, Sāriputta, in that thicket of thorny plants, this would happen: whoever entered that thicket with unextinguished lust, mostly their hairs would stand on end. So, Sāriputta, during those cold winter nights, in the middle of the dark fortnight, when snow was falling, during such nights I spent the night in the open air and the day in the thicket; during the last month of summer, I spent the day in the open air and the night in the thicket. And furthermore, Sāriputta, this unprecedented verse occurred to me, never heard before: 'Alone in a thicket of thorns, soaked and shivering; naked, not sitting on a fire-seat, a seeker, a sage.'
translations.mn12:51: So, Sāriputta, I made my bed in charnel grounds, using bones as a pillow. And furthermore, Sāriputta, when I approached village outskirts, people would spit, urinate, throw dust on me, and insert splinters into my ear canals. Yet, Sāriputta, I never recognized any evil thought arising in me toward them. This, Sāriputta, was my abiding in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'Purification comes through food.' They said to me: 'Live on beans.' So they eat beans, eat bean flour, drink bean water—enjoying various kinds of bean preparations. But I, Sāriputta, consumed only one kind of bean as food. Perhaps, Sāriputta, you might think: 'Surely, at that time, there were many beans.' But, Sāriputta, that should not be seen in that way. Even then, beans were as scarce as they are now. But, Sāriputta, due to consuming only one kind of bean, my body became extremely emaciated. Just as the knotted joints of a withered vine or creepers; so too my limbs became due to that minimal nourishment. Just like a deep rut; so too my buttocks became due to that minimal nourishment. Just as the keel of a boat; so too my backbone stood out due to that minimal nourishment. Just like the roof-rafters of an old shed, sagging and drooping; so too my ribs became sagging and drooping due to that minimal nourishment. Just as deep in a pond, the water-plants deep below are barely visible; so too in the hollows of my eyes, the eyeballs appeared deep-set and barely visible due to that minimal nourishment. Just as a bitter gourd, cut and dried by wind and sun, shrivels up; so too my scalp became shriveled and withered due to that minimal nourishment. So, Sāriputta, thinking 'I will reduce the skin of my belly,' I grasped only the backbone; thinking 'I will reduce the backbone,' I grasped only the belly skin, until my belly skin clung to my backbone due to that minimal nourishment. So, Sāriputta, when I thought 'I will pass urine or excrement,' I fell down right there due to that minimal nourishment. So, Sāriputta, while breathing in and out, I massaged my limbs with my hands. And as I massaged my limbs with my hands, the roots of my hair, rotted at the roots, fell away from my body due to that minimal nourishment.
translations.mn12:56: By that conduct, that practice, that severe asceticism, I did not attain any superior human quality, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why is that? Because I had not yet attained that noble wisdom which is noble, which leads out, which leads the wise one rightly to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'Purification comes through wandering (samsara).' But, Sāriputta, that kind of wandering is not easy to find which I had not already wandered through during this long course of time, except for the Pure Abodes. And, Sāriputta, if I were to be reborn among the gods of the Pure Abodes, I would not return to this world again.
translations.mn12:6: Indeed, Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have this sequence of Dhamma regarding me: 'Truly, the Blessed One experiences various kinds of miraculous abilities: being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one; appearing and vanishing; going unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as though through space; diving in and out of the earth as though it were water; walking on water without sinking as though on dry land; flying cross-legged through the air like a bird; with his hand touching and stroking the sun and moon, so powerful and mighty; and even reaching with his body to the Brahma world.'
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'Purification comes through sacrifice.' But, Sāriputta, that kind of sacrifice is not easy to find which I had not already performed during this long course of time, whether by a crowned king, a warrior, or a great brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'Purification comes through fire-worship.' But, Sāriputta, that kind of fire is not easy to find which I had not already worshipped during this long course of time, whether by a crowned king, a warrior, or a great brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: Indeed, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and say: 'As long as a person is young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth and in the first stage of life, then he is endowed with the highest degree of wisdom and capability. But when that person becomes aged, old, burdened with years, advanced in life, and has reached old age—eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old—then from that wisdom and capability decline.' Now, Sāriputta, this should not be viewed in that way. For now, Sāriputta, I myself am aged, old, burdened with years, advanced in life, and eighty years have passed for me. Yet, Sāriputta, there are four disciples of mine who live a hundred years, who will live a hundred years, endowed with the highest degree of mindfulness, energy, and wisdom. Just as, Sāriputta, a skilled archer, well trained and experienced, could easily shoot a light arrow across a horizontal palm-leaf roof, so too are these four disciples, exceedingly mindful, exceedingly energetic, exceedingly resolute, and endowed with the highest degree of wisdom. They would repeatedly question me, taking up the four foundations of mindfulness, and whenever questioned, I would explain to them; and having been explained, they would retain it, but would not ask me further questions again. Apart from eating, drinking, chewing, tasting, defecating, urinating, and alleviating fatigue, the teaching of the Tathāgata never ceases, the exposition of the Tathāgata's words and phrases never ceases, the Tathāgata's readiness in answering questions never ceases. Then, when the hundred years of these four disciples have passed, they would pass away. Even if you were to carry me on a couch, Sāriputta, there would be no change in the Tathāgata's wisdom and capability.
translations.mn12:7: This too, Sāriputta, will not be part of the doctrine of that foolish man Sunakkhatta concerning me: 'The Blessed One hears both divine and human sounds with his divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human.'
translations.mn12:8: This too, Sāriputta, will not be part of the doctrine of that foolish man Sunakkhatta concerning me: 'The Blessed One knows the minds of other beings and individuals with his mind—he knows a mind with lust as having lust, a mind without lust as without lust; a mind with hatred as having hatred, a mind without hatred as without hatred; a mind with delusion as having delusion, a mind without delusion as without delusion; a contracted mind as contracted, a distracted mind as distracted; an exalted mind as exalted, a non-exalted mind as non-exalted; an inferior mind as inferior, a superior mind as superior; a concentrated mind as concentrated, an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; a liberated mind as liberated, an unliberated mind as unliberated.'
translations.mn12:9: Indeed, Sāriputta, these ten are the Tathāgata's powers, with which the Tathāgata, endowed, claims the foremost position, roars his lion's roar in assemblies, and sets in motion the brahmin-wheel. What are the ten?
