translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, young man, a certain woman or man is not a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, fragrances, unguents, bedding, housing, or lamps to ascetics or brahmins. Having performed such a deed, having undertaken it, upon the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a bad destination, in a state of suffering, in perdition, in hell. If upon the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a bad destination, in a state of suffering, in perdition, in hell, but come to the human state, then wherever they are reborn, they are of little fortune. This, young man, is the practice that leads to little fortune: not being a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, fragrances, unguents, bedding, housing, or lamps to ascetics or brahmins.
translations.mn135:2: Then the young man Subha, the son of Todeyya, went to the Blessed One; on arrival, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting to one side, the young man Subha, the son of Todeyya, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their actions, young man, heirs of their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings, namely, in terms of inferiority and superiority.
translations.mn135:3: "What, venerable Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why among human beings who are born as humans, inferiority and superiority are seen? For, venerable Gotama, some humans are seen with short life spans, others with long life spans; some are seen frequently ill, others rarely ill; some are seen unattractive, others attractive; some are seen with little influence, others with great influence; some are seen with little fortune, others with great fortune; some are seen of low birth, others of high birth; some are seen as dull-witted, others as wise. What, venerable Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why among human beings who are born as humans, inferiority and superiority are seen?"
translations.mn135:4: "Beings are owners of their actions, young man, heirs of their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings, namely, in terms of inferiority and superiority." "I do not understand the meaning of this statement of the venerable Gotama, spoken in brief without detailed explanation. May the venerable Gotama please teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I may understand the meaning of this statement of his, spoken in brief without detailed explanation." "Then listen, young man, pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," the young man Subha, the son of Todeyya, replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: Here, young man, a certain woman or man is one who kills living beings, is cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and harming, without compassion for living creatures. With that action completed and undertaken in this way, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. If instead, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell, but come to the human state, then wherever they are reborn, they are short-lived. This, young man, is the practice that leads to short life: namely, being one who kills living beings, is cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and harming, without compassion for living creatures.
translations.mn135:6: But here, young man, a certain woman or man, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from taking life; they are one who lays down the rod, lays down the weapon, full of conscience, compassionate, trembling for the welfare of all living beings. With that action completed and undertaken in this way, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, even in the heavenly world. If instead, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world, but come to the human state, then wherever they are reborn, they are long-lived. This, young man, is the practice that leads to long life: namely, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstaining from taking life; being one who lays down the rod, lays down the weapon, full of conscience, compassionate, trembling for the welfare of all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: Now, bhikkhus, when such a householder strives and exerts himself, his wealth increases. Then he experiences suffering and sorrow over the safeguarding of his wealth: 'May my wealth not be seized by kings, nor by thieves, nor burned by fire, nor carried off by water, nor taken by unloved heirs.' Yet, while he thus guards and protects it, his wealth is seized by kings, or by thieves, or burned by fire, or carried off by water, or taken by unloved heirs. He grieves, is distressed, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught: 'What was mine is now gone.' This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted entirely in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:11: Furthermore, bhikkhus, due to sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders, mothers with sons quarrel, sons with mothers, fathers with sons, sons with fathers, brothers with brothers, brothers with sisters, sisters with brothers, friends with friends. Engaged in quarrels, disputes, and conflicts, they attack one another with fists, clods, sticks, and weapons. There they suffer death or death-like pain. This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted entirely in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:12: Furthermore, bhikkhus, due to sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, taking up sword and shield, fitting the quiver, they rush into battle with arrows swiftly flying, spears swiftly hurled, swords flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, struck by spears, and have their heads cut off by swords. There they suffer death or death-like pain. This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted entirely in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:13: Furthermore, bhikkhus, due to sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, taking up sword and shield, fitting the quiver, they rush forth as assistants in siege warfare, with arrows swiftly flying, spears swiftly hurled, swords flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, struck by spears, drenched with boiling liquids, crushed by battering rams, and have their heads cut off by swords. There they suffer death or death-like pain. This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted entirely in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:15: Furthermore, bhikkhus, due to sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, they engage in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Having engaged in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. This too, bhikkhus, is a future danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, rooted entirely in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:16: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: For whoever, bhikkhus, ascetics or brahmins, do not understand as they really are the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, it is impossible that they would fully comprehend sensual pleasures themselves, or lead others to such full comprehension, or that one practicing rightly would fully comprehend sensual pleasures. But whoever, bhikkhus, ascetics or brahmins, do understand as they really are the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, it is possible that they would fully comprehend sensual pleasures themselves, lead others to such full comprehension, or that one practicing rightly would fully comprehend sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:18: And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in forms? Suppose, bhikkhus, a noble girl, or a brahmin girl, or a householder's daughter, fifteen or sixteen years old, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair—would she, bhikkhus, at that time, be beautiful and graceful in appearance? 'Yes, venerable sir.' That pleasure and joy which arises in dependence on such beauty and grace—this is the gratification in forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, bhikkhus, is the drawback of forms? Here, bhikkhus, one might see that very same sister at a later time, whether eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, born of old age, decrepit, broken like a roof tile, bent over, supported by a staff, trembling, frail, having reached advanced age, with broken teeth, grey and scanty hair, bald-headed, with wrinkled skin, with limbs bent and spotted. What do you think, bhikkhus, has that former beauty and charm disappeared, and has the drawback become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then, bhikkhus, a number of bhikkhus having dressed in the morning, took their bowls and robes and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: 'It is too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī; why don't we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?' Then those bhikkhus went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects; and after cordial greetings and polite conversation, they sat down to one side. When they were seated, those wanderers of other sects said to those bhikkhus:
translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, bhikkhus, one might see that very same sister sick, suffering, severely ill, lying in her own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some, being laid down by others. What do you think, bhikkhus, has that former beauty and charm disappeared, and has the drawback become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, bhikkhus, one might see that very same sister's body thrown on a charnel ground— a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by tendons; a skeleton smeared with flesh and blood, without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by tendons; a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by tendons; bones scattered in all directions— some hand bones, some foot bones, some shin bones, some thigh bones, some pelvic bones, some spinal bones, some shoulder bones, some neck bones, some skull bones. What do you think, bhikkhus, has that former beauty and charm disappeared, and has the drawback become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, bhikkhus, one might see that very same sister's body thrown on a charnel ground— bones white like conch shells, bones heaped up, bones weathered for three years, bones decomposed into dust. What do you think, bhikkhus, has that former beauty and charm disappeared, and has the drawback become evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:3: 'The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches the full understanding of sensual pleasures; we too teach the full understanding of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches the full understanding of forms; we too teach the full understanding of forms. The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches the full understanding of feelings; we too teach the full understanding of feelings. Then, friends, what is the difference, what is the distinction, what makes the distinction between the ascetic Gotama and us, in terms of teaching the Dhamma or instruction?'
translations.mn13:30: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from forms? It is the removal and abandonment of desire and lust for forms—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in feelings? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, filled with rapture and pleasure. At that time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells having entered the first jhāna with thought and examination, born of seclusion, filled with rapture and pleasure, he does not intend harm to himself, nor to others, nor to both; at that time he feels only painless feeling. Bhikkhus, I say that painless feeling is the highest gratification in feelings.
translations.mn13:36: And what, bhikkhus, is the drawback of feelings? That which is, bhikkhus, feeling impermanent, suffering, subject to change—this is the drawback of feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from feelings? It is the removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those bhikkhus neither approved nor rejected the wanderers' statement; without approving or rejecting, they rose from their seats and departed: 'We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
translations.mn13:6: 'Those wanderers of other sects, bhikkhus, who speak thus should be addressed: "What, friends, is the gratification, what is the drawback, what is the escape from sensual pleasures? What is the gratification, what is the drawback, what is the escape from forms? What is the gratification, what is the drawback, what is the escape from feelings?" When asked thus, bhikkhus, those wanderers of other sects will neither be able to answer properly nor avoid confusion. Why is that? Because it is beyond their range. I do not see, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathāgata, a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.mn13:8: And what, monks, is the drawback of sensual pleasures? Here, monks, a clansman earns a living by some craft—whether by counting, calculating, farming, trading, herding, archery, service to the king, or by a craft he has mastered—exposed to cold and heat, harassed by flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, suffering from hunger and thirst, worn out. This too, monks, is a visible drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as its cause.
translations.mn13:9: And if, monks, this clansman, striving and exerting himself thus, does not succeed in obtaining those possessions, he grieves, he grieves, he laments, beats his breast, weeps, and falls into confusion: 'Vain indeed was my effort, fruitless my striving.' This too, monks, is a visible drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, dependent on sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as its cause.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadhan country and arrived at Rājagaha. He went to Bhaggava the potter and said to him:
translations.mn140:12: 'One should not neglect wisdom, one should guard truth, one should cultivate generosity, one should train only in tranquility'—so has this been said. In reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, monk, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal, it may be external. And what, monk, is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, personal, hard, solid, and grasped—such as head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, or whatever else is internal, personal, hard, solid, and grasped—this is called, monk, the internal earth element. Both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element. 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self'—thus should one see this as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing this as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element, and the mind turns away from the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, monk, is the water element? The water element may be internal, it may be external. And what, monk, is the internal water element? Whatever is internal, personal, fluid, and grasped—such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, oil of the joints, urine, or whatever else is internal, personal, fluid, and grasped—this is called, monk, the internal water element. Both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element. 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self'—thus should one see this as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing this as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element, and the mind turns away from the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, monk, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal, it may be external. And what, monk, is the internal fire element? Whatever is internal, personal, fiery, and grasped—such as that by which one is warmed, by which one ages, by which one is burned, by which food and drink are properly digested, or whatever else is internal, personal, fiery, and grasped—this is called, monk, the internal fire element. Both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element. 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self'—thus should one see this as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing this as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element, and the mind turns away from the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, monk, is the air element? The air element may be internal, it may be external. And what, monk, is the internal air element? Whatever is internal, personal, airy, and grasped—such as winds going upward, winds going downward, winds in the abdomen, winds in the belly, winds moving through the limbs, in-breaths and out-breaths, or whatever else is internal, personal, airy, and grasped—this is called, monk, the internal air element. Both the internal air element and the external air element are simply the air element. 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self'—thus should one see this as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing this as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element, and the mind turns away from the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, monk, is the space element? The space element may be internal, it may be external. And what, monk, is the internal space element? Whatever is internal, personal, spacious, and grasped—such as the ear-hole, the nostril, the mouth opening, the passage through which food and drink are swallowed, the place where food and drink remain, the passage through which food and drink exit, or whatever else is internal, personal, spacious, hollow, open, not contacted by flesh and blood, and grasped—this is called, monk, the internal space element. Both the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element. 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self'—thus should one see this as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing this as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element, and the mind turns away from the space element.
translations.mn140:2: "If you, Bhaggava, would let us stay in your workshop for one night." "It is not convenient for me, sir. There is a renunciant who arrived first and has taken up residence. If he permits it, you may stay, sir, as you please."
translations.mn140:20: Then only equanimity remains, purified, bright, malleable, workable, and radiant. Just as, bhikkhu, a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice would heat a crucible, having heated the crucible would pour molten gold into its mouth, and from time to time would blow on it, from time to time sprinkle it with water, from time to time closely examine it; then that gold would become well refined, thoroughly refined, purified, free from dross, malleable, workable, and radiant, and whatever form he wished—whether a bracelet, earrings, a necklace, or a gold chain—he could make it serve his purpose. So too, bhikkhu, then only equanimity remains, purified, bright, malleable, workable, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he knows: 'It is impermanent'; he knows: 'It is not clung to'; he knows: 'It is not delighted in'. If he feels a painful feeling, he knows: 'It is impermanent'; he knows: 'It is not clung to'; he knows: 'It is not delighted in'. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows: 'It is impermanent'; he knows: 'It is not clung to'; he knows: 'It is not delighted in'.
translations.mn140:29: 'Wisdom should not be neglected, truth should be upheld, generosity should be cultivated, and peace alone should he train in'—this is what was said. This is how it should be understood.
translations.mn140:3: At that time, a householder's son named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith in the Blessed One. He arrived at that potter's workshop and spent the first rains-residence there. Then the Blessed One went to the Venerable Pukkusāti and said to him: 'If it suits you, bhikkhu, let us dwell in this potter's workshop for one night.' 'It is at your disposal, venerable sir, the potter's workshop. May the venerable one dwell there as he likes.'
translations.mn140:30: 'Where views do not arise, there the sage is said to be at peace'—this is what was said. In reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:31: 'I am' is a view, bhikkhu, 'I am this' is a view, 'I shall be' is a view, 'I shall not be' is a view, 'I shall be material' is a view, 'I shall be immaterial' is a view, 'I shall be percipient' is a view, 'I shall be non-percipient' is a view, 'I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient' is a view. A view, bhikkhu, is a disease, a view is a boil, a view is a dart. The sage is said to be at peace, bhikkhu, only upon completely transcending all views. Indeed, bhikkhu, the peaceful sage is not born, does not age, does not die, does not tremble, does not yearn. For him, bhikkhu, there is no craving by which he might be born; being un-born, how could he age? Being un-aged, how could he die? Being undying, how could he tremble? Being un-trembling, what could he yearn for?
translations.mn140:32: 'Where views do not arise, there the sage is said to be at peace'—this is what was said. This is how it should be understood. Bhikkhu, retain this brief exposition of the six elements I have given you.
translations.mn140:33: Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, rising from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said to the Blessed One: 'I have erred, venerable sir, I have strayed, I have done what is unskilful, in that I failed to recognize the Blessed One, who should be addressed respectfully. May the Blessed One accept my confession of this fault, for restraint in the future.' 'Indeed, bhikkhu, you have erred, you have strayed, you have done what is unskilful, in that you failed to recognize me, who should be addressed respectfully. But since, bhikkhu, you have seen your fault as a fault and have confessed it according to the Dhamma, we accept it. For growth in this noble discipline, bhikkhu, is one who sees a fault as a fault, confesses it according to the Dhamma, and exercises restraint in the future.'
translations.mn140:34: 'Venerable sir, may I receive ordination in the presence of the Blessed One?' 'But bhikkhu, is your bowl and robe complete?' 'No, venerable sir, my bowl and robe are not complete.' 'Bhikkhu, the Tathāgatas do not ordain one whose bowl and robe are incomplete.'
translations.mn140:35: Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, having approved and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and set out in search of a bowl and robes. Then, while the Venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, he was gored to death by a stray cow.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter's workshop, prepared a straw bed in one corner, sat down, folded his legs crosswise, straightened his body, and established mindfulness in front of him. The Blessed One spent most of the night sitting. The Venerable Pukkusāti also spent most of the night sitting. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'This householder's son behaves admirably. Why don't I question him?' Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: 'For the sake of whom, bhikkhu, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? In whose Dhamma do you delight?' 'There is, venerable sir, the ascetic Gotama, a Sakyan, who went forth from the Sakyan clan. Of that Blessed One Gotama this excellent reputation has spread: "Indeed, the Blessed One is accomplished, fully enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed." It is for the sake of that Blessed One that I have gone forth. He is my teacher. In his Dhamma I delight.' 'But where now, bhikkhu, does that Blessed One, the accomplished, fully enlightened one, dwell?' 'There is, venerable sir, a city named Sāvatthī in the northern regions. There the Blessed One, the accomplished, fully enlightened one, now dwells.' 'Have you ever seen that Blessed One before? And if you saw him, would you recognize him?' 'No, venerable sir, I have never seen that Blessed One before; and even if I saw him, I would not recognize him.'
translations.mn140:6: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “This young man has gone forth for my sake. Why don’t I teach him the Dhamma?” Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Pukkusāti: “I will teach you the Dhamma, monk. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the venerable Pukkusāti replied in assent to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn140:7: "This person, monk, consists of six elements, six sense bases, eighteen mental investigations, and four foundations of mindfulness. Where views do not arise, and when views do not arise, the sage is said to be at peace. One should not neglect wisdom, should guard truth, cultivate generosity, and train only in tranquility." This is the summary of the analysis of the elements.
translations.mn146:12: "This is a simile I have made, sisters, to convey the meaning. This is the meaning here: 'The inner fleshly body,' sisters, is a designation for these six internal sense bases; 'the outer skin-covered body,' sisters, is a designation for these six external sense bases; 'the inner sinews, the inner bones, the inner tendons,' sisters, is a designation for delight and lust; 'the sharp knife of wisdom,' sisters, is a designation for noble wisdom—the noble wisdom that cuts through, penetrates, pierces, and thoroughly pierces internal defilements, internal fetters, and internal bonds.
translations.mn146:13: These seven, sisters, are the factors of enlightenment. When developed and cultivated, a monk dwells having realized with his own knowledge the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, in this very life. What seven? Here, sisters, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of principles … the enlightenment factor of energy … the enlightenment factor of rapture … the enlightenment factor of tranquility … the enlightenment factor of concentration … the enlightenment factor of equanimity, dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. These seven, sisters, are the factors of enlightenment. When developed and cultivated, a monk dwells having realized with his own knowledge the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, in this very life."
translations.mn146:14: Then the venerable Nandaka, having instructed those nuns with this exhortation, dismissed them: "Go now, sisters; the time has come." Then those nuns, having approved and welcomed the words of the venerable Nandaka, rose from their seats, paid homage to him, circumambulated him, and went to the Blessed One. Approaching him, they paid homage and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those nuns were addressed by the Blessed One: "Go now, nuns; the time has come." Then those nuns, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, departed.
translations.mn146:3: At that time, the elder monks were giving regular instruction to the nuns. The venerable Nandaka did not wish to give regular instruction to the nuns. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Who, Ānanda, is giving regular instruction to the nuns today?" "Sir, all have given regular instruction to the nuns. This venerable Nandaka does not wish to give regular instruction to the nuns."
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka: "Instruct the nuns, Nandaka; guide the nuns, Nandaka; give the nuns, brahmin, a Dhamma talk." "Yes, sir," the venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. Then, having dressed in the morning, he took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned after the meal, he went alone to the royal park. Those nuns saw the venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and brought water for his feet. The venerable Nandaka sat down on the appointed seat. Sitting down, he washed his feet. Then the nuns paid homage to the venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Nandaka said to them:
translations.mn146:5: "There will be a question-and-answer session, sisters. Those who know should say: 'We know,' and those who do not know should not say: 'We do not know.' And if anyone has doubt or uncertainty, I alone should be asked: 'Sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?'" "Sir, we are already pleased and delighted with just this much—that the Venerable Nandaka is willing to conduct the session."
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this thought occurred to his mind: "Rāhula’s qualities conducive to liberation are mature. Why don’t I lead Rāhula on to the destruction of the taints?" Then, having dressed in the morning, the Blessed One took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned after the meal, he addressed the venerable Rāhula: "Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula; let us go to the Andhavana for the day’s abode." "Yes, sir," the venerable Rāhula replied, and taking his sitting cloth, he followed behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: At that time, thousands of deities were following the Blessed One, thinking: 'Today the Blessed One will lead the Venerable Rāhula to the destruction of the taints.' Then the Blessed One, having entered the Blind Men's Grove, sat down at the foot of a certain tree on a seat made ready. The Venerable Rāhula too, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down at one side. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Rāhula, who was sitting at one side: 'What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, sir.' 'But what is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?' 'Suffering, sir.' 'But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"?' 'No, sir.'
translations.mn148:16: This, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the arising of identity—when one regards the eye as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."
translations.mn148:2: "I will teach you the Dhamma, bhikkhus, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I will make known the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life, namely, the six sextets. Listen to this, attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, sir," those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: This, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the cessation of identity—when one does not regard the eye as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."
translations.mn148:3: "The six internal sense bases should be understood, the six external sense bases should be understood, the six classes of consciousness should be understood, the six classes of contact should be understood, the six classes of feeling should be understood, the six classes of craving should be understood.
translations.mn148:34: With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When touched by a pleasant feeling, one does not delight, welcome, or remain attached to it. His underlying tendency to lust does not lie dormant. When touched by a painful feeling, one does not grieve, lament, or weep, nor does he fall into confusion. His underlying tendency to aversion does not lie dormant. When touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he clearly understands its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and its escape. His underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie dormant. Indeed, bhikkhus, one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust in pleasant feeling, eliminated the underlying tendency to aversion in painful feeling, and eradicated the underlying tendency to ignorance in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—having abandoned ignorance and produced true knowledge—will be one who makes an end of suffering in this very life. This is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with eye-consciousness, with eye-contact, with feeling, and with craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be fully understood by direct knowledge? It should be said: the five aggregates subject to clinging, namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These are the phenomena to be fully understood by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence—these are the phenomena to be abandoned by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight—these are the phenomena to be developed by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be realized by direct knowledge? Knowledge and liberation—these are the phenomena to be realized by direct knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: "I will teach you the Great Sixfold Base, bhikkhus. Listen to this, attend closely, I will speak." "Yes, sir," those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: "Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are, not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is, not knowing and not seeing the feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact as it really is, one becomes attached to the eye, to forms, to eye-consciousness, to eye-contact, and to that feeling. For one who dwells attached, bound, deluded, and contemplating gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging increase in the future. His craving—which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there—grows. His bodily anxieties grow, his mental anxieties grow; his bodily torments grow, his mental torments grow; his bodily fevers grow, his mental fevers grow. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: For one who dwells attached, bound, deluded, and contemplating gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging increase in the future. His craving—which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there—grows. His bodily anxieties grow, his mental anxieties grow; his bodily torments grow, his mental torments grow; his bodily fevers grow, his mental fevers grow. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: And indeed, bhikkhus, one knows and sees the eye as it really is, one knows and sees forms as they really are, one knows and sees eye-consciousness as it really is, one knows and sees eye-contact as it really is, and whatever feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too one knows and sees as it really is. One does not delight in the eye, does not delight in forms, does not delight in eye-consciousness, does not delight in eye-contact, and does not delight in whatever feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact. Abiding with no delight, no attachment, no delusion, and contemplating the danger, the five aggregates subject to clinging diminish for such a one. His craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, is abandoned. His bodily anxieties are abandoned, mental anxieties are abandoned; bodily distresses are abandoned, mental distresses are abandoned; bodily fevers are abandoned, mental fevers are abandoned. He experiences bodily ease and mental ease.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines with the mind, the mind inclines in that direction. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines the thought of renunciation, having abandoned sensual thought, having made the thought of renunciation predominant, his mind inclines towards that thought of renunciation. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines the thought of non-ill-will … If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines the thought of non-harming, having abandoned the thought of harming, having made the thought of non-harming predominant, his mind inclines towards that thought of non-harming.
translations.mn19:12: Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of summer, when all the grass and vegetation have dried up, a cowherd would guard the cows, and whether he is at the foot of a tree or in an open space, his mindfulness is constantly present: 'These are the cows.' So too, bhikkhus, mindfulness was constantly present: 'These are the dhammas.'
translations.mn19:13: And indeed, bhikkhus, my energy was aroused and unslacking, mindfulness was established and not confused, the body was calm and unexcited, the mind was concentrated and unified.
translations.mn19:14: Thus, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, accompanied by rapture and happiness.
translations.mn19:24: This, bhikkhus, was the third knowledge attained by me in the last watch of that night: ignorance was destroyed, true knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—just as it should be for a diligent, ardent, and resolute one.
translations.mn19:25: Just as, bhikkhus, in a forest wilderness there is a large, deep marsh covered with reeds and rushes. A large herd of elephants dwells depending on it. Then someone would arise who is harmful, unbeneficial, and dangerous. He would block the safe, good, pleasant path, open up a bad path, cover the clear path, and set up a thicket. In this way, that large herd of elephants would later come to ruin and disaster. But then, bhikkhus, someone else would arise in that same large herd of elephants who is beneficial, helpful, and safe. He would open up the safe, good, pleasant path, block the bad path, clear away the thicket, and remove the undergrowth. In this way, that large herd of elephants would later attain growth, increase, and expansion.
translations.mn19:26: This simile, bhikkhus, has been made by me to illustrate the meaning. And this is the meaning here: 'Large, deep marsh covered with reeds and rushes'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the sensual pleasures. 'Large herd of elephants'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for beings. 'A person harmful, unbeneficial, dangerous'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the Evil One, the Wicked One. 'Bad path'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the wrong eightfold path, namely: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. 'Thicket'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for lust and greed. 'Undergrowth'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for ignorance. 'A person beneficial, helpful, safe'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. 'The safe, good, pleasant path'—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, bhikkhus, I have opened the safe, good, pleasant path, blocked the bad path, cleared away the thicket, and removed the undergrowth.
translations.mn19:3: While I, bhikkhus, was dwelling thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, a sensual thought arose. I understood thus: 'This sensual thought has arisen in me. This leads to self-affliction, to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the factors of vexation, and does not lead to Nibbāna.' Reflecting thus, 'It leads to self-affliction,' it subsided in me, bhikkhus; reflecting thus, 'It leads to the affliction of others,' it subsided in me, bhikkhus; reflecting thus, 'It leads to the affliction of both,' it subsided in me, bhikkhus; reflecting thus, 'It is obstructive to wisdom, belongs to the factors of vexation, and does not lead to Nibbāna,' it subsided in me, bhikkhus. And I, bhikkhus, abandoned the sensual thought that had arisen, eliminated it, destroyed it, and made it cease.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines with the mind, the mind inclines in that direction. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines sensual thought, having abandoned the thought of renunciation, having made sensual thought predominant, his mind inclines towards that sensual thought. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines ill-will thought … If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks upon and examines harmful thought, having abandoned the thought of non-harming, having made harmful thought predominant, his mind inclines towards that harmful thought.
translations.mn19:7: Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the sky is clear and the clouds have dispersed, a cowherd would guard his cows, and he would drive them back, turn them back, restrain them, and keep them within bounds with a stick from here and there. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the cowherd sees danger in their wandering—slaughter, bondage, punishment, or censure. So too, bhikkhus, I saw the danger, drawback, and defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit, purity, and advantage in wholesome states.
translations.mn19:8: To me, bhikkhus, while living thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, a thought of renunciation arises. I understand thus: 'This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It leads neither to self-affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it is wise, unobstructed, and leads to Nibbāna.' If, bhikkhus, I were to repeatedly think and ponder on it by night, I would see no fear arising from that. If by day, I would see no fear arising from that. If both by night and day, I would see no fear arising from that. Yet, if I were to keep on thinking and pondering for too long, my body would become fatigued. When the body is fatigued, the mind becomes restless. When the mind is restless, it moves away from concentration. So, bhikkhus, I would steady my mind internally, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it. Why is that? 'So that my mind does not become restless.'
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭha, in the Subhagavana, at the root of a sāla tree. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: He perceives Brahmā as Brahmā; perceiving Brahmā as Brahmā, he regards himself as Brahmā, regards himself as belonging to Brahmā, regards himself as having come from Brahmā, regards himself as having reached Brahmā, and delights in Brahmā. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:11: He perceives the Radiant Devas as the Radiant Devas; perceiving the Radiant Devas as the Radiant Devas, he regards himself as belonging to the Radiant Devas, regards himself as in the Radiant Devas, regards himself as having come from the Radiant Devas, regards himself as having reached the Radiant Devas, and delights in the Radiant Devas. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:123: Even a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the spiritual life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—he too perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not regard himself as earth, does not regard himself as belonging to earth, does not regard himself as coming from earth, does not regard himself as having reached earth, and does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because of the destruction of delusion, being free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: He perceives the Devas of Refulgent Glory as the Devas of Refulgent Glory; perceiving the Devas of Refulgent Glory as the Devas of Refulgent Glory, he regards himself as belonging to the Devas of Refulgent Glory, regards himself as in the Devas of Refulgent Glory, regards himself as having come from the Devas of Refulgent Glory, regards himself as having reached the Devas of Refulgent Glory, and delights in the Devas of Refulgent Glory. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:14: He perceives the All-pervading as the All-pervading; perceiving the All-pervading as the All-pervading, he regards himself as the All-pervading, regards himself as belonging to the All-pervading, regards himself as having come from the All-pervading, regards himself as having reached the All-pervading, and delights in the All-pervading. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:147: Even the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not regard himself as earth, does not regard himself as belonging to earth, does not regard himself as coming from earth, does not regard himself as having reached earth, and does not delight in earth. Why is that? I say it is because it has been fully understood by the Tathāgata.
translations.mn1:171: Even the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not regard himself as earth, does not regard himself as belonging to earth, does not regard himself as coming from earth, does not regard himself as having reached earth, and does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because he knows: 'Craving is the root of suffering; existence leads to birth, and for what has been born, aging and death.' Therefore, bhikkhus, I say: 'The Tathāgata, through the complete destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishment of all craving, has awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment.'
translations.mn1:19: He perceives the seen as the seen; perceiving the seen as the seen, he regards himself as the seen, regards himself as belonging to the seen, regards himself as having come from the seen, regards himself as having reached the seen, and delights in the seen. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:2: “I will teach you, bhikkhus, the exposition on the root of all things. Listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: He perceives the heard as the heard; perceiving the heard as the heard, he regards himself as the heard, regards himself as belonging to the heard, regards himself as having come from the heard, regards himself as having reached the heard, and delights in the heard. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:22: He perceives the cognized as the cognized; perceiving the cognized as the cognized, he regards himself as the cognized, regards himself as belonging to the cognized, regards himself as having come from the cognized, regards himself as having reached the cognized, and delights in the cognized. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:23: He perceives oneness as oneness; perceiving oneness as oneness, he regards himself as oneness, regards himself as belonging to oneness, regards himself as having come from oneness, regards himself as having reached oneness, and delights in oneness. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:24: He perceives diversity as diversity; perceiving diversity as diversity, he regards himself as diversity, regards himself as belonging to diversity, regards himself as having come from diversity, regards himself as having reached diversity, and delights in diversity. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:25: He perceives all as all; perceiving all as all, he regards himself as all, regards himself as belonging to all, regards himself as having come from all, regards himself as having reached all, and delights in all. Why is that? I say it is because it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:27: Even a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who is a trainee, who has not yet reached the mental goal, who is striving for the supreme security from bondage— he too perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he should not regard himself as earth, should not regard himself as belonging to earth, should not regard himself as coming from earth, should not regard himself as having reached earth, and should not delight in earth. Why is that? I say it is because it is to be fully understood.
translations.mn1:3: “Here, bhikkhus, an unlearned worldling who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble Dhamma, untrained in the noble Dhamma, who has not seen the good persons, is unskilled in the qualities of good persons, untrained in the qualities of good persons—perceives earth as earth; perceiving earth as earth, he conceives earth as 'mine', identifies with earth, conceives 'I am earth', conceives 'earth is like this for me', and delights in earth. And why is that? I say because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:4: He perceives water as water; perceiving water as water, he conceives water as 'mine', identifies with water, conceives 'I am water', conceives 'water is like this for me', and delights in water. And why is that? I say because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:5: He perceives fire as fire; perceiving fire as fire, he conceives fire as 'mine', identifies with fire, conceives 'I am fire', conceives 'fire is like this for me', and delights in fire. And why is that? I say because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:51: But even a bhikkhu who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, who has lived the spiritual life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—he too perceives earth as earth; but having fully understood earth as earth, he does not conceive earth as 'mine', does not identify with earth, does not conceive 'I am earth', does not conceive 'earth is like this for me', and does not delight in earth. And why is that? I say because it has been fully understood.
translations.mn1:7: He perceives beings as beings; perceiving beings as beings, he conceives beings as 'mine', identifies with beings, conceives 'I am beings', conceives 'beings are like this for me', and delights in beings. And why is that? I say because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:8: He perceives gods as gods; perceiving gods as gods, he conceives gods as 'mine', identifies with gods, conceives 'I am gods', conceives 'godhood is like this for me', and delights in gods. And why is that? I say because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn1:9: He perceives Pajāpati as Pajāpati; perceiving Pajāpati as Pajāpati, he conceives Pajāpati as 'mine', identifies with Pajāpati, conceives 'I am Pajāpati', conceives 'Pajāpati is like this for me', and delights in Pajāpati. And why is that? I say because it has not been fully understood.
translations.mn20:2: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to higher mind should from time to time reflect on five themes. What are the five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever of my statements you understand the meaning of, hold on to that in that way. And whatever of my statements you do not understand the meaning of, you should question me about it, or those bhikkhus who are competent.
translations.mn22:14: The Dhamma I have taught you is like a raft, bhikkhus; it is for crossing over, not for holding onto. Even the Dhammas should be abandoned, how much more so the wrong things.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: 'Might there be, venerable sir, fear and dread when there is nothing external?' 'There might be, bhikkhus,' said the Blessed One. 'Here, a bhikkhu is of such a view: \"May I have it, may it be mine; may I have it, may I obtain it.\" He grieves, laments, weeps, beats his breast, and falls into confusion. Thus, bhikkhu, there is fear and dread when there is nothing external.'
translations.mn22:19: 'Might there be, venerable sir, no fear and dread when there is nothing external?' 'There might be, bhikkhus,' said the Blessed One. 'Here, a bhikkhu is not of such a view: \"May I have it, may it be mine; may I have it, may I obtain it.\" He does not grieve, does not lament, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion. Thus, bhikkhu, there is no fear and dread when there is nothing external.'
translations.mn22:20: 'Might there be, venerable sir, fear and dread when there is nothing internal?' 'There might be, bhikkhus,' said the Blessed One. 'Here, a bhikkhu holds such a view: \"This world is the self; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, I shall stand firm like this forever.\" He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the complete destruction of all underlying tendencies to views, to the stilling of all formations, to the relinquishing of all attachments, to the destruction of craving, to fading away, to cessation, to Nibbāna. Then he thinks: \"I shall be annihilated, I shall be destroyed, I shall not exist.\" He grieves, laments, weeps, beats his breast, and falls into confusion. Thus, bhikkhu, there is fear and dread when there is nothing internal.'
translations.mn22:23: Bhikkhus, take up that self-doctrine which, when taken up, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise. Bhikkhus, do you see such a self-doctrine which, when taken up, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise?
translations.mn22:24: Bhikkhus, rely on that basis of views which, when relied upon, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise. Bhikkhus, do you see such a basis of views which, when relied upon, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise?
translations.mn22:25: Bhikkhus, is there 'self' in reality such that 'what is mine' may exist?
translations.mn22:27: Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever kind of form there is—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom, as it really is, thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Whatever kind of feeling there is … Whatever kind of perception there is … Whatever kind of formations there are … Whatever kind of consciousness there is—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom, as it really is, thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; and when liberated, there is the knowledge: 'I am liberated.' He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, lived is the holy life, done is what had to be done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.mn22:30: This bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who has lifted the pole, one who has removed the crossbar, one who has pulled up the peg, one who is free of obstacles, one who is noble, banner-lowered, burden-laid-down, unentangled.
translations.mn22:31: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has lifted the pole? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's ignorance has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with so that it can no longer arise in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has lifted the pole.
translations.mn22:32: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has removed the crossbar? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's repeated becoming and the cycle of rebirth has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with so that it can no longer arise in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has removed the crossbar.
translations.mn22:33: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has pulled up the peg? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's craving has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with so that it can no longer arise in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has pulled up the peg.
translations.mn22:34: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu free of obstacles? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's five lower fetters have been abandoned, their roots cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they can no longer arise in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is free of obstacles.
translations.mn22:35: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu noble, banner-lowered, burden-laid-down, unentangled? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's conceit of 'I am' has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with so that it can no longer arise in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is noble, banner-lowered, burden-laid-down, unentangled.
translations.mn22:38: Now, bhikkhus, if others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata feels neither joy nor pleasure nor mental elation. And, bhikkhus, when others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata thinks: 'What was formerly fully understood, now such actions are being performed.'
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, bhikkhus, even if others revile, reproach, scold, and harass you, you should not harbor hatred, resentment, or mental discomfort. Therefore, bhikkhus, even if others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate you, you should not feel joy, pleasure, or mental elation. Therefore, bhikkhus, even if others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate you, you should reflect thus: 'What was formerly fully understood, now such actions are being performed.'
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours; abandoning it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.
translations.mn22:42: Thus well-expounded by me, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma—open, revealed, evident, without barriers. In this well-expounded Dhamma, bhikkhus, taught openly, revealed, evident, without barriers, those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and are liberated by perfect wisdom—there is no more designation of round for them.
translations.mn22:43: Thus well-expounded by me, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma—open, revealed, evident, without barriers. In this well-expounded Dhamma, bhikkhus, taught openly, revealed, evident, without barriers, those bhikkhus whose five lower fetters are abandoned are all reborn spontaneously, there attaining final Nibbāna, not subject to return from that world.
translations.mn22:44: Thus well-expounded by me, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma—open, revealed, evident, without barriers. In this well-expounded Dhamma, bhikkhus, taught openly, revealed, evident, without barriers, those bhikkhus whose three fetters are abandoned and whose greed, hate, and delusion are weakened are all once-returners, who will come back to this world only once more and then make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: Thus well-expounded by me, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma—open, revealed, evident, without barriers. In this well-expounded Dhamma, bhikkhus, taught openly, revealed, evident, without barriers, those bhikkhus whose three fetters are abandoned are all stream-enterers, not liable to fall into states of woe, fixed in destiny, headed for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:46: Thus well-expounded by me, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma—open, revealed, evident, without barriers. In this well-expounded Dhamma, bhikkhus, taught openly, revealed, evident, without barriers, all those bhikkhus who are followers of the Dhamma, followers of faith, are headed for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:6: “Who indeed, you foolish man, has understood this Dhamma as I have taught it? Have I not, you foolish man, repeatedly explained defilements as obstacles? And yet, by indulging in them, you are creating an obstacle for yourself. Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be of little satisfaction, much suffering, much distress, and greater danger. Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a skeleton… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a lump of flesh… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a torch of dry grass… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a pit of glowing embers… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a dream… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like borrowed goods… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like the fruits of a tree… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a sword and a stake… sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a snake’s head—full of suffering, full of distress, and greater danger. Furthermore, you, foolish man, by wrongly grasping, have slandered us, harmed yourself, and generated much demerit. This will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time,”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus, could this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who is obsessed with the simile of the raft, possibly understand the Dhamma and discipline?” “How could he, venerable sir? It is not possible, venerable sir.” When this was said, bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was obsessed with the simile of the raft, became silent, ashamed, crestfallen, with downcast eyes, dejected, and without a reply, and sat there. Then the Blessed One, knowing bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was obsessed with the simile of the raft, to be silent, ashamed, crestfallen, with downcast eyes, dejected, and without a reply, said to him: “You will come to understand, you foolish man, the evil of your wrong view by your own experience. I will now question the bhikkhus.”
translations.mn22:9: That someone, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from sensual perception, apart from sensual thought, would still indulge in sensual pleasures—this is not possible.
translations.mn26:10: And what, bhikkhus, do you call something subject to sorrow? Sons and wives are subject to sorrow, servants are subject to sorrow, goats and sheep are subject to sorrow, fowls and pigs are subject to sorrow, elephants, cattle, horses, and mules are subject to sorrow. These, bhikkhus, are attachments that are subject to sorrow. Here, one who is bound, deluded, and deeply immersed, being himself subject to sorrow, seeks only what is subject to sorrow.
translations.mn26:11: And what, bhikkhus, do you call something defiling? Sons and wives are defiling, servants are defiling, goats and sheep are defiling, fowls and pigs are defiling, elephants, cattle, horses, and mules are defiling, gold and silver are defiling. These, bhikkhus, are attachments that are defiling. Here, one who is bound, deluded, and deeply immersed, being himself defiled, seeks only what is defiling. This, bhikkhus, is the ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: So too, bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, when I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth, I sought only what is subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, I sought only what is subject to aging; being myself subject to illness, I sought only what is subject to illness; being myself subject to death, I sought only what is subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, I sought only what is subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement, I sought only what is subject to defilement. Then it occurred to me: ‘Why do I, being myself subject to birth, seek only what is subject to birth? Why, being myself subject to aging, seek only what is subject to aging? Why, being myself subject to illness, seek only what is subject to illness? Why, being myself subject to death, seek only what is subject to death? Why, being myself subject to sorrow, seek only what is subject to sorrow? Why, being myself subject to defilement, seek only what is subject to defilement? Suppose that I, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in birth, were to seek the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in aging, were to seek the ageless, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in illness, were to seek the disease-free, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in death, were to seek the deathless, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in sorrow, were to seek the sorrowless, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in defilement, were to seek the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna?’
translations.mn26:14: Then, bhikkhus, some time later, while still young, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my parents were unwilling and weeping with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: Then, bhikkhus, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the unsurpassed state of peace, I wandered gradually through the Magadhan countryside until I arrived at Uruvelā Senānigama. There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a charming grove, a clear flowing river with fine sand, delightful and well situated, and villages all around. It occurred to me: ‘Indeed, this stretch of land is delightful, the grove is charming, the river flows clearly with fine sand, well situated and delightful, and there are villages all around. This is surely suitable for the striving of a clansman intent on effort.’ Then, bhikkhus, I sat down right there: ‘This is enough for striving.’
translations.mn26:21: Then, bhikkhus, having understood Brahma's request and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha's eye. And, bhikkhus, as I surveyed the world with the Buddha's eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and dull faculties, with good qualities and bad qualities, easy to be taught and hard to be taught, some dwelling seeing fear in the next world and evil deeds, some not dwelling seeing fear in the next world and evil deeds. Just as in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, remain submerged under the water, some lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, stand level with the water, and some lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, rise up above the water, unstained by the water; so too, bhikkhus, as I surveyed the world with the Buddha's eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and dull faculties, with good qualities and bad qualities, easy to be taught and hard to be taught, some dwelling seeing fear in the next world and evil deeds, some not dwelling seeing fear in the next world and evil deeds. Then, bhikkhus, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse: 'The door to the deathless is open; let those who have ears show faith. I will not speak to the malicious; O Brahmā, let wise men listen to the sublime Dhamma.' Then, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking 'I have made an opportunity for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,' having paid homage to me, circumambulated me, and disappeared right there.
translations.mn26:25: Bhikkhus, the wanderer Upaka saw me on the road between the Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Seeing me, he said to me: 'Your faculties are clear, friend, your complexion is pure and bright. In whose name have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve?' When this was said, bhikkhus, I addressed the wanderer Upaka in verses: 'I am unconquered by anything, I know all, I am unattached to all things; having abandoned craving, I am liberated by the destruction of craving. Having realized it myself, to whom should I point? I have no teacher, nor is there anyone equal to me in this world with its devas. There is no one like me. I am the arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed teacher. I am the only one rightly self-awakened, cooled and extinguished. I go to the city of Kāsi to set in motion the wheel of Dhamma; in this world that has grown dark, I will beat the drum of the deathless.' 'So you claim, friend, to be an arahant, a conqueror without end.' 'Only those are conquerors like me who have attained the destruction of the taints. The evil things are conquered by me; therefore, Upaka, I am a conqueror.' When this was said, bhikkhus, the wanderer Upaka said 'May you succeed, friend,' shook his head, took a side path, and departed.
translations.mn26:26: Then, bhikkhus, I proceeded gradually on my journey until I reached the deer park at Isipatana, Benares, where the group of five bhikkhus were. The bhikkhus saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they said to one another: 'Here comes the ascetic Gotama, who gave up effort, indulged in luxury, and reverted to luxury. He should not be honored, nor should we rise up for him or receive his bowl and robe. But a seat should be prepared; if he wishes, he may sit down.' But as I approached, the bhikkhus could not maintain their agreement. Some came forward and received my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, some brought water for my feet. Yet they addressed me by name and as 'friend'.
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, I said to the bhikkhus of the group of five: 'Do you know of me, bhikkhus, having previously developed such a radiant state as this?' 'No, indeed, venerable sir.' 'I am, bhikkhus, the arahant, the rightly self-awakened one. Lend ear, bhikkhus, the deathless has been attained. I will instruct you, I will teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon realize for yourselves, in this very life, the unsurpassed goal of the holy life—having directly known and realized it—where for which sons of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.'
translations.mn26:29: I was unable, bhikkhus, to fully instruct the bhikkhus of the group of five. Two bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I would instruct, while three bhikkhus went for alms. Whatever the three bhikkhus brought back from their alms round, we six would live on that. Then three bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I would instruct, while two bhikkhus went for alms. Whatever the two bhikkhus brought back from their alms round, we six would live on that.
translations.mn26:30: Then, bhikkhus, the bhikkhus of the group of five, being instructed and advised by me, understanding that they themselves were subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna—attained the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna. Understanding that they themselves were subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, seeking the ageless, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna—attained the ageless, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna. Understanding that they themselves were subject to illness … to death … to sorrow … to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna—attained the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna. Then knowledge arose in them: 'Unshakable is our liberation; this is the last birth; there is no more becoming.'
translations.mn26:31: These, bhikkhus, are the five sensual pleasures. What are the five? Forms cognizable by the eye, agreeable, pleasing, charming, delightful, enticing, connected with sensual pleasure; sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body, agreeable, pleasing, charming, delightful, enticing, connected with sensual pleasure. These, bhikkhus, are the five sensual pleasures.
translations.mn26:34: Just as, bhikkhus, a forest deer moving about in the wilderness walks safely, stands safely, sits safely, lies down safely. Why is that? Because it has escaped the hunter’s path, bhikkhus. So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus, to have become invisible, sightless to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:35: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of thought and examination, attains internal confidence, unification of mind, and enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without thought and examination, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:36: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly aware, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.’ He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:37: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:38: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite space. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:39: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, completely transcending the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One approached the brahmin Rammaka’s hermitage. At that time, several bhikkhus were sitting together in Rammaka’s hermitage engaged in Dhamma talk. The Blessed One stood outside the gatehouse waiting for the discussion to end. When the Blessed One knew the discussion had ended, he coughed and knocked on the door. The bhikkhus opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered Rammaka’s hermitage and sat down on the prepared seat. Seated, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What were you discussing now, bhikkhus, as you sat together? And what conversation was interrupted?” “Venerable sir, our Dhamma talk was about you, and then the Blessed One arrived.” “Good, bhikkhus. It is fitting for you, bhikkhus, sons of good families who have gone forth from home into homelessness, to sit together engaged in Dhamma talk. When you gather together, bhikkhus, you should do two things—engage in Dhamma talk or maintain noble silence.
