translations.mn26:40: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, completely transcending the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the dimension of nothingness. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:41: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, completely transcending the dimension of nothingness, enters and dwells in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He is said to have blinded Māra, bhikkhus … to the Evil One.
translations.mn26:5: There are these two quests, bhikkhus— the noble quest and the ignoble quest. And what, bhikkhus, is the ignoble quest? Here, bhikkhus, someone who is subject to birth seeks what is subject to birth; being subject to aging, he seeks what is subject to aging; being subject to illness, he seeks what is subject to illness; being subject to death, he seeks what is subject to death; being subject to sorrow, he seeks what is subject to sorrow; being subject to defilement, he seeks what is subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, bhikkhus, is subject to birth? A wife and children are subject to birth, servants are subject to birth, goats and sheep are subject to birth, chickens and pigs are subject to birth, elephants, cattle, horses, and mules are subject to birth, gold and silver are subject to birth. These, bhikkhus, are conditions subject to birth. Here, one who is himself subject to birth, seeks what is subject to birth, deluded, confused, deeply immersed.
translations.mn27:12: A householder or householder’s son, or someone reborn in some other family, hears that Dhamma. Hearing that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Endowed with that faith, he reflects thus: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; the life of one gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?’ Then, after some time, having abandoned a small fortune or a large fortune, having abandoned a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on ochre robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having gone forth in this way, having completed the training and livelihood of monks, he abstains from killing living beings, laying aside the rod and the sword, he dwells restrained, full of pity, compassionate toward all living beings. He abstains from taking what is not given, refraining from theft; he is one who takes only what is given, expecting only what is given. He dwells with purity thus attained. He abstains from unchastity and lives the holy life, abstinent, far removed from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse. He abstains from false speech, refraining from falsehood; he is truthful, reliable, not deceptive among people. He abstains from divisive speech, refraining from speech that divides; having heard something here, he does not repeat it there to cause division, and having heard something there, he does not repeat it here to cause division. Thus he is one who reunites those who are divided, a promoter of harmony, who delights in harmony, who speaks words that promote harmony. He abstains from harsh speech, refraining from harsh words; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, reaching the heart, courteous, agreeable to many, and pleasing to many. He abstains from idle chatter, refraining from frivolous talk; he speaks at the proper time, speaks truth, speaks on what is good, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the discipline; he speaks words that are worth remembering, timely, reasonable, concise, and meaningful. He abstains from injuring seeds and plants, eats only one meal a day, abstains from eating at the wrong time, abstains from dancing, singing, music, and watching shows, abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and applying cosmetics, abstains from high and large beds, abstains from accepting gold and silver, abstains from accepting raw grain, abstains from accepting raw meat, abstains from accepting women and girls, abstains from accepting male and female slaves, abstains from accepting goats and sheep, abstains from accepting chickens and pigs, abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mules, abstains from accepting fields and land, abstains from sending or engaging in messages, abstains from buying and selling, abstains from using false measures, weights, and scales, abstains from fraud, cheating, and deceit, abstains from mutilating, killing, binding, robbery, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with simple robes to protect the body and with almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these things with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies only with its wings as its burden; so too, the monk is content with simple robes to protect the body and with almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these things with him. Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.
translations.mn27:15: When he sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp at signs or details. Whatever unwholesome, evil states of longing and dejection might arise in one who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained—toward the prevention of such states he practices restraint, he guards the eye faculty, and achieves restraint over the eye faculty. Hearing a sound with the ear… smelling an odor with the nose… tasting a flavor with the tongue… touching a tangible with the body… cognizing a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at signs or details. Whatever unwholesome, evil states of longing and dejection might arise in one who dwells with the mind faculty unrestrained—toward the prevention of such states he practices restraint, he guards the mind faculty, and achieves restraint over the mind faculty. Endowed with this noble restraint over the faculties, he experiences within himself an unpolluted happiness.
translations.mn27:16: He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning, when looking ahead and looking away, when bending and extending the limbs, when wearing robes and carrying the bowl, when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, when defecating and urinating, when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
translations.mn27:17: Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment, endowed with this noble restraint over the faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to secluded dwellings: the wilderness, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a rocky cave, a charnel ground, a forest, an open space, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: Having returned from his almsround after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, straightening his body, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Abandoning greed for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning dullness and drowsiness, he dwells free from dullness and drowsiness, mindful and clearly comprehending, perceiving light; he purifies his mind from dullness and drowsiness. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells without restlessness, with a mind inwardly tranquil; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells with doubt cut off, free from perplexity, confident and assured in skillful qualities; he purifies his mind from doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, mental defilements that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness. This too, Brahmin, is called the path of the Tathāgata, frequented by the Tathāgata, cherished by the Tathāgata. Yet even so, the noble disciple does not yet reach the goal: ‘The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well.’
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus!' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was leaving Sāvatthī in a large carriage drawn by mules during the midday heat. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the wanderer Pilotika: 'Now, from where, reverend sir, does Venerable Vacchāyana come during this midday heat?' 'I come from the presence of the ascetic Gotama, sir.' 'What does Venerable Vacchāyana think? Does he regard the ascetic Gotama as wise and learned?' 'How could I, sir, know whether the ascetic Gotama is wise and learned? Only one like him could know the wisdom and learning of the ascetic Gotama.' 'Indeed, Venerable Vacchāyana greatly praises the ascetic Gotama.' 'How could I, sir, praise the ascetic Gotama? The ascetic Gotama is supreme among gods and humans, praiseworthy and blameless.' 'But, Venerable Vacchāyana, seeing what benefit are you so devoted to the ascetic Gotama?'
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly aware, experiencing pleasure with the body, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'One who is equanimous and mindful, dwelling in pleasure.' This too is called, brahmin ... the community of the Blessed One's disciples who are well-practiced.
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of thought and examination, attains inner confidence, unification of mind, without thought or examination, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna. This too is called, brahmin ... the community of the Blessed One's disciples who are well-practiced.
translations.mn27:3: 'Just as, sir, a skilled elephant-trainer might enter an elephant forest and see in the forest a large elephant footprint, long and wide. He would conclude: 'Indeed, this must be a great elephant.' So too, sir, when I saw in the ascetic Gotama these four footprints, then I came to certainty: 'The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the community of the Blessed One's disciples is well-practiced.'
translations.mn27:4: What are the four? Here, sir, I see some warrior-scholars, skilled in debate, like sharp weapons, wandering about, breaking through wrong views with their wisdom. They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama will arrive at such-and-such village or town.' They prepare a question: 'We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If he answers thus, we will argue in this way. If he answers otherwise, we will argue in that way.' They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama has arrived at such-and-such village or town.' They go to the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, encourages, inspires, and gladdens them with a Dhamma talk. When instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a Dhamma talk, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama their question, much less argue with him. Rather, they become disciples of the ascetic Gotama. When I, sir, saw in the ascetic Gotama this first footprint, then I came to certainty: 'The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the community of the Blessed One's disciples is well-practiced.'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to the Blessed One. Approaching him, he exchanged greetings. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Seated, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the wanderer Pilotika. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: 'Brahmin, the elephant footprint simile is not yet fully expanded in detail. But, brahmin, I will explain how the elephant footprint simile is fully expanded. Listen, pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, with purity of mindfulness and equanimity. This too is called, brahmin, the footprint of the Tathāgata, the resort of the Tathāgata, the dwelling of the Tathāgata. Yet even so, the noble disciple does not yet reach certainty: 'The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the community of the Blessed One's disciples is well-practiced.'
translations.mn28:10: If, friend, a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, and equanimity rooted in skillfulness does not become established, he becomes agitated and experiences distress: 'Indeed, I am without gain; indeed, I have no gain; indeed, I have obtained what is hard to obtain, yet equanimity rooted in skillfulness does not become established in me when I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way.' Just as, friend, a female slave seeing her master becomes agitated and distressed; so too, friend, if a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, and equanimity rooted in skillfulness does not become established, he becomes agitated and experiences distress: 'Indeed, I am without gain; indeed, I have no gain; indeed, I have obtained what is hard to obtain, yet equanimity rooted in skillfulness does not become established in me when I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way.' But if, friend, a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, and equanimity rooted in skillfulness becomes established, he is satisfied thereby. Even so much, friend, is already a great accomplishment for a bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element becomes agitated. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friend, when in the great ocean the waters recede hundreds of leagues, two hundred leagues, three hundred leagues, four hundred leagues, five hundred leagues, six hundred leagues, seven hundred leagues. There comes a time, friend, when in the great ocean the water stands seven palm-trees high, six palm-trees, five, four, three, two, or just one palm-tree in height. There comes a time, friend, when in the great ocean the water stands seven men high, six men, five, four, three, two, or just one man in height. There comes a time, friend, when in the great ocean the water stands half a man high, waist-high, knee-high, or ankle-high. There comes a time, friend, when in the great ocean there is not even as much water as would fill the hollow of a hand. For, indeed, friend, the impermanence, the tendency to decay, the tendency to decline, and the tendency to change in the external water element will thus become manifest.
translations.mn28:13: What then, for this short-lived body sustained by craving, could be 'I am,' 'mine,' or 'I exist'?
translations.mn28:14: If, friend, a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, and equanimity rooted in skillfulness becomes established, he is satisfied thereby.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friend, when the external fire element becomes agitated. It burns villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. It burns until it reaches a place devoid of fuel—whether green or dry land, rocky ground, or water, or a pleasant stretch of countryside—then it goes out for lack of fuel. There comes a time, friend, when people seek fire even from a hen's foot or the dung of a young calf. For, indeed, friend, the impermanence, the tendency to decay, the tendency to decline, and the tendency to change in the external fire element will thus become manifest. What then, for this short-lived body sustained by craving, could be 'I am,' 'mine,' or 'I exist'?
translations.mn28:18-20: Then indeed, he does not exist there ... If, friend, a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, and equanimity rooted in skillfulness becomes established, he is satisfied thereby. Even so much, friend, is already a great accomplishment for a bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:2: Just as, friend, whatever footprints of living beings there are, all those come together in the elephant's footprint, and the elephant's footprint is declared supreme among them because of its great size; so too, friend, all wholesome qualities are included in the Four Noble Truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friend, when the external air element becomes agitated. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friend, when in the last month of summer people seek wind even under palm trees or in the shade, and they do not even desire to see grass. For, indeed, friend, the impermanence, the tendency to decay, the tendency to decline, and the tendency to change in the external air element will thus become manifest. What then, for this short-lived body sustained by craving, could be 'I am,' 'mine,' or 'I exist'? Then indeed, he does not exist there.
translations.mn28:23: If others speak harshly, revile, anger, or harass that bhikkhu, he understands thus: 'This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me. It is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.' He sees that contact is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. His mind, taking the elements as its object, moves forward, becomes confident, settled, and resolved.
translations.mn28:24: And if, friend, other people behave toward that bhikkhu in ways that are disagreeable, unpleasant, and disagreeable—by contact with hands, contact with stones, contact with sticks, or contact with knives—he understands thus: 'Such is this body; in this body contacts with hands occur, contacts with stones occur, contacts with sticks occur, contacts with knives occur. Yet the Blessed One has already said in the Simile of the Saw: “Even if, bhikkhus, bandits were to sever one limb at a time with a two-handled saw, one who gave rise to mental irritation on that account would not be practicing my teaching.” My energy will be aroused and unsluggish, mindfulness established and unmuddled, body tranquil and unexcited, mind collected and unified. Now let contacts with hands occur in this body, let contacts with stones occur, let contacts with sticks occur, let contacts with knives occur. This is how the teaching of the Buddhas is to be honored.'
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friend, space enclosed by wood, vine, grass, and clay is called a hut; so too, friend, space enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin is called material form.
translations.mn28:27: If, friend, the internal eye is intact but external forms do not come into range, and there is no corresponding mental engagement, then the manifestation of that corresponding consciousness does not occur. If, friend, the internal eye is intact and external forms come into range, but there is no corresponding mental engagement, then the manifestation of that corresponding consciousness does not occur. But when, friend, the internal eye is intact, external forms come into range, and there is corresponding mental engagement, then the manifestation of that corresponding consciousness occurs.
translations.mn28:28: Whatever material form there is of such a being, that is included in the aggregate of form as clinging; whatever feeling, that is included in the aggregate of feeling as clinging; whatever perception, that is included in the aggregate of perception as clinging; whatever mental formations, those are included in the aggregate of mental formations as clinging; whatever consciousness, that is included in the aggregate of consciousness as clinging. He understands thus: 'Thus indeed is the inclusion, the gathering, the coming together of these five aggregates subject to clinging. Yet the Blessed One has already said: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” For these five aggregates subject to clinging are dependently originated. The craving, attachment, inclination, and obsession with these five aggregates subject to clinging is the origin of suffering. The removal and abandonment of craving and lust for these five aggregates subject to clinging is the cessation of suffering.' So much, friend, is already sufficient for a bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friend, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. And what, friend, are the five aggregates subject to clinging? They are: the aggregate of form as clinging, the aggregate of feeling as clinging, the aggregate of perception as clinging, the aggregate of mental formations as clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness as clinging.
translations.mn28:37: If the internal mind is intact, but external phenomena do not come into range, and there is no corresponding mental engagement, then the manifestation of that corresponding consciousness does not occur.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element becomes agitated. At that time, the external earth element disappears. For, friend, the impermanence of the external earth element, its tendency to decay, to decline, and to change, will then become apparent. But what need would there be for such a tiny, craving-clung body to say 'I am' or 'mine' or 'I exist'? Indeed, it would not even exist there.
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, on Vulture's Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta's departure. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus in reference to Devadatta:
translations.mn29:3: Here, bhikkhus, a certain clansman, inspired by faith, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, thinking: 'I am oppressed by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am oppressed by suffering, surrounded by suffering. May the cessation of this entire mass of suffering be known!' Having gone forth in this way, he acquires gains, honor, and fame. But with those gains, honor, and fame, he is neither satisfied nor fulfilled. With those gains, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. With those gains, honor, and fame, he does not become intoxicated, heedless, or negligent. Remaining heedful, he strives for the perfection of virtue. With that perfection of virtue, he becomes satisfied and fulfilled. With that perfection of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others: 'I am virtuous, of good conduct; but these other bhikkhus are immoral, of bad conduct.' With that perfection of virtue, he becomes intoxicated, heedless, and negligent. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering. Just as, bhikkhus, a man seeking heartwood, desiring heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passing over the heartwood of a large tree, passing over the sapwood, cutting off the bark and outer layers, departs carrying them, thinking it is heartwood; and a clear-sighted man seeing him would say: 'Surely this good man does not know heartwood, does not know sapwood, does not know bark, does not know outer layers, does not know twigs and leaves. Just so this good man, seeking heartwood, desiring heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passing over the heartwood of a large tree, passing over the sapwood, cutting off the bark and outer layers, departs carrying them, thinking it is heartwood; yet he will not experience the benefit of heartwood.'
translations.mn2:10: And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena that should not be attended to, which one does not attend to? Those phenomena, bhikkhus, by which, when one attends to them, unarisen sensual taints arise, or arisen sensual taints increase; unarisen taints of existence arise, or arisen taints of existence increase; unarisen taints of ignorance arise, or arisen taints of ignorance increase—these are the phenomena that should not be attended to, which one does not attend to. And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena that should be attended to, which one attends to? Those phenomena, bhikkhus, by which, when one attends to them, unarisen sensual taints do not arise, or arisen sensual taints are abandoned; unarisen taints of existence do not arise, or arisen taints of existence are abandoned; unarisen taints of ignorance do not arise, or arisen taints of ignorance are abandoned—these are the phenomena that should be attended to, which one attends to. By not attending to those phenomena that should not be attended to, and by attending to those phenomena that should be attended to, unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: He wisely attends: 'This is suffering,' he wisely attends: 'This is the origin of suffering,' he wisely attends: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' he wisely attends: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' When he thus wisely attends, three fetters are abandoned: identity view, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals. These, bhikkhus, are called taints to be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Taints to be abandoned by restraint. And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells guarding the sense door of the eye after wisely reflecting. Those taints and afflictions that would arise in one who dwells unguarded in the sense door of the eye do not arise in one who dwells guarded in the sense door of the eye. He dwells guarding the sense door of the ear after wisely reflecting ... the nose ... the tongue ... the body ... the mind after wisely reflecting. Those taints and afflictions that would arise in one who dwells unguarded in the sense door of the mind do not arise in one who dwells guarded in the sense door of the mind. Those taints and afflictions that would arise in one who dwells unrestrained do not arise in one who dwells restrained. These, bhikkhus, are called taints to be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: He wisely reflects and uses almsfood: 'Not for fun, not for indulgence, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the support and maintenance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thus: I will restrain old feelings and not arouse new feelings, and I will be healthy, blameless, and live in comfort.'
translations.mn2:16: He wisely reflects and uses medicinal requisites for the sick: 'Only for the endurance of arisen bodily afflictions, for maximum freedom from discomfort.'
translations.mn2:17: Those taints and afflictions that would arise in one who does not use them would not arise in one who uses them. These, bhikkhus, are called taints to be abandoned by use.
translations.mn2:3: "It is by knowing and seeing, bhikkhus, that I declare the destruction of taints, not without knowing, not without seeing. And what, bhikkhus, do I know and see when I declare the destruction of taints? Wise attention and unwise attention. When one attends unwise, bhikkhus, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase; but when one attends wisely, bhikkhus, unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena that should not be attended to, which one attends to? Those phenomena, bhikkhus, by which, when one attends to them, unarisen sensual taints arise, or arisen sensual taints increase; unarisen taints of existence arise, or arisen taints of existence increase; unarisen taints of ignorance arise, or arisen taints of ignorance increase—these are the phenomena that should not be attended to, which one attends to. And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena that should be attended to, which one does not attend to? Those phenomena, bhikkhus, by which, when one attends to them, unarisen sensual taints do not arise, or arisen sensual taints are abandoned; unarisen taints of existence do not arise, or arisen taints of existence are abandoned; unarisen taints of ignorance do not arise, or arisen taints of ignorance are abandoned—these are the phenomena that should be attended to, which one does not attend to.
translations.mn2:7: By attending to those phenomena that should not be attended to, and by not attending to those phenomena that should be attended to, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase. He thus attends unwisely: 'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?' Or he is now internally in doubt about the present: 'Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go?'
translations.mn2:8: When that person pays attention unwisely, one of the six views arises: 'I have a self'—this view arises in them as true and accurate; or 'I have no self'—this view arises in them as true and accurate; or 'I perceive self by means of self'—this view arises in them as true and accurate; or 'I perceive what is not self by means of self'—this view arises in them as true and accurate; or 'I perceive self by means of what is not self'—this view arises in them as true and accurate; or else they have this view: 'This self of mine, the speaker, the experiencer, who here and there experiences the results of good and bad deeds, is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will endure forever just like that.' This is called, bhikkhus, the mass of views, the grasping of views, the jungle of views, the tangle of views, the agitation of views, the fetter of views. Bound by the fetter of views, bhikkhus, the unlearned worldling does not gain release from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; 'he does not gain release from suffering,' I say.
translations.mn2:9: And, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple—who sees the noble ones, skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who sees the good persons, skilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, well-trained in the Dhamma of the good persons—clearly understands which phenomena are fit to be attended to and which are unfit to be attended to. Understanding which phenomena are fit to be attended to and which are unfit to be attended to, he does not attend mentally to those phenomena that are unfit to be attended to, and he does attend mentally to those phenomena that are fit to be attended to.
translations.mn31:10: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But do you, Anuruddha, being heedful, ardent, and resolute, attain to a higher human quality, a noble distinction in knowledge and vision, a peaceful abiding?” “What should there be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, we attain and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, as far as we wish. This, venerable sir, is the higher human quality, the noble distinction in knowledge and vision, the peaceful abiding attained by us while being heedful, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.mn31:11-13: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, do you attain to another higher human quality, a noble distinction in knowledge and vision, a peaceful abiding?” “What should there be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, we attain and dwell in the second jhāna, which is without thought and examination, with internal confidence and unification of mind, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure, as far as we wish. Beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, this other higher human quality, noble distinction in knowledge and vision, peaceful abiding is attained by us.”
translations.mn31:14: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, do you attain to another higher human quality, a noble distinction in knowledge and vision, a peaceful abiding?” “What should there be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, we dwell with detachment from rapture, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing pleasure with the body, having entered the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘One who is equanimous and mindful, dwelling happily.’ As far as we wish, we attain and dwell in the third jhāna. Beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, this other higher human quality, noble distinction in knowledge and vision, peaceful abiding is attained by us.”
translations.mn31:15: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, do you attain to another higher human quality, a noble distinction in knowledge and vision, a peaceful abiding?” “What should there be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, we attain and dwell in the fourth jhāna, beyond pleasure and pain, with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, neither painful nor pleasant, with purity of mindfulness and equanimity, as far as we wish. Beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, this other higher human quality, noble distinction in knowledge and vision, peaceful abiding is attained by us.”
translations.mn31:16: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, do you attain to another higher human quality, a noble distinction in knowledge and vision, a peaceful abiding?” “What should there be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, we attain and dwell in the dimension of infinite space, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking: ‘Infinite is space,’ as far as we wish. Beyond this abiding, beyond the stilling of this abiding, this other higher human quality, noble distinction in knowledge and vision, peaceful abiding is attained by us.”
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove.
translations.mn31:3: Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from seclusion and approached the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove. The park-keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar and, on seeing him, said to the Blessed One: “Do not enter this park, ascetic. There are three sons of good families dwelling here, enjoying themselves. Do not disturb their peaceful abiding.”
translations.mn31:4: The Venerable Anuruddha heard the park-keeper speaking with the Blessed One. Hearing him, he said to the park-keeper: “Do not stop the Blessed One, friend park-keeper. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then the Venerable Anuruddha went to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila, and said to them: “Come, venerable ones, come, venerable ones, our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”
translations.mn31:5: Then Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One. One received the Blessed One's alms bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one brought water for the feet. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Then those venerable ones paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Venerable Anuruddha, seated to one side: "Is it comfortable for you, Anuruddha? Is it bearable? And are you not wearying from going for alms?"
translations.mn31:6: "Are you, Anuruddha, living in harmony, cordial, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, regarding one another with kindly eyes?" "Indeed, sir, we live in harmony, cordial, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, regarding one another with kindly eyes." "But how, Anuruddha, do you live in harmony, cordial, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, regarding one another with kindly eyes?"
translations.mn31:9: "Indeed, sir, we dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute." "But how, Anuruddha, do you dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute?" "Here, sir, whichever of us returns first from the village on alms-round prepares the seats, brings water for drinking and washing, and places the chamber pot. Whichever returns later, if there is any leftover food and he wishes, he eats; if he does not wish, he either leaves it where it is or pours it into water where there are no living beings. Then he puts away the seats, removes the drinking and washing water, removes the chamber pot, and sweeps the dining area. Whoever sees a water pot, a food container, or a spittoon empty and useless, fills it. If it is too heavy, he calls another with a gesture and they carry it together using both hands, but we never, sir, break into speech because of fatigue. For five hours, sir, we spend the entire night in Dhamma discussion. Thus, sir, we dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute."
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: "I am truly confident in Master Gotama. For Master Gotama is one with developed body and developed mind."
translations.mn36:12: "What else could it be, Aggivessana? Here, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: 'Household life is crowded and dusty; the life of a renunciant is open and free. It is not easy, living in a house, to lead a holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?'"
translations.mn36:2: At that time, the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his outer robe and, taking his bowl and robes, was about to enter Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: "Then this thought occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Suppose I were to clench my teeth, press my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and with my mind restrain, suppress, and overwhelm my mind?' So I, Aggivessana, clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and with my mind restrained, suppressed, and overwhelmed my mind. While I was doing so, Aggivessana, sweat came out from my armpits. Just as a strong man might grasp a weaker man by the head or shoulders and restrain, suppress, and overwhelm him; so too, Aggivessana, while I was clenching my teeth, pressing my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and with my mind restraining, suppressing, and overwhelming my mind, sweat came out from my armpits. Yet my energy was roused and unrelaxed, mindfulness was established and unmuddled, and my body was aroused but untranquil, due to the predominance of pain from such striving. Still, even such painful feelings as arose did not obsess my mind."
translations.mn36:26: Some devas, seeing me, said: 'The ascetic Gotama is dead.' Some said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.' Some said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying; he is an arahant, and this is the way an arahant dwells.'
translations.mn36:27: "Then this thought occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Suppose I were to practice complete abstinence from food?' Then, Aggivessana, some devas approached me and said: 'Do not, good sir, practice complete abstinence from food. If you do, we will pour divine energy into you through your pores, and you will survive on that.' Then this thought occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'If I were to accept complete fasting, and these devas were to pour divine energy into me through my pores, and I were to survive on that, it would be a falsehood for me.' So I, Aggivessana, rejected those devas, saying, 'Leave.'
translations.mn36:30: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced severe, sharp, and painful feelings due to self-mortification, this was the utmost; there was nothing beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience such feelings, this will be the utmost; there will be nothing beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins now experience such feelings, this is the utmost; there is nothing beyond this. Yet, by means of this severe self-mortification, I do not attain the superhuman states, the special knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there perhaps be another path to enlightenment?'
translations.mn36:28: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Why don't I eat only a little food at a time, just a small amount—perhaps a few beans, lentils, or chickpeas, or even vetch?' So I, Aggivessana, ate only a little food at a time, just a small amount—perhaps a few beans, lentils, chickpeas, or vetch. As I thus ate only a little food, my body became extremely emaciated. My limbs became like the jointed segments of vine or bamboo; my buttocks like a camel's hoof; my spine protruding like a string of beads; my ribs, gaunt and jutting, like the rafters of a dilapidated shed; my eyes, sunk deep in their sockets, like water reflections at the bottom of a deep well; my scalp shriveled and withered like a green gourd dried by wind and sun. When I wished to touch my belly skin, I grasped my spine; when I wished to touch my spine, I grasped my belly skin, so closely had my skin clung to my bones due to such minimal nourishment. When I wished to pass urine or excrement, I collapsed right there due to such minimal nourishment. As I breathed in and out, I felt my bones rubbing against each other. Due to such minimal nourishment, my body hair, rotted at the roots, fell off my body.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son, pacing back and forth, walking up and down, approached the Great Wood, to the hall with the pointed roof. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: 'Here comes Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son, a boastful speaker, one who prides himself on his wisdom, praised and esteemed by many. This one, sir, seeks to disparage the Buddha, disparage the Dhamma, disparage the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One, out of compassion, sit for a moment.' The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after the exchange of courteous and amiable talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was the first knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night: ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—just as it should for a diligent, ardent, and self-resolute one. Even such pleasant feelings that arose did not invade my mind.
translations.mn36:32: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Why should I fear that pleasure which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?' It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'I should not fear that pleasure which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.'
translations.mn36:38: With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfections, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected my many past abodes, with their aspects and details: one birth, two births... many births... thus with their details and characteristics, I recollected my various past abodes.
translations.mn36:34: So, Aggivessana, having taken coarse food and gained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, with thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Even such pleasant feelings that arose did not invade my mind.
translations.mn36:29: Some people, Aggivessana, seeing me, would say: 'Gotama the ascetic is black.' Some people would say: 'Gotama the ascetic is not black, he is blue-black.' Some people would say: 'Gotama the ascetic is neither black nor blue-black, but his skin is the color of a bruise.' So thoroughly emaciated, Aggivessana, was my body, so purified, so transparent, so wasted, due to such minimal nourishment.
translations.mn36:4: There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who devote themselves to the development of the body, not to the development of the mind. They, Master Gotama, experience bodily pain and suffering. It has happened before, Master Gotama, that one struck by severe bodily pain remains mindful, yet his body may become rigid like a log, his heart may burst, blood may gush from his mouth, and he may fall into madness or mental confusion. For him, Master Gotama, the mind is subject to the body, governed by the body's condition. Why is that? Because the mind has not been developed. But there are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who devote themselves to the development of the mind, not to the development of the body. They, Master Gotama, experience mental pain and suffering. It has happened before, Master Gotama, that one struck by severe mental pain remains mindful, yet his body may become rigid like a log, his heart may burst, blood may gush from his mouth, and he may fall into madness or mental confusion. For him, Master Gotama, the body is subject to the mind, governed by the mind's condition. Why is that? Because the body has not been developed. To me, Master Gotama, it occurs: 'Surely the disciples of Master Gotama devote themselves to the development of the mind, not to the development of the body.'
translations.mn36:40: With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, according to their actions...
translations.mn36:42: With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew as it actually is: 'This is suffering,' 'This is the origin of suffering,' 'This is the cessation of suffering,' 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' I directly knew as it actually is: 'These are the taints,' 'This is the origin of the taints,' 'This is the cessation of the taints,' 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.'
translations.mn36:43: With such knowledge and vision, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there came the knowledge: 'Liberated.' I directly knew: 'Destroyed is birth, lived is the holy life, done is what had to be done, there is no more of this state of being.'
translations.mn36:45: I do indeed, Aggivessana, know that I teach the Dhamma to countless assemblies. Yet someone might think: 'The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma only concerning me.' But that, Aggivessana, should not be regarded in that way; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others solely for the purpose of making it known. And I, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, in that same earlier state of concentration as my object, internally compose and settle my mind, unify and concentrate it, so that I dwell quite secluded.
translations.mn36:46: "I do know, Aggivessana, that in the last month of the hot season, after returning from almsround in the afternoon, I spread out the fourfold folded robe, lay down on my right side in the lion's posture, mindful and fully aware, and fell asleep." "But, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins would say this is a state of delusion," "Aggivessana, one is not therefore deluded or undeluded just by that. But, Aggivessana, whether one is deluded or undeluded, listen well, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, sir," Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son replied. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn36:47: "Whoever, Aggivessana, has not abandoned the taints that defile, lead to renewed existence, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—I call such a one deluded. For, Aggivessana, because of the taints not being abandoned, one is deluded. Whoever, Aggivessana, has abandoned the taints that defile, lead to renewed existence, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—I call such a one undeluded. For, Aggivessana, because of the taints being abandoned, one is undeluded. For the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that defile, lead to renewed existence, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, their roots destroyed, like a palm stump cut off, no longer subject to arising in the future. Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree with its crown cut off can never grow again; so too, Aggivessana, for the Tathāgata the taints that defile, lead to renewed existence, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, their roots destroyed, like a palm stump cut off, no longer subject to arising in the future."
translations.mn36:5: "But, Aggivessana, have you heard of the practice of bodily development?" "Such as Nanda the bull, Kisa Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla—these naked ascetics, of loose conduct, refusing to accept alms handed directly, not accepting food from a pot, from a pan, from between two mortars, from where a pestle is, from where two are eating, from a pregnant woman, from a nursing woman, from a woman living with a man, not accepting food invited, not accepting food from where a dog is present, not accepting food where flies swarm, not eating fish, not eating meat, not drinking alcohol or fermented liquor or water that has been stood overnight. They are one-meal-eaters, or two-meal-eaters... up to seven-meal-eaters. They live on one gift, or two gifts... up to seven gifts. They eat one-day-old food, or two-day-old food... up to seven-day-old food. Thus they dwell devoted to a regimen of periodic eating, up to half a month."
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is the body developed and the mind developed? Here, Aggivessana, a well-instructed noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not become lustful or obsessed with pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, he does not grieve, lament, or weep, nor does he fall into confusion. For him, Aggivessana, even when a pleasant feeling has arisen, the mind does not become overwhelmed due to the development of the body; even when a painful feeling has arisen, the mind does not become overwhelmed due to the development of the mind. Whoever, Aggivessana, has both these aspects so developed that even when a pleasant feeling has arisen the mind does not become overwhelmed due to the development of the body, and even when a painful feeling has arisen the mind does not become overwhelmed due to the development of the mind—this, Aggivessana, is how one has a developed body and a developed mind.
translations.mn38:15: These four, bhikkhus, are the nutriments for the sustenance of beings that already exist, and for the support of those seeking birth. What four? Coarse or fine material food as the first, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth.
translations.mn38:19: "Good, bhikkhus. Thus, bhikkhus, you should also say, and I also say—when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus comes the entire mass of suffering into being."
translations.mn38:13: "Is it true, bhikkhus, that what exists is rightly seen with correct wisdom as it actually is?" "Yes, sir." "Is it true, bhikkhus, that the nutriment by which it arises is rightly seen with correct wisdom as it actually is?" "Yes, sir." "Is it true, bhikkhus, that the cessation of what exists, due to the cessation of that nutriment, is rightly seen with correct wisdom as it actually is?" "Yes, sir."
translations.mn36:8: And how, Aggivessana, is the body undeveloped and the mind undeveloped? Here, Aggivessana, an unlearned ordinary person experiences a pleasant feeling. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, he becomes lustful and falls into attachment to pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, he grieves, laments, weeps, beats his breast, and falls into confusion. For him, Aggivessana, when a pleasant feeling has arisen, the mind becomes overwhelmed due to the undeveloped body; when a painful feeling has arisen, the mind becomes overwhelmed due to the undeveloped mind. Whoever, Aggivessana, has both these aspects so undeveloped that when a pleasant feeling has arisen the mind becomes overwhelmed due to the undeveloped body, and when a painful feeling has arisen the mind becomes overwhelmed due to the undeveloped mind—this, Aggivessana, is how one has an undeveloped body and an undeveloped mind.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus comes the entire mass of suffering into being.
translations.mn38:10: "If, bhikkhus, one does not know this that exists, does doubt arise from uncertainty?" "Yes, sir." "If, bhikkhus, one does not know the nutriment by which it arises, does doubt arise from uncertainty?" "Yes, sir." "If, bhikkhus, one does not know the cessation of what exists, due to the cessation of that nutriment, does doubt arise from uncertainty?" "Yes, sir."
translations.mn38:14: "If you, bhikkhus, were to grasp, cling to, grasp as mine, and regard as self this view so purified and so clear, would you understand my teaching, given as a simile of a raft, as for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?" "No, sir." "If you, bhikkhus, do not grasp, do not cling, do not grasp as mine, and do not regard as self this view so purified and so clear, would you understand my teaching, given as a simile of a raft, as for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?" "Yes, sir."
translations.mn36:6: "But what, Aggivessana, do you achieve with that alone?" "Not much, indeed, Gotama. Sometimes, Gotama, they eat large amounts of food, consume large amounts of meals, recline on large luxurious couches, drink large quantities of beverages. They claim strength, speak of strength, boast of strength." "Aggivessana, what you abandon in the past and accumulate later causes increase and decrease in this body. But, Aggivessana, have you heard of mental development?" When questioned by the Blessed One about mental development, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son did not respond.
translations.mn38:12: "Is it true, bhikkhus, that for you there is no doubt here regarding what exists?" "Yes, sir." "Is it true, bhikkhus, that for you there is no doubt here regarding the nutriment by which it arises?" "Yes, sir." "Is it true, bhikkhus, that for you there is no doubt here regarding the cessation of what exists, due to the cessation of that nutriment?" "Yes, sir."
translations.mn38:11: "Is it true, bhikkhus, that when one sees what exists as it actually is with correct wisdom, doubt is abandoned?" "Yes, sir." "Is it true, bhikkhus, that when one sees the nutriment by which it arises as it actually is with correct wisdom, doubt is abandoned?" "Yes, sir." "Is it true, bhikkhus, that when one sees the cessation of what exists, due to the cessation of that nutriment, as it actually is with correct wisdom, doubt is abandoned?" "Yes, sir."
translations.mn38:2: At that time, a bhikkhu named Sāti, the son of a Keṇṭaka, had arisen with this harmful view: 'Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: it is this very consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, not another.'
translations.mn38:20: With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all cease. Thus is there the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: "Well said, bhikkhus. Indeed, bhikkhus, you should speak in this way, and I also speak thus: when this is not, that does not exist; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is, with the cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all cease. Thus is there the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:23: "Would you, bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, run after the past: 'Were we in the past? Were we not in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?'" "No, sir." "Would you, bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, run after the future: 'Shall we be in the future? Shall we not be in the future? What shall we be in the future? How shall we be in the future? Having been what, what shall we become in the future?'" "No, sir."
translations.mn38:25: "Well said, bhikkhus. I have brought you, bhikkhus, to this Dhamma that is evident, immediate, inviting one to come and see, effective, to be personally experienced by the wise. This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is evident, immediate, inviting one to come and see, effective, to be personally experienced by the wise—such is the meaning of what was said, and this is why it was said.
translations.mn38:26: There is, bhikkhus, the concurrence of three things for the descent of the embryo. Here, if the mother and father come together, but the mother is not in season and the being to be reborn does not present itself, then there is no descent of the embryo. Here, if the mother and father come together, the mother is in season, but the being to be reborn does not present itself, then there is no descent of the embryo. But when, bhikkhus, the mother and father come together, the mother is in season, and the being to be reborn presents itself—then with the concurrence of these three things, the descent of the embryo occurs.
translations.mn38:27: That embryo, bhikkhus, the mother carries in her womb for nine or ten months, with great care and heavy burden. At the end of nine or ten months, she gives birth, with great care and heavy burden. When born, the child is nourished by her own blood. That blood, bhikkhus, in the Noble One's discipline, is called mother's milk.
translations.mn38:28: Then, bhikkhus, as the boy grows and his faculties mature, he plays with such toys as are fit for boys, such as a toy plough, a toy pot, a toy winnowing basket, a toy cart, a toy bow.
translations.mn38:39: He, having abandoned these five hindrances, mental defilements that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, accompanied by rapture and pleasure. Furthermore, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu, with the stilling of thought and examination, attains internal confidence and unification of mind, without thought and examination, born of concentration, and enters and dwells in the second jhāna… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna.
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "What do you think, bhikkhus, can this bhikkhu Sāti, the Keṇṭaka's son, be considered as having any standing in this Dhamma and discipline?" "How could he, sir? No, sir." When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, the Keṇṭaka's son, became silent, ashamed, crestfallen, with downcast eyes, brooding, without a reply, and sat there. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the bhikkhu Sāti, the Keṇṭaka's son, was silent, ashamed, crestfallen, with downcast eyes, brooding, without a reply, said to the bhikkhu Sāti, the Keṇṭaka's son: "You will come to understand, foolish man, the consequences of this evil view of yours. I will now question the bhikkhus."
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Do you too, bhikkhus, understand the Dhamma as I have taught it in the same way as this bhikkhu Sāti, the Keṇṭaka's son, who, having wrongly grasped it, misrepresents us, harms himself, and accumulates much demerit?" "No, sir. For, sir, the Blessed One has explained consciousness as dependently arisen in many ways; there is no arising of consciousness without conditions." "Good, good, bhikkhus. It is good that you understand the Dhamma I have taught in this way. For, bhikkhus, I have explained consciousness as dependently arisen in many ways; there is no arising of consciousness without conditions. But this bhikkhu Sāti, the Keṇṭaka's son, having wrongly grasped it, misrepresents us, harms himself, and accumulates much demerit. This will lead that foolish man to harm and suffering for a long time."
translations.mn38:9: Do you see, bhikkhus, that it is real?” – “Yes, venerable sir.” – “Do you see, bhikkhus, that it arises dependent on nutriment?” – “Yes, venerable sir.” – “Do you see, bhikkhus, that when nutriment ceases, the real thing ceases, being subject to cessation?” – “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large community of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a Brahmin village of the Kosalans named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householder, does one transgress the Dhamma and live wrongly with the mind? Here, householder, someone is covetous; he covets the wealth of others: 'Oh, that what belongs to others might be mine!' He has a mind filled with ill will and evil intentions: 'May these beings be slain or destroyed or cut off or perish, or may they not exist at all!' He holds wrong view, distorted perception: 'There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves and proclaim this world and the next.' Thus, householder, one transgresses the Dhamma and lives wrongly with the mind. Because of such transgression of Dhamma and wrong conduct, householder, some beings after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householder, does one practice the Dhamma and live rightly with the body? Here, householder, someone, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from killing; he lays down the rod, lays down the weapon; he is conscientious, full of compassion, and lives sympathizing with the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned stealing, he abstains from taking what is not given; whatever belongs to others, in the village or in the forest, he does not take it as stolen property. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from improper sexual behavior; he does not engage in sexual intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, clan, Dhamma, or who are married, guarded by a penalty, or even adorned with a garland as a sign. Thus, householder, one practices the Dhamma and lives rightly with the body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householder, does one practice the Dhamma and live rightly with speech? Here, householder, someone, having abandoned false speech, abstains from lying. When brought before a court, assembly, family gathering, group, or royal court, and questioned as a witness, saying: 'Come, good man, say what you know,' he speaks falsely if he knows nothing, saying: 'I don’t know'; if he knows, he says: 'I know'; if he hasn’t seen, he says: 'I haven’t seen'; if he has seen, he says: 'I have seen.' Thus, for the sake of oneself, others, or for a trivial gain, he does not speak deliberate falsehood. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive talk; having heard something in one place, he does not repeat it elsewhere to break those apart; having heard something elsewhere, he does not repeat it to these people to break them apart. Thus he is one who reunites those divided, a promoter of harmony, who enjoys harmony, delights in harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh language; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, reaching the heart, courteous, desired by many, and agreeable to many. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from pointless talk; he speaks at the right time, speaks truth, speaks meaning, speaks Dhamma, speaks about discipline; he speaks words worth remembering, timely, reasonable, concise, and beneficial. Thus, householder, one practices the Dhamma and lives rightly with speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householder, does one practice the Dhamma and live rightly with the mind? Here, householder, someone is free from covetousness; he does not covet the wealth of others: 'Oh, that what belongs to others might be mine!' He is free from ill will, with pure mental intentions: 'May these beings be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress; may they live happily, taking care of themselves.' He has right view, correct perception: 'There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves and proclaim this world and the next.' Thus, householder, one practices the Dhamma and lives rightly with the mind. Because of such practice of Dhamma and right conduct, householder, some beings after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If a householder who practices the Dhamma and lives rightly wishes: 'Oh, that after death, when the body breaks up, I might be reborn among the great warrior nobles!'—this is possible; he may indeed be reborn among the great warrior nobles after death. Why is that? Because he practices the Dhamma and lives rightly.
translations.mn41:3: Then the Brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Blessed One; and on approaching, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after the courteous and amiable talk, sat down at one side; some raised their hands in salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some announced their name and clan to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some sat down at one side in silence. When they were seated at one side, the Brahmin householders of Sālā said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn41:4: "What, Master Gotama, is the reason, what is the cause, why some beings after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell? And what, Master Gotama, is the reason, what is the cause, why some beings after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world?"
translations.mn41:43: If, householder, one desires to be righteous and virtuous: 'Oh, that I might realize for myself, with direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and abide in it, having realized it in this very life!'—there is the possibility that one who is righteous and virtuous might realize, with direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and abide in it, having realized it in this very life. Why is that? Because such a one is righteous and virtuous.
translations.mn41:5: It is because of unrighteous and immoral conduct, householder, that some beings, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. It is because of righteous and moral conduct, householder, that some beings, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, even in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:6: We do not understand, sir, the meaning of this brief statement of the Blessed One, which has not been explained in detail. May the Blessed One please teach the Dhamma in such a way that we may understand the meaning of his brief statement, which has not been explained in detail.
translations.mn41:8: And how, householder, is there threefold bodily unrighteous and immoral conduct? Here, householder, someone is one who takes life, brutal and bloody-handed, devoted to killing and slaughter, showing no compassion to living beings. He is one who takes what is not given. Whatever belongs to another, whatever is another's property, in a village or in the wilderness, he takes it as stolen goods. He is one who engages in sexual misconduct. He has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, clan, Dhamma, or who are married, guarded by law, or even adorned with a garland of flowers. Thus, householder, there is threefold bodily unrighteous and immoral conduct.
translations.mn41:9: And how, householder, is there fourfold verbal unrighteous and immoral conduct? Here, householder, someone is one who speaks falsely. When brought before a group, an assembly, a family gathering, a clan gathering, or a royal court, and questioned as a witness: 'Come, good man, tell what you know,' he says, knowing nothing: 'I know,' or knowing, says: 'I don't know,' or not seeing, says: 'I see,' or seeing, says: 'I don't see.' Thus, speaking falsely deliberately, for his own sake, for another's sake, or for some trifling worldly reason. He is one who speaks divisively. Having heard something here, he repeats it elsewhere to cause division, or having heard something there, he repeats it here to cause division among people. Thus, he is a breaker of unity, a sower of discord, delighting in disputes, taking pleasure in conflict, and speaking words that create division. He is one who speaks harshly. He speaks words that are rough, harsh, cutting, offensive to others, provoking anger, and leading away from concentration. He is one who indulges in idle chatter. He speaks at the wrong time, speaks falsehoods, speaks what is useless, speaks contrary to the Dhamma and discipline, and speaks words that are meaningless, untimely, inappropriate, and unbeneficial. Thus, householder, there is fourfold verbal unrighteous and immoral conduct.
translations.mn4:20: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'Why don't I stay in those dwellings—on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight—that are known and noted, such as shrines in monasteries, shrines in forests, shrines under trees, haunted places, and places where wild animals dwell? Perhaps I might see that fear and dread.' Then, brahmin, at a later time, on those nights—on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight—I stayed in such dwellings: shrines in monasteries, shrines in forests, shrines under trees, haunted places, and places where wild animals dwell. And while I was dwelling there, brahmin, a path might appear, a peacock might drop a twig, or the wind might scatter dried leaves. Then it occurred to me: 'Is this that fear and dread coming?' Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'Why do I dwell depending on something else for fear? Why don't I face that fear and dread as it really is, just as it comes, and subdue it as it really is?' Then, brahmin, while I was walking back and forth, that fear and dread came. And I did not stop walking, nor did I sit down or lie down, until I had subdued that fear and dread while still walking. Then, brahmin, while I was standing, that fear and dread came. And I did not walk, nor did I sit down or lie down, until I had subdued that fear and dread while still standing. Then, brahmin, while I was sitting, that fear and dread came. And I did not lie down, nor did I stand up or walk, until I had subdued that fear and dread while still sitting. Then, brahmin, while I was lying down, that fear and dread came. And I did not sit up, nor did I stand up or walk, until I had subdued that fear and dread while still lying down.
translations.mn4:22-26: Indeed, brahmin, my energy was aroused and unsluggish, mindfulness was established and not confused, the body was calmed and not disturbed, and the mind was concentrated and unified. Then, brahmin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, I entered and dwelled in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, without thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelled equanimous, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing pleasure with the body, I entered and dwelled in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'One who is equanimous and mindful, dwelling happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, I entered and dwelled in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: With this mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed the mind to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected my many kinds of past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a complexion, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; then passing away from there, I was reborn here. Here I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a complexion, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; then passing away from here, I was reborn there.' Thus with their aspects and particulars, I recollected many past lives.
translations.mn4:28: This, brahmin, was the first knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night: ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—just as it should for a diligent, striving, and resolute person.
translations.mn4:29: With this mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed the mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood beings according to their actions: 'These worthy beings, who were endowed with bad bodily conduct, bad verbal conduct, and bad mental conduct, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view—after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the lower realms, hell.
