But these worthy beings, who were endowed with good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct, who did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view—after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood them according to their actions.
translations.mn4:3: Even before my enlightenment, while I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, this occurred to me, brahmin: 'Truly, the forest and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, are difficult to attain; seclusion is hard, solitude is unpleasant. I suppose the forests steal away the mind of a bhikkhu who has not attained concentration.'
translations.mn4:30: This, brahmin, was the second knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night: ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—just as it should for a diligent, striving, and resolute person.
translations.mn4:34: Perhaps this might occur to you, brahmin: 'Surely the ascetic Gotama is still not free from lust, hatred, and delusion, and that is why he frequents the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places.' But, brahmin, that should not be seen in that way. Seeing two reasons, brahmin, I frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places—seeing my own present happiness in dwelling, and out of compassion for future generations.'
translations.mn4:4: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'Any ascetics or brahmins who, with impure bodily conduct, frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, due to the taint of impure bodily conduct, those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, with impure bodily conduct; I am one of pure bodily conduct. Among those noble ones who, with pure bodily conduct, frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, I am one.' Seeing this purity of bodily conduct within myself, brahmin, I felt even greater enthusiasm for dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'Any ascetics or brahmins who, with impure verbal conduct... with impure mental conduct... with impure livelihood, frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, due to the taint of impure livelihood, those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience unwholesome fear and dread.'
translations.mn4:6: But I do not frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, with impure livelihood; I am one of pure livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: Among those noble ones who, with pure livelihood, frequent the forests and wilderness, the remote dwelling places, I am one.' Seeing this purity of livelihood within myself, brahmin, I felt even greater enthusiasm for dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Beluvagāma in Vesālī. At that time, Dasama the householder, a native of Aṭṭhakanāgara, had arrived in Pāṭaliputta on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a monk, completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite space. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the dimension of infinite space is conditioned and intentionally formed. Whatever is conditioned and intentionally formed is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He knows this. Standing firm there, he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a monk, completely transcending the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' enters and dwells in the dimension of nothingness. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the dimension of nothingness is conditioned and intentionally formed. Whatever is conditioned and intentionally formed is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He knows this. Standing firm there, he realizes the destruction of the taints. If he does not realize the destruction of the taints, then, with that very passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, he destroys the five lower fetters and is reborn spontaneously, there attaining final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is the one thing declared by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees, in which a heedful, ardent, and resolute monk, while dwelling, has his mind unliberated yet liberated, the taints not yet destroyed yet destroyed, and attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanagara said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Just as, venerable sir, a man seeking one treasure opening might discover eleven treasure openings; so too, venerable sir, I, seeking one door to the deathless, have obtained eleven doors to the deathless through meditation. Just as, venerable sir, a man's house has eleven doors, and if that house were on fire, he could save himself through any one of those doors; so too, venerable sir, through any one of these eleven doors to the deathless, I shall be able to save myself. Indeed, venerable sir, those of other sects will go seeking their teacher's fee; how then could I not honor the Venerable Ānanda?'
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanagara approached a certain monk at Kukkuṭārāma, and having approached, he paid homage to that monk and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanagara said to that monk: 'Where, venerable sir, is the Venerable Ānanda dwelling now? We wish to see him.' 'He, householder, the Venerable Ānanda, is dwelling in the village of Beluvagāmaka near Vesālī.'
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanagara, having finished his business in Pāṭaliputta, went to Vesālī, to the village of Beluvagāmaka, to the presence of the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanagara said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Is there, venerable sir Ānanda, one thing declared by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees, in which a heedful, ardent, and resolute monk, while dwelling, has his mind unliberated yet liberated, the taints not yet destroyed yet destroyed, and attains the unsurpassed security from bondage?' 'Yes, householder, there is one thing declared by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees, in which a heedful, ardent, and resolute monk, while dwelling, has his mind unliberated yet liberated, the taints not yet destroyed yet destroyed, and attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.' 'But what, venerable sir Ānanda, is that one thing declared by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees, in which a heedful, ardent, and resolute monk, while dwelling, has his mind unliberated yet liberated, the taints not yet destroyed yet destroyed, and attains the unsurpassed security from bondage?'
translations.mn52:4: Here, householder, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and happiness. He reflects thus: 'This first jhāna is conditioned and intentionally formed. Whatever is conditioned and intentionally formed is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He knows this. Standing firm there, he realizes the destruction of the taints. If he does not realize the destruction of the taints, then, with that very passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, he destroys the five lower fetters and is reborn spontaneously, there attaining final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is the one thing declared by the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees, in which a heedful, ardent, and resolute monk, while dwelling, has his mind unliberated yet liberated, the taints not yet destroyed yet destroyed, and attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a monk dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. So above, below, across, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects thus: 'This liberation of mind by loving-kindness is conditioned and intentionally formed. Whatever is conditioned and intentionally formed is impermanent, subject to cessation.' He knows this. Standing firm there, he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn54:18: Suppose, householder, there were a pit filled with glowing embers, full of live coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come along who wanted to live, not die, who desired happiness and recoiled from suffering. Two strong men would seize him by the arms and drag him toward the pit of embers. What do you think, householder, would that man twist and turn his body this way and that?” “Yes, sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, sir, I understand that this man would fall into that pit of embers, and as a result he would meet death or deadly pain.” “In just the same way, householder, the noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures are said by the Blessed One to be like a pit of embers, full of suffering, full of despair, and the danger here is even greater.’ Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, … he develops equanimity alone.
translations.mn54:23: Such a noble disciple, householder, having attained this unsurpassed purity of equanimity and mindfulness, with the divine eye, which is pure and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … and understands beings according to their deeds.
translations.mn54:24: Such a noble disciple, householder, having attained this unsurpassed purity of equanimity and mindfulness, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, right here and now, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells therein.
translations.mn60:10: Now, householder, those ascetics and brahmins who speak and hold such a view: ‘There is giving … there are those who declare this world and the next after realizing them for themselves’—one may expect of them that, having completely abandoned these three unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—they will undertake and practice these three wholesome states: good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, and good conduct by mind. Why is that? Because these venerable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, drawback, and defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit, purity, and advantage in wholesome states.
translations.mn60:12: Now, householder, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If there is another world, then this good man, upon the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Even if there is no other world, let these ascetics and brahmins speak the truth; still, this good man is praised in the present life by the wise: “A virtuous person, of right view, one who affirms the existence of merit.” If indeed there is another world, then this good man gains advantage in both respects: he is praised by the wise in this life, and upon the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this doctrine, well grasped and well undertaken, stands firm, encompassing both sides, and he abandons evil conduct.'
translations.mn60:13: There are, householder, some ascetics and brahmins who speak and hold such a view: ‘One who acts or causes others to act, one who cuts or causes others to cut, one who burns or causes others to burn, one who causes sorrow or causes others to cause sorrow, one who causes fatigue or causes others to cause fatigue, one who trembles or causes others to tremble, one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks up families, steals wealth, makes others celibate, stands in the way of others, commits adultery, or speaks falsely—by doing these things, one does no evil. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to turn all the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil from that, no coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the south bank of the Ganges slaughtering, killing, cutting, burning, and cooking, there would be no evil from that, no coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the north bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, and causing to sacrifice, there would be no merit from that, no coming of merit. By giving, self-control, restraint, and truthfulness, there is no merit, no coming of merit.’
translations.mn60:14: Among these very ascetics and brahmins, some ascetics and brahmins hold the opposite view; they say to them: ‘One who acts or causes others to act … one who speaks falsely—by doing these things, one does evil. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to turn all the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, there would be evil from that, there would be a coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the south bank of the Ganges slaughtering, killing, cutting, burning, and cooking, there would be evil from that, there would be a coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the north bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, and causing to sacrifice, there would be merit from that, there would be a coming of merit. By giving, self-control, restraint, and truthfulness, there is merit, there is a coming of merit.’ What do you think, householder, do these ascetics and brahmins hold mutually contradictory views?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn60:16: When action exists, yet one holds the view ‘there is no action,’ that is wrong view for him. When action exists, yet one intends ‘there is no action,’ that is wrong intention for him. When action exists, yet one speaks the words ‘there is no action,’ that is wrong speech for him. When action exists, yet one declares ‘there is no action,’ he contradicts those arahants who affirm action. When action exists, yet one causes others to believe ‘there is no action,’ that is false proclamation of the Dhamma for him. And by means of that false proclamation of the Dhamma, he disparages himself and reviles others. Thus his former good conduct is already abandoned, and bad conduct is present—this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, contradiction of the noble ones, false proclamation of the Dhamma, self-disparagement, and reviling of others. Thus these many evil, unwholesome states arise due to wrong view.
translations.mn60:17: There, householders, a wise person reflects thus: 'If there is no action, then this good man will fare well after the breakup of the body; but if there is action, then this good man will be reborn after death in a bad destination, a realm of suffering, hell. Yet even if there is no action, let it be that these ascetics and brahmins speak the truth; still, this good man is blameworthy in the sight of the wise in this very life—a man of bad conduct, wrong view, one who denies action.' If indeed there is action, then this good man incurs blame in both respects: he is blameworthy in the sight of the wise in this very life, and after the breakup of the body he will be reborn in a bad destination, a realm of suffering, hell. Thus this incomplete doctrine, wrongly grasped, spreads like a disease, abandoning the wholesome state.
translations.mn60:19: Indeed, if action exists, then the view 'there is action' is correct; that will be right view. Indeed, if action exists, then the thought 'there is action' is correct; that will be right intention. Indeed, if action exists, then the speech 'there is action' is correct; that will be right speech. Indeed, if action exists, then declaring 'there is action' does not contradict the arahants who affirm action. Indeed, if action exists, then proclaiming 'there is action' to others establishes the true Dhamma. And with that establishment of the true Dhamma, one neither exalts oneself nor disparages others. Thus, one's previous bad conduct is already abandoned, and good conduct is established—this right view, right intention, right speech, the non-opposition to the noble ones, the establishment of the true Dhamma, non-self-exaltation, non-disparagement of others. Thus, these many wholesome qualities arise dependent on right view.
translations.mn60:21: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; without cause, without condition, beings become defiled. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; without cause, without condition, beings are purified. There is no strength, no effort, no human capacity, no human striving; all beings, all living creatures, all beings, all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, controlled by destiny, circumstance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.'
translations.mn60:22: Among these very ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins hold the opposite view. They say: 'There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; with cause and condition, beings become defiled. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; with cause and condition, beings are purified. There is strength, there is effort, there is human capacity, there is human striving; not all beings, not all living creatures, not all beings, not all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, controlled by destiny, circumstance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.' What do you think, householders, are these ascetics and brahmins opposed to one another in their views?
translations.mn60:29: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'There is no such thing as the formless realms in their entirety.'
translations.mn60:30: Among these very ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins hold the opposite view. They say: 'There are the formless realms in their entirety.' What do you think, householders, are these ascetics and brahmins opposed to one another in their views?
translations.mn60:32: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold and proclaim this view: 'There is no complete cessation of existence.'
translations.mn60:35: These four types of persons, householders, exist and are found in the world. What four? Here, householders, one person is self-afflicted, devoted to the practice of self-mortification. Here, householders, one person afflicts others, devoted to the practice of afflicting others. Here, householders, one person is both self-afflicted and afflicts others, devoted to both self-mortification and afflicting others. Here, householders, one person is neither self-afflicted nor devoted to self-mortification, nor does he afflict others or engage in afflicting others; he, without self-affliction, without afflicting others, in this very life attains dispassion, cessation, coolness, and experiences happiness, dwelling with a mind become divine.
translations.mn60:36: And which person, householders, is self-afflicted, devoted to the practice of self-mortification? Here, householders, one person is naked, living in the open, licking his hands, not coming when called, not stopping when told, not accepting food from a pot, from a pan, from a doorstep, from where a stick is being wielded, from where a pestle is being used, where two people are eating, from where a pregnant woman, a nursing mother, or a woman with a man, is eating, from where food is specifically set aside, from where an invitation has been made; he accepts no food offered by hand, no food from a village, no food from a town; he wears rag-robes, a single cloth, a double cloth, hemp garments, hempen cloth, garments of refuse rags, a deer-skin, a garment of bark, a mat of grass, a wood-shaving garment, a head-hair blanket, an animal-hair blanket, an owl's wing garment; he plucks out his hair and beard, practicing the vow of pulling out hair; he stands continuously, refusing seats; he squats continuously, exerting himself in effort; he uses a brush of bristles, living on alms; he lives in the forest, feeding on fruits and tubers; he lives on roots and fruits, subsisting on wild food; he wears a loincloth of bark, or a mat of grass, or a wood-shaving garment; he lives with matted hair, smeared with dirt, devoted to the veneration of fire; he performs various kinds of self-mortifying practices. Such a person is called one who is self-afflicted, devoted to the practice of self-mortification.
translations.mn60:37: And which person, householders, afflicts others, devoted to the practice of afflicting others? Here, householders, one person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a hunter of deer, a fowler, a fisherman, a thief, a soldier, a tax-collector, or one engaged in any other cruel occupation. Such a person is called one who afflicts others, devoted to the practice of afflicting others.
translations.mn60:38: And which person, householders, is both self-afflicted and afflicts others, devoted to both self-mortification and afflicting others? Here, householders, one person is a king, a crowned warrior, who, relying on his power, seizes others' property, saying: 'Seize this man's property!' 'Seize this man's wife!' 'Seize this man's children!' 'Seize this man's relatives!' 'Imprison this man!' 'Torture this man!' 'Execute this man!' And those who are punished, terrified by punishment, terrified by fear, with faces turned upward, weeping, perform the required tasks. Such a person is called one who is both self-afflicted and afflicts others, devoted to both self-mortification and afflicting others.
translations.mn60:39: And which person, householders, is neither self-afflicted nor devoted to self-mortification, nor does he afflict others or engage in afflicting others; he, without self-affliction, without afflicting others, in this very life attains dispassion, cessation, coolness, and experiences happiness, dwelling with a mind become divine?
translations.mn60:4: Is there, householders, any teacher pleasing to you in whom you have established confident faith?
translations.mn60:5: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and say: 'There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good or bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and proclaim this world and the next.'
translations.mn60:6: And indeed, householders, among these ascetics and brahmins, there are some who hold the opposite view. They say: 'There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is another world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and proclaim this world and the next.' What do you think, householders: are these ascetics and brahmins who hold opposite views to one another?' 'Yes, sir.'
translations.mn63:8: And why, Mālukyaputta, has this been left undeclared by me? Because it is not beneficial, not fundamental to the spiritual life, not conducive to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. That is why it has been left undeclared by me.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, completely transcending all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'infinite is space', attains and dwells in the base of infinite space. Whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness there present... he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as disease, as a boil, as a dart, as trouble, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as not-self. He turns his mind away from those states and directs his mind towards the deathless element: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Established there, he attains the destruction of the taints; if the taints are not destroyed, then with that very delight in the Dhamma, with that very joy in the Dhamma, he is reborn spontaneously, and there he will attain final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking 'infinite is consciousness', attains and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. Whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness there present... he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as disease, as a boil, as a dart, as trouble, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as not-self. He turns his mind away from those states and directs his mind towards the deathless element: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Established there, he attains the destruction of the taints; if the taints are not destroyed, then with that very delight in the Dhamma, with that very joy in the Dhamma, he is reborn spontaneously, and there he will attain final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: "Do you, bhikkhus, remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?" When this was said, the Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: "I, sir, remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One." "But how, Mālukyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?" "Identity view, sir, as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One, I remember; doubt, sir, as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One, I remember; clinging to rules and observances, sir, as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One, I remember; sensual desire, sir, as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One, I remember; ill will, sir, as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One, I remember. Thus, sir, I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One."
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it." "Then listen, Ānanda, and pay close attention; I will speak," said the Blessed One. "Yes, sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: And whoever, Ānanda, follows the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, and by means of that path, that practice, sees, understands, or abandons the five lower fetters—this is possible.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which consists of thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Whatever material form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness there present, he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as disease, as a boil, as a dart, as trouble, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as not-self. He turns his mind away from those states and directs his mind towards the deathless element: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Established there, he attains the destruction of the taints; if the taints are not destroyed, then with that very delight in the Dhamma, with that very joy in the Dhamma, he is reborn spontaneously, and there he will attain final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If a bhikkhu wishes: 'May I experience various kinds of supernormal powers: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though on dry land; may I fly cross-legged through the air like a bird; may I with my hand touch and stroke the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; may I wield bodily mastery even up to the Brahmā world,' then he should fulfill the precepts, develop the mind, be devoted to solitude, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
translations.mn6:15: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May I hear both divine and human sounds with the purified divine ear element surpassing the human—whether far or near,' he should fulfill the precepts, …pe… frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:16: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May I understand the minds of other beings, other persons, with my mind—knowing a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' knowing a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust'; knowing a mind with hate as 'a mind with hate,' knowing a mind without hate as 'a mind without hate'; knowing a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion,' knowing a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion'; knowing a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind,' knowing a scattered mind as 'a scattered mind'; knowing an exalted mind as 'an exalted mind,' knowing an unexalted mind as 'an unexalted mind'; knowing a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind,' knowing an unsurpassed mind as 'an unsurpassed mind'; knowing a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind,' knowing an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind'; knowing a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind,' knowing an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind,'—he should fulfill the precepts, …pe… frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:2: “Live accomplished in virtue, bhikkhus, accomplished in the Pātimokkha; restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with good conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest fault, having undertaken the training rules, train in them.
translations.mn6:3: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May I be dear and agreeable, respected and esteemed by my fellow practitioners,' he should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to inner mental stillness, not neglecting jhāna, endowed with insight, frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:6: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May those of my relatives and blood-relations who have passed away, who have died, recall me with a confident mind, and may that be very fruitful and beneficial for them,' he should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to inner mental stillness, not neglecting jhāna, endowed with insight, frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:7: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May I be able to endure displeasure, and may displeasure not overcome me; may I dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen displeasure,' he should fulfill the precepts, …pe… frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:8: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May I be able to endure fear and dread, and may fear and dread not overcome me; may I dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen fear and dread,' he should fulfill the precepts, …pe… frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:9: If a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, should wish: 'May I easily, without difficulty, without trouble, attain the four jhānas that are noble attainments of mental excellence, the peaceful dwellings in this very life,' he should fulfill the precepts, …pe… frequent secluded dwellings.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kāsi country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn70:11: “Because, bhikkhus, I know and have seen and realized and directly experienced with wisdom: 'When one dwells having attained this kind of neutral feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, unwholesome qualities diminish and wholesome qualities increase,' therefore I say: 'Dwell having attained this kind of neutral feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.'
translations.mn70:12: I do not say to all bhikkhus, bhikkhus, 'You should practice heedfulness.' Nor do I say to all bhikkhus, bhikkhus, 'You should not practice heedfulness.' Those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the spiritual life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated by perfect wisdom—towards such bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I say: 'You should not practice heedfulness.' Why is that? Because they have already done what is to be done with heedfulness. They are incapable of negligence.
translations.mn70:13: And those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are learners, who have not attained the mental goal, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—towards such bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I say: 'You should practice heedfulness.' Why is that? So that these venerable ones, dwelling in suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and restraining the faculties, may attain, for the sake of which sons of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—the unsurpassed culmination of the spiritual life: having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, may they dwell having attained it in this very life. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness in these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I say: 'You should practice heedfulness.'
translations.mn70:14: These seven persons, bhikkhus, exist in the world. What seven? The one liberated both ways, the wisdom-liberated one, the body-witness, the one attained to view, the faith-liberated one, the Dhamma-follower, the faith-follower.
translations.mn70:15: And who, bhikkhus, is the person liberated both ways? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells having touched with the body those liberations that are formless, transcending forms, and his taints are destroyed by wisdom. This, bhikkhus, is called the person liberated both ways. Towards this bhikkhu, bhikkhus, I say: 'You should not practice heedfulness.' Why is that? Because he has already done what is to be done with heedfulness. He is incapable of negligence.
translations.mn70:17: And who, bhikkhus, is the body-witness? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells having touched with the body those liberations that are formless, transcending forms, and by wisdom some of his taints are destroyed. This, bhikkhus, is called the body-witness. Towards this bhikkhu, bhikkhus, I say: 'You should practice heedfulness.' Why is that? So that this venerable one, dwelling in suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and restraining the faculties, may attain, for the sake of which sons of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—the unsurpassed culmination of the spiritual life: having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, may they dwell having attained it in this very life. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness in this bhikkhu, bhikkhus, I say: 'You should practice heedfulness.'
translations.mn70:2: “Monks, I myself eat apart from the evening meal. And while eating apart from the evening meal, monks, I perceive little affliction, little discomfort, lightness, strength, and ease in living. Come, you too, monks, eat apart from the evening meal. And while you too, monks, eat apart from the evening meal, you will perceive little affliction, little discomfort, lightness, strength, and ease in living.” “Yes, sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn70:20: And who, monks, is a follower of the Dhamma? Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having touched with the body those liberations that are formless, transcending form, yet by means of wisdom some taints are destroyed for him, and the teachings declared by the Tathāgata are just barely accepted by him through wisdom; and he possesses these qualities: faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, and wisdom faculty. This, monks, is called a person who is a follower of the Dhamma. Even for this monk, monks, I say, 'There is work to be done with diligence.' Why is that? Perhaps this venerable one, resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing the faculties, might—having realized for himself in this very life, through direct knowledge—the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—live having realized it.” This, monks, is the fruit of diligence I see for this monk, and therefore I say, 'There is work to be done with diligence.'
translations.mn70:22: I do not say, monks, that attainment of knowledge is through the beginning alone; rather, monks, attainment of knowledge comes through gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress.
translations.mn70:23: And how, monks, does attainment of knowledge come through gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress? Here, monks, one inspired by faith approaches, having approached one attends closely, attending closely one hears the Dhamma, having heard the Dhamma one retains it, retaining the teachings one examines their meaning, examining the meaning one accepts the teachings through reflective acceptance, through acceptance of the teachings enthusiasm arises, with enthusiasm one makes effort, making effort one weighs things carefully, having weighed one strives, striving with aroused mind one realizes the ultimate truth with the body, and sees it clearly with wisdom.
translations.mn70:24: If, monks, that faith had not been; if, monks, that approaching had not been; if, monks, that close attendance had not been; if, monks, that listening had not been; if, monks, that hearing of Dhamma had not been; if, monks, that retention of Dhamma had not been; if, monks, that examination of meaning had not been; if, monks, that acceptance of Dhamma through reflective acceptance had not been; if, monks, that enthusiasm had not been; if, monks, that effort had not been; if, monks, that weighing had not been; if, monks, that striving had not been—then, monks, it would be for the purpose of going astray, for the purpose of wrong practice, monks. How far, monks, have these foolish men strayed from this Dhamma and Discipline!
translations.mn70:25: There is, monks, a fourfold declaration, by which a wise person, on seeing it, would quickly understand the meaning. I will set it forth for you; will you understand my meaning?” “But how could we, sir, understand the meaning of the Dhamma without knowing it?”
translations.mn70:26: “Even that teacher, monks, who is devoted to material gain, who is an heir of material things, who lives attached to material pleasures, does not constantly resort to such a thought as this: 'May it be so, then we will do it; or may it not be so, then we will not do it.' How much more so, monks, the Tathāgata, who lives entirely detached from material things.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering gradually in Kāsi, arrived at a town of the Kāsi people named Kīṭāgiri. There the Blessed One dwelt at Kīṭāgiri, in the town of the Kāsi people.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time, the bhikkhus named Assaji and Punabbasuka were dwelling as residents at Kīṭāgiri. Then several bhikkhus approached the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka, and having approached, they said to them: 'Friends, the Blessed One eats apart from the evening meal, and so does the bhikkhu Saṅgha. And while eating apart from the evening meal, friends, they perceive little affliction, little discomfort, lightness, strength, and ease in living. Come, you too, friends, eat apart from the evening meal. And while you too, friends, eat apart from the evening meal, you will perceive little affliction, little discomfort, lightness, strength, and ease in living.' When this was said, the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka said to those bhikkhus: 'We, friends, eat in the evening, in the morning, during the day, and at improper times. While we eat in the evening, in the morning, during the day, and at improper times, we perceive little affliction, little discomfort, lightness, strength, and ease in living. Why should we abandon what is evident for what is time-bound? We will eat in the evening, in the morning, during the day, and at improper times.'
translations.mn70:7: “Do you not know, monks, that I have taught the Dhamma in this way: that for one who experiences such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but for another experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase; for one who experiences such a painful feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but for another experiencing such a painful feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase; for one who experiences such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but for another experiencing such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kuru people at Kammāsadamma, a town of the Kurus, in the hermitage of the brahmin of the Bharadvāja clan, on a straw-thatched shelter.
translations.mn75:10: Indeed, Magandiya, when I was formerly a householder, I was surrounded and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye, agreeable, pleasing, charming, attractive, connected with sensual desire, delightful; sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body, agreeable, pleasing, charming, attractive, connected with sensual desire, delightful. I, Magandiya, had three palaces: one for the cold season, one for the hot season, and one for the rainy season. In the rainy season palace, I was attended by minstrels, all women, for four months without descending to the lower palace. Later, having truly understood the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures, I abandoned sensual craving, dispelled sensual fever, and dwelled with a mind free from thirst, internally peaceful. I saw other beings who were not free from sensual desire, being devoured by sensual craving, tormented by sensual fever, indulging in sensual pleasures. I did not envy them, nor did I delight therein. Why is that? I, Magandiya, delighting in that delight which is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—even having attained a divine happiness—delighting in that delight, I do not envy the inferior, nor do I delight therein.
translations.mn75:12: Just so, Magandiya, when I was formerly a householder, I was surrounded and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye, agreeable, pleasing, charming, attractive, connected with sensual desire, delightful; sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body, agreeable, pleasing, charming, attractive, connected with sensual desire, delightful. Later, having truly understood the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures, I abandoned sensual craving, dispelled sensual fever, and dwelled with a mind free from thirst, internally peaceful. I saw other beings who were not free from sensual desire, being devoured by sensual craving, tormented by sensual fever, indulging in sensual pleasures. I did not envy them, nor did I delight therein. Why is that? I, Magandiya, delighting in that delight which is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—even having attained a divine happiness—delighting in that delight, I do not envy the inferior, nor do I delight therein.
translations.mn75:13: Suppose, Magandiya, a man afflicted with sores, his body ulcerated, suffering and tormented by boils, scratching his sores with his nails, and burning his body with a hot iron. His friends, companions, relatives, and kin would summon a physician or surgeon. That physician or surgeon would apply medicine. Relying on that medicine, the man would be freed from his sores, become healthy, happy, comfortable, and independent, going wherever he wished. Then he would see another man afflicted with sores, his body ulcerated, suffering and tormented by boils, scratching his sores with his nails, burning his body with a hot iron. What do you think, Magandiya: would that man envy the other man for being burned with a hot iron or for using medicine?
translations.mn75:16: Just so, Magandiya, in the past sensual pleasures were accompanied by painful contact, great affliction, and great fever; in the future sensual pleasures will be accompanied by painful contact, great affliction, and great fever; even now, in the present, sensual pleasures are accompanied by painful contact, great affliction, and great fever. And these beings, Magandiya, not free from sensual desire, being devoured by sensual craving, tormented by sensual fever, with faculties impaired, turn upside down in regarding sensual pleasures as happiness.
translations.mn75:17: Suppose, Magandiya, a man afflicted with sores, his body ulcerated, suffering and tormented by boils, scratching his sores with his nails, burning his body with a hot iron. The more, Magandiya, that such a man with sores, his body ulcerated, suffering and tormented by boils, scratches his sores with his nails and burns his body with a hot iron, the more those sores become foul, stinking, and putrid; yet there remains a trace of pleasure and gratification—the itching of the sores. Just so, Magandiya, beings not free from sensual desire, being devoured by sensual craving, tormented by sensual fever, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more, Magandiya, that beings not free from sensual desire, being devoured by sensual craving, tormented by sensual fever, indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their sensual craving increases, and they are tormented by sensual fever; yet there remains a trace of pleasure and gratification—dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn75:18: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, has any king or royal minister ever been seen or heard of who, endowed and provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure, being served and waited upon, yet having abandoned sensual craving, quenched sensual fever, free from thirst, with a peaceful mind within, has lived, is living, or will live?
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Kammāsadamma for alms. Having walked for alms in Kammāsadamma and returned from the alms round after the meal, he approached a certain forest grove for the day's abode. Having entered the grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's rest.
translations.mn75:22: "I am deeply impressed, sir Gotama. May the Venerable Gotama teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I may realize health and see Nibbāna." "Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man born blind; he would not see black and white forms, he would not see blue forms, yellow forms, red forms, or brown forms, he would not see what is even or uneven, he would not see constellations, he would not see the moon and sun. His friends and companions, relatives and kin, would summon a skilled physician or surgeon. That physician or surgeon would prepare medicine for him. But even with that medicine, he would neither produce eyes nor purify eyes. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that doctor not be subject to mere fatigue and trouble?" "Yes, sir Gotama." "In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna,' you would neither understand health nor see Nibbāna. That would be my fatigue, that would be my vexation."
translations.mn75:24: In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna,' you would understand health and see Nibbāna. Then, with the arising of vision in you, the passion, desire, and delight in the five aggregates subject to clinging would be abandoned. Moreover, this would occur to you: 'Indeed, for a long time I have been deceived, cheated, and misled by this mind. For I clung to form, I clung to feeling, I clung to perception, I clung to formations, I clung to consciousness. With clinging as condition, existence arose; with existence as condition, birth arose; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus arises this whole mass of suffering.'"
translations.mn75:25: "I am deeply impressed, sir Gotama. May the Venerable Gotama teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I may rise from this seat with joy." "Then, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with good persons. When you, Māgaṇḍiya, associate with good persons, you will hear the true Dhamma; when you hear the true Dhamma, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know and see for yourself—these are the diseases, the boils, the arrows. Here, diseases, boils, and arrows cease without remainder. With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus ceases this entire mass of suffering."
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, sir Gotama! Excellent, sir Gotama! Just as one might set upright what has been overturned, reveal what has been hidden, show the way to one who is lost, or place a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes can see forms, so too has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by the Venerable Gotama. I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the bhikkhu Saṅgha. May I receive ordination under the Venerable Gotama, may I receive higher ordination?"
translations.mn75:27: "Whoever, Māgaṇḍiya, previously belonging to another sect, desires ordination and higher ordination in this Dhamma and discipline, first undergoes a probation period of four months. After four months have passed, if the bhikkhus are keen-minded, they grant ordination and higher ordination for bhikkhuhood. However, individual temperaments are recognized here." "If, sir, those previously belonging to another sect who desire ordination and higher ordination undergo a probation period of four months, and after four months have passed, the keen-minded bhikkhus grant ordination and higher ordination for bhikkhuhood, then I will undergo a probation period of four years. After four years have passed, let the keen-minded bhikkhus grant me ordination and higher ordination for bhikkhuhood."
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, walking back and forth, wandering from place to place, approached the Brahmin Bhāradvāja's fire-hut. The wanderer Māgaṇḍiya saw the straw bedding prepared in the Brahmin Bhāradvāja's fire-hut. Seeing it, he said to the Brahmin Bhāradvāja: 'Whose, I wonder, is this straw bedding prepared in the honorable Bhāradvāja's fire-hut? It seems fit for a monk's bed.'
translations.mn75:6: Then the Blessed One, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, heard the conversation between the Brahmin Bhāradvāja and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the Brahmin Bhāradvāja's fire-hut; approaching, he sat down on the prepared straw bedding. Then the Brahmin Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; approaching, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the Brahmin Bhāradvāja, who was seated to one side: 'Did you, Bhāradvāja, have some conversation just now with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya regarding this very straw bedding?' When this was said, the Brahmin Bhāradvāja, feeling remorseful and with body covered in goosebumps, said to the Blessed One: 'Indeed, venerable Gotama, that is exactly what I wished to report to you. And yet, venerable Gotama, you have already declared it without being told.'
translations.mn75:7: Then the conversation between the Blessed One and the Brahmin Bhāradvāja came to an end. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, walking back and forth, wandering from place to place, approached where the Brahmin Bhāradvāja's fire-hut was, where the Blessed One was; approaching, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, who was seated to one side:
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Sanctuary.
translations.mn77:10: Indeed, Udāyi, there are five other qualities by which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and dwell relying upon me. What five? Here, Udāyi, my disciples develop virtue highly: 'The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the highest perfection in virtue.'
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path to my disciples; as they practice accordingly, my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and grief in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and grief in the world. And among my disciples, many dwell accomplished in higher knowledge and penetration.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path to my disciples; as they practice accordingly, my disciples develop the four right efforts. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu generates desire, strives, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome qualities; for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome qualities; for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and for the maintenance, non-decline, augmentation, fulfillment, and development of arisen wholesome qualities. And among my disciples, many dwell accomplished in higher knowledge and penetration.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path to my disciples; as they practice accordingly, my disciples develop the four bases of psychic power. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional effort; develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional effort; develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind and volitional effort; develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional effort. And among my disciples, many dwell accomplished in higher knowledge and penetration.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path to my disciples; as they practice accordingly, my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the faculty of faith, leading to tranquility, leading to awakening; develops the faculty of energy … develops the faculty of mindfulness … develops the faculty of concentration … develops the faculty of wisdom, leading to tranquility, leading to awakening. And among my disciples, many dwell accomplished in higher knowledge and penetration.
translations.mn77:2: At that time, several renowned wanderers were dwelling in the wanderers' park near Morani, such as Annabhāra, Varadharu, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other renowned wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path to my disciples; as they practice accordingly, my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, dependent on seclusion, dispassion, cessation, culminating in release; develops the enlightenment factor of discrimination of dhammas … develops the enlightenment factor of energy … develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility … develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, dependent on seclusion, dispassion, cessation, culminating in release. And among my disciples, many dwell accomplished in higher knowledge and penetration.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path for my disciples, by practicing which my disciples develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops right view, develops right thought, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right concentration. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the utmost perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path for my disciples, by practicing which my disciples develop the eight liberations. One who is embodied perceives forms: this is the first liberation. One with internal perception of form sees forms externally: this is the second liberation. One is exclusively concentrated on the beautiful: this is the third liberation. With the complete transcending of all perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'space is infinite': this is the fourth liberation. With the complete transcending of the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'consciousness is infinite': this is the fifth liberation. With the complete transcending of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness, thinking 'there is nothing': this is the sixth liberation. With the complete transcending of the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: this is the seventh liberation. With the complete transcending of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling: this is the eighth liberation. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the utmost perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path for my disciples, by practicing which my disciples develop the ten kasiṇas. One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable; one perceives the water kasiṇa … one perceives the fire kasiṇa … one perceives the air kasiṇa … one perceives the blue kasiṇa … one perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one perceives the red kasiṇa … one perceives the white kasiṇa … one perceives the space kasiṇa … one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the utmost perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught the path for my disciples, by practicing which my disciples develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, accompanied by rapture and happiness. He suffuses, permeates, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this rapture and happiness. Just as, Udāyi, a skilled bath attendant or his apprentice would sprinkle bath powder with water, kneading it gradually into a moistened ball so that the bath powder is saturated, saturated within and without, yet not dripping with moisture; so too, Udāyi, the bhikkhu suffuses, permeates, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this rapture and happiness.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyi, the bhikkhu, with the stilling of thought and examination, attains internal confidence and unification of mind, and enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without thought and examination, born of concentration, accompanied by rapture and happiness. He suffuses, permeates, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this rapture and happiness. Just as, Udāyi, a deep lake filled with clear water, has no inlet from the east, west, north, or south, and no rain is falling into it at intervals from the sky; yet from that very lake, cool streams well up and suffuse, permeate, fill, and pervade the entire lake with cool water, so that no part of the lake remains untouched by cool water; so too, Udāyi, the bhikkhu suffuses, permeates, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this rapture and happiness.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyi, the bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, and experiences in the body that happiness of which the noble ones declare, 'One dwells in equanimity, mindful, experiencing happiness,' and enters and dwells in the third jhāna. He suffuses, permeates, fills, and pervades this very body with the happiness free from rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this raptureless happiness. Just as, Udāyi, in a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, some of the blue, red, or white lotuses born in the water, growing in the water, not rising above the surface, are nurtured underwater, and from their tips to their roots are thoroughly soaked, permeated, filled, and pervaded with cool water; so too, Udāyi, the bhikkhu suffuses, permeates, fills, and pervades this very body with the happiness free from rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this raptureless happiness.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyi, the bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits suffusing this very body with a purified, bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this purified, bright mind. Just as, Udāyi, a person wrapped from head to foot with a white cloth would have no part of his entire body untouched by the white cloth; so too, Udāyi, the bhikkhu sits suffusing this very body with a purified, bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by this purified, bright mind. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the utmost perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Blessed One, having robed himself in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'It is too far to go into Rājagaha for alms. Why don't I rather go to the Moranivāpa park, where the wanderer Sakuludāyī is?'
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples hear with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, heavenly and human, whether near or far. Just as, Udāyī, a strong conch blower could make himself heard in all four directions; so too, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples hear with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, heavenly and human, whether near or far. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples recollect various past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a complexion; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the span of my life; and passing away from there, I arose there. There too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a complexion; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the span of my life; and passing away from there, I have been reborn here.' Thus they recollect their manifold past lives with their details and characteristics. Just as, Udāyī, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village, and then return from that village back to his own village; and he would know: 'I went from my own village to that village, there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, was silent thus; from there I went to that other village, there too I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, was silent thus; now I have returned from that village back to my own village.' So too, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples recollect their manifold past lives with their details and characteristics. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and they understand beings according to their deeds: 'These beings, endowed with bad bodily conduct, bad verbal conduct, and bad mental conduct, revilers of noble ones, holding wrong view, performing deeds rooted in wrong view—upon the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. Or these beings, endowed with good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct, not revilers of noble ones, holding right view, performing deeds rooted in right view—upon the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand beings according to their deeds. Just as, Udāyī, there are two houses with doors; a clear-sighted man standing in the middle could see people entering and leaving, walking and moving about; so too, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand beings according to their deeds ... and among my disciples, many dwell having attained the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples, with the destruction of the taints, attain and dwell in taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves in this very life. Just as, Udāyī, a clear, transparent, and undisturbed lake in a mountain cleft would allow a clear-sighted man standing on the bank to see oysters, pebbles, and shoals of fish moving or resting; and he would know: 'This lake is clear, transparent, and undisturbed, and there are oysters, pebbles, and shoals of fish moving and resting.' So too, Udāyī, the path has been taught by me to my disciples, by practising which my disciples, with the destruction of the taints, attain and dwell in taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves in this very life. And among my disciples, many dwell having attained the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One went to the wanderer Sakuludāyī. And the wanderer Sakuludāyī said to the Blessed One: 'Come, venerable sir! Welcome, venerable sir! It is a long time since the Blessed One has found the opportunity to come here. Please sit down, venerable sir; this seat is prepared.' The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then the wanderer Sakuludāyī took a low seat and sat down to one side. And the Blessed One said to the wanderer Sakuludāyī, who was sitting to one side: 'What discussion, Udāyī, were you engaged in just now? And what conversation was left unfinished?'
translations.mn77:7: "How many qualities, Udāyī, do you see in me, by which my disciples honour, respect, revere, and venerate me, and dwell relying on me?"
translations.mn77:9: “If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is of little need, and he praises having little need,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, still, Udāyī, there are disciples of mine who eat once a day, or every half-day, or every seven days, or every half-month. Yet I myself, Udāyī, sometimes eat even less than that with this alms bowl, sometimes more. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is of little need, and he praises having little need,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, those of my disciples who eat once a day, or every half-day, or every seven days, or every half-month would not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me in this way, nor would they dwell relying upon me. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he praises contentment with any kind of robe,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, still, Udāyī, there are disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearing rough robes, who gather discarded rags from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or dung heaps, and make them into outer robes and wear them. Yet I myself, Udāyī, sometimes wear robes given by householders—strong, thick, coarse, without fine hair. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he praises contentment with any kind of robe,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, those of my disciples who are rag-robe wearers, wearing rough robes, who gather discarded rags from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or dung heaps, and make them into outer robes and wear them, would not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me in this way, nor would they dwell relying upon me. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of alms food, and he praises contentment with any kind of alms food,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, still, Udāyī, there are disciples of mine who are alms-food eaters, going on a fixed round, delighting in gleanings, who, having entered a householder’s home, even when invited to sit, do not accept food. Yet I myself, Udāyī, sometimes eat when invited, eating rice with fine curry, various soups, and various seasonings. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of alms food, and he praises contentment with any kind of alms food,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, those of my disciples who are alms-food eaters, going on a fixed round, delighting in gleanings, who, having entered a householder’s home, even when invited to sit, do not accept food, would not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me in this way, nor would they dwell relying upon me. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with any kind of lodging,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, still, Udāyī, there are disciples of mine who dwell at the root of trees, in the open air, who do not enter a shelter even for eight months. Yet I myself, Udāyī, sometimes dwell in roofed buildings, well-plastered and well-swept, windproof, with closed windows and doors. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with any kind of lodging,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, those of my disciples who dwell at the root of trees, in the open air, who do not enter a shelter even for eight months, would not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me in this way, nor would they dwell relying upon me. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he praises seclusion,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, still, Udāyī, there are disciples of mine who are forest-dwellers, fond of remote lodgings, who occupy remote forest and woodland places as secluded dwellings, and come into the midst of the Saṅgha only once every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Yet I myself, Udāyī, sometimes dwell surrounded by bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male and female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, wanderers, and their disciples. If, Udāyī, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he praises seclusion,' and were to dwell relying upon me in that way, those of my disciples who are forest-dwellers, fond of remote lodgings, who occupy remote forest and woodland places as secluded dwellings, and come into the midst of the Saṅgha only once every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, would not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me in this way, nor would they dwell relying upon me. Thus, Udāyī, my disciples do not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me with these five qualities, nor do they dwell relying upon me.
translations.mn7:11: ‘Just as if my four floods—vomiting, excrement, urine, and semen—had been expelled and rejected,’ he gains understanding of meaning, gains understanding of Dhamma, gains joy connected with Dhamma; joyful, rapture arises; with rapture, the body calms; with a calm body, he feels pleasure; with pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He dwells having suffused one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will.
translations.mn7:17: He understands: 'There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, and there is this noble deliverance beyond mere perception.'
translations.mn7:18: With such knowledge, with such vision, his mind is liberated from the taints of sensual desire, from the taints of existence, and from the taints of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, lived is the holy life, done is what had to be done, there is no more of this state of being.' This, monks, is called 'a monk washed inwardly by washing.'
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja was seated not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One: 'Does Master Gotama go to bathe in the Bāhuka River?' 'What, brahmin, is the use of the Bāhuka River? What can the Bāhuka River do?' 'The Bāhuka River is held in high regard by many, Master Gotama; the Bāhuka River is considered meritorious by many, Master Gotama; many people carry off their evil deeds by bathing in the Bāhuka River.'
translations.mn7:2: Just as, monks, a cloth stained and soiled would not take dye properly—whether blue, yellow, red, or pink—because of its impurity. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth. So too, monks, when the mind is defiled, a bad destination may be expected. Just as, monks, a clean and bright cloth would properly take dye—whether blue, yellow, red, or pink—because of its purity. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth. So too, monks, when the mind is undefiled, a good destination may be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja in verse: 'The Bāhuka and Adhikakka, Gayā and Sundarikā, Sarasvatī and Payāga, and the Bāhumatī River—even a fool who goes there is not purified. What will Sundarikā do, what will Payāga or the Bāhuka River do? Evil deeds committed by a wicked person, those rivers cannot wash away. For the pure, the fast is always pure, for the pure the observance is always pure; for one pure and of pure conduct, the precepts are always fulfilled. Wash here, O brahmin, and bring safety to all beings. If you do not speak falsely, if you do not harm any living being, if you do not take what is not given, and are faithful and free from stinginess, why trouble to go to Gayā? Even water itself becomes your Gayā.'
translations.mn7:3: And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind?
