Covetousness and unrighteous greed are defilements of the mind; ill will is a defilement of the mind; anger is a defilement of the mind; resentment is a defilement of the mind; hypocrisy is a defilement of the mind; arrogance is a defilement of the mind; envy is a defilement of the mind; stinginess is a defilement of the mind; deceit is a defilement of the mind; fraudulence is a defilement of the mind; obstinacy is a defilement of the mind; aggressiveness is a defilement of the mind; conceit is a defilement of the mind; excessive conceit is a defilement of the mind; intoxication is a defilement of the mind; heedlessness is a defilement of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally experienced by the wise.'
translations.mn7:7: endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples who have practiced well, who have practiced straight-forwardly, who have practiced correctly, who have practiced properly—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering among the Kuru people with a large community of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a Kuru town named Thullakoṭṭhita.
translations.mn82:11: Then the friends of the young man Raṭṭhapāla went to his parents and said: 'Sir, this young man Raṭṭhapāla is lying down on the ground right there, saying: "I will die right here, or I will go forth." If you do not allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the household life into homelessness, he will die right there. But if you allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the household life into homelessness, you will see him even after he has gone forth. If the young man Raṭṭhapāla does not find delight in going forth, what other course will he have? He will return here. Please allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the household life into homelessness.' 'We allow it, dear ones, we allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the household life into homelessness. But after going forth, he should inform his parents.' Then the friends of the young man Raṭṭhapāla went to him and said: 'Get up, good Raṭṭhapāla, you have been permitted by your parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness. And after going forth, you should inform your parents.'
translations.mn82:12: Then the young man Raṭṭhapāla, rising up and taking his belongings, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated there, the young man Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, I have been permitted by my parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness. May the Blessed One ordain me.'
translations.mn82:20: Then, knowing that Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had accepted the invitation, his father went to his own dwelling, had a large heap of gold and silver made, covered it with mats, and said to the former wife of Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'Come, daughter-in-law, adorn yourself with the ornaments with which the young man Raṭṭhapāla used to delight, and go to him adorned.'
translations.mn82:16: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, arranged his dwelling, took his bowl and robe, and set out on a wandering journey towards Thullakoṭṭhika. Wandering gradually, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dwelt in the royal deer park of King Korabya at Thullakoṭṭhika. Then, in the morning, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. While walking for alms with proper attention, he approached his father's dwelling.
translations.mn82:18: Now at that time, a female servant related to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla wanted to throw away a soiled lump of dough. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to that servant: 'Sister, if it is fit to be discarded, pour it into my bowl.' Then, as the servant poured the soiled lump of dough into Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, she noticed the mark of hands, feet, and limbs. Then the servant went to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother and said to her: 'Know this, lady: your son Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.' 'If, dear, you speak truly, I will give you what you wish.' Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother went to his father and said to him: 'Know this, householder: it seems the young man Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.'
translations.mn82:22: Then, in the morning, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to his father's dwelling. Having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then his father uncovered the heap of gold and silver and said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother's wealth, this is from your grandfather, this is from your great-grandfather. You can, dear Raṭṭhapāla, enjoy the pleasures and also do meritorious deeds. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to the household life and enjoy pleasures and do meritorious deeds.' 'If you would do as I say, householder, load this heap of gold and silver onto a cart, drive it out, and throw it into the middle of the river current. Why is that? Because sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair will arise from that, householder.'
translations.mn82:13: The young man Raṭṭhapāla did not obtain ordination and higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One. Then, soon after Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's higher ordination, while he was still newly ordained, the Blessed One, having stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he wished, set out on a wandering journey towards Sāvatthī. Wandering gradually, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One dwelt in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.
translations.mn82:21: Then, when that night had passed, Raṭṭhapāla's father had excellent food and drink prepared in his own dwelling and informed Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.'
translations.mn82:17: Now at that time, Raṭṭhapāla's father was pacing up and down in the central hall. He saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar. Seeing him, he said: 'Because of these bald-headed ascetics, our only beloved son has gone forth.' Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla received neither a gift nor a refusal at his father's dwelling; instead, he received only abuse from another.
translations.mn82:19: Now at that time, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was using the soiled lump of dough leaning on the root of a tree. Then Raṭṭhapāla's father approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla and said to him: 'Are you really, dear Raṭṭhapāla, using a soiled lump of dough? Shouldn't you, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to your own home?' 'How could we, householder, who have gone forth from home to homelessness, return to our home? We are homeless, householder. I came to your house, householder, but received neither a gift nor a refusal; instead, I received only abuse from another.' 'Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go home.' 'Enough, householder, my meal duty is done today.' 'Then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, please accept an invitation to eat at home tomorrow.' Venerable Raṭṭhapāla consented in silence.
translations.mn82:14: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, quickly realized—by himself, directly knowing and attaining—the supreme goal of the holy life for which sons of good families rightly go forth from home into homelessness, even in this very life. 'Destroyed is birth, lived is the holy life, done is what had to be done, there is no more of this state'—he understood. And indeed, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:23: Then the former wives of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, each taking hold of his feet, said to him: 'What kind of celestial nymphs, sir, are those on account of which you have gone forth into homelessness?' 'We do not, sisters, go forth into homelessness on account of nymphs,' he replied. 'The venerable Raṭṭhapāla speaks in terms of spiritual kinship!' With that they fainted right there and fell down.
translations.mn82:24: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: 'If, householder, food is to be given, then give it; do not harass me.' 'Eat, my son Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is finished,' he replied. Then the father of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla personally fed and satisfied the venerable Raṭṭhapāla with delicious food and drink. Then, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having eaten, with bowl in hand, standing right there, spoke these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then, standing right there after uttering these verses, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla went to Migacīra, the park of King Korabya; having arrived, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abode.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Korabya said to the hunter: 'Clear, good hunter, the Migacīra parkland; we shall go to see the pleasant grounds.' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' the hunter replied, and while clearing the Migacīra park, he saw the venerable Raṭṭhapāla seated at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abode. Seeing him, he went to King Korabya, and said to him: 'Your park is now clean, Your Majesty. Here is a man named Raṭṭhapāla, a gentleman from a leading family in this very Thullakoṭṭhika, of whom you have often heard spoken highly; he is seated at the foot of a tree.' 'Then enough, good hunter, with preparing the park. Now we ourselves will pay homage to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla,' said the king.
translations.mn82:28: Then King Korabya, having said, 'Whatever food and drink has been prepared there, let all of it be released,' had excellent carriages yoked, mounted his chief carriage, and with fine carriages proceeded from Thullakoṭṭhika, with great royal splendor, to visit the venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Having gone as far as the carriage could go, he dismounted and walked on foot, surrounded by a magnificent retinue, to where the venerable Raṭṭhapāla was; having arrived, he exchanged courteous greetings with him. After exchanging polite and congenial talk, he stood to one side. Standing there, King Korabya said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'Let the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla please sit on this seat prepared for him.' 'Enough, great king, you may sit down; I will sit on my own seat,' replied Raṭṭhapāla. So King Korabya sat down on the appointed seat. Seated, King Korabya said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: "These four, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are the misfortunes because of which some people, having shaved off their hair and beard, putting on ochre robes, go forth from the household life into homelessness. What are the four? The misfortune of old age, the misfortune of illness, the misfortune of wealth, and the misfortune of relatives."
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika went to the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after pleasant and polite conversation, sat down at one side; some raised their hands in salutation and sat down at one side; some announced their name and clan in the Blessed One's presence and sat down at one side; and some sat down at one side in silence. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika were seated, the Blessed One instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened them with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: "These four, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are the misfortunes because of which some people, having shaved off their hair and beard, putting on ochre robes, go forth from the household life into homelessness. These misfortunes are not present in your case. What then, Master Raṭṭhapāla, having known, seen, or heard, have you gone forth from the household life into homelessness?"
translations.mn82:35: "Indeed, great king, the Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, has declared four teachings, which having known, seen, and heard, I went forth from the household life into homelessness. What are the four?"
translations.mn82:4: At that time, a young man named Raṭṭhapāla, a son of a leading family in that very Thullakoṭṭhika, was seated in that assembly. Then it occurred to the young man Raṭṭhapāla: 'In whatever way I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not possible while living in a house to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:6: Then the householder Raṭṭhapāla, not long after the large group of brahmins and householders had departed, went to the Blessed One, and on arrival, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: 'Insofar as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure, like a polished shell. I wish, sir, to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. May I receive ordination and higher ordination in the Blessed One’s presence. May the Blessed One ordain me.' 'But Raṭṭhapāla, have you been given permission by your mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness?' 'No, sir, I have not been given permission by my mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness.' 'Raṭṭhapāla, the Tathāgatas do not ordain one who has not been given permission by his mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness.' 'Very well, sir, I will do just that: I will act in such a way that my mother and father will give me permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness.'
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large company of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Opāsāda. There the Blessed One stayed in the Devavana, the Sālā forest, to the north of Opāsāda.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, approached the Blessed One. On arrival, he exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging these polite and friendly words, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: Now at that time the Blessed One was seated conversing on some appropriate topic with a number of elderly brahmins. At that time there was a young student named Kāpaṭika, youthful, with shaven head, about sixteen years of age, of noble birth, proficient in the three Vedas, with mastery of the indexes, phonology, grammar, the fourth Vedāṅga, and history as the fifth; skilled, intelligent, and well-spoken, endowed with knowledge of omens and the marks of the great man, seated in that assembly. While the elder brahmins were conversing with the Blessed One, he repeatedly interrupted the conversation. Then the Blessed One rebuked the young Kāpaṭika: 'Let the Venerable Bhāradvāja not interrupt the elder brahmins while they are conversing. Let the Venerable Bhāradvāja wait for the conclusion of the discussion.' When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Blessed One: 'Let the Blessed One not rebuke the young Kāpaṭika. The young Kāpaṭika is a householder’s son, very learned, wise, eloquent, and capable of debating with the Blessed One on this matter.'
translations.mn95:2: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was residing in Opāsāda, a village granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal fief, a gift of the king, a brahmin estate, complete with seven hundred ploughs, thorny fences, and water from tanks.
translations.mn95:20: When he does not find anything in himself corresponding to those defiling qualities, he places faith in them; with faith arisen he approaches, on approaching he serves, serving he lends ear, with attentive ear he hears the Dhamma, having heard the Dhamma he retains it, reflecting on the meaning of the teachings retained, the teachings, upon reflection, are accepted, acceptance of the teachings gives rise to desire, desire gives rise to zeal, with zeal he exerts himself, exerting himself he weighs, weighing he strives, striving with body and mind he directly realizes the supreme truth and sees it clearly with wisdom. This much, Bhāradvāja, is the realization of truth, this much is the experience of truth, and this much do we describe as the realization of truth; but the attainment of truth has not yet occurred.'
translations.mn95:33: 'But what, Master Gotama, is the benefit of approaching? We ask Master Gotama about the benefit of approaching.' 'Faith, Bhāradvāja, is the great benefit of approaching. If faith did not arise, one would not approach. Because faith arises, therefore one approaches. Therefore faith is the great benefit of approaching.'
translations.mn9:11: And what, friends, is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, and what is the path leading to the cessation of nutriment? These four nutriments, friends, sustain beings existing and support those seeking birth. What four? Physical food, coarse or fine; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. With the arising of craving comes the arising of nutriment; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of nutriment; this noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of nutriment, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment, and thus understands the path leading to the cessation of nutriment, he abandons the underlying tendency to lust, removes the underlying tendency to aversion, eradicates the underlying tendency to the view 'I am,' abandons ignorance, produces knowledge, and right here in this very life makes an end of suffering. Even so much, friends, is a noble disciple one of right view, one whose view is upright, endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, one who has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.mn95:5: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was sleeping during the day in the upper chamber. The brahmin Caṅkī saw the brahmins and householders from Opāsāda leaving the upper chamber, gathering in groups, and heading northward to the Devavana, the Sālavana. Seeing this, he asked Khatta: "Well then, good Khatta, where are the brahmins and householders from Opāsāda going, having left the upper chamber, gathering in groups, and heading northward to the Devavana, the Sālavana?"
translations.mn9:15: But what, friends, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering, in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering— this, friends, is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friends, is the origin of suffering? It is that craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there, that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence— this, friends, is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it— this, friends, is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friends, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, that is, right view … right concentration— this, friends, is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: 'Right view, right view,' it is said, friend. To what extent, friend, does a noble disciple possess right view, have upright view, be endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and have entered this true Dhamma?" "We have come from afar, friend, to learn the meaning of this statement from the Venerable Sāriputta. May the Venerable Sāriputta himself explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the bhikkhus will remember it." "Then listen, friends, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: "Good, friends," those bhikkhus, having approved and rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta's statement, asked him a further question: "But could there be, friend, another way in which a noble disciple possesses right view, has upright view, is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has entered this true Dhamma?"
translations.mn9:3: "Whenever, friends, a noble disciple understands unwholesome states, understands the roots of unwholesome states, understands wholesome states, and understands the roots of wholesome states— to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view, has upright view, is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has entered this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: But what, friends, is unwholesome, what is the root of unwholesome, what is wholesome, what is the root of wholesome? Killing living beings, friends, is unwholesome, taking what is not given is unwholesome, sexual misconduct is unwholesome, false speech is unwholesome, divisive speech is unwholesome, harsh speech is unwholesome, idle chatter is unwholesome, covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, wrong view is unwholesome— this, friends, is called unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friends, is the root of unwholesome? Greed is the root of unwholesome, hatred is the root of unwholesome, delusion is the root of unwholesome— this, friends, is called the root of unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friends, is the root of wholesome? Non-greed is the root of wholesome, non-hatred is the root of wholesome, non-delusion is the root of wholesome— this, friends, is called the root of wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: But what, friends, is taint, what is the origin of taint, what is the cessation of taint, what is the path leading to the cessation of taint? These three, friends, are taints— the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of ignorance. With the origin of ignorance, the taints originate; with the cessation of ignorance, the taints cease; this very Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of taints, that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: Whenever, friends, a noble disciple thus understands unwholesome states, thus understands the roots of unwholesome states, thus understands wholesome states, thus understands the roots of wholesome states, he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, eradicates the underlying tendency to hatred, destroys the underlying tendency to the view 'I am,' abandons ignorance and arouses true knowledge, and right in this very life attains the cessation of suffering— to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view, has upright view, is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has entered this true Dhamma,"
translations.sn1.10:2: "For those dwelling in the wilderness, the peaceful brahmacārins, who eat only one meal a day, by what virtue are they praised?"
translations.sn1.10:3: "They do not grieve over the past, they do not yearn for the future; they live with what is present— by this virtue they are praised.
translations.sn1.17:1: "Difficult is the life of a novice, difficult is the life of a trainee, difficult indeed is the life of a monk; there are many obstacles there, where the fool becomes discouraged."
translations.sn1.17:2: "How could one practice the monastic life, if one does not restrain the mind? At every step one would falter, following the flow of thoughts.
translations.sn1.17:3: "Like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, the bhikkhu should draw in his thoughts; unattached and not seeking support elsewhere, he who is fully extinguished would not be blamed by anyone."
translations.sn1.18:1: "There is a man restrained by shame, found in the world; who disregards blame, like a noble horse ignoring the whip."
translations.sn1.18:2: "Those who always dwell mindful, restrained by shame, will reach the end of suffering, moving evenly amidst unevenness."
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then, when the night had advanced, a certain devatā of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that devatā addressed the Blessed One: "How, sir, have you crossed the flood?" "I have crossed the flood, friend, by not standing still, by not struggling." "But how, sir, have you, not standing still, not struggling, crossed the flood?" "When I, friend, stand still, then I sink; when I, friend, struggle, then I am swept away. Thus, friend, by not standing still, by not struggling, I have crossed the flood."
translations.sn1.1:2: "Long have I seen a brahmin, fully extinguished, not standing, not striving, who has crossed the flood, unattached in the world."
translations.sn1.1:3: This said, the devatā. The Teacher was pleased. Then that devatā, knowing "The Teacher is pleased with me," having paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and thereupon disappeared.
translations.sn1.20:1: Thus have I heard — at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha in the Tapodārāma. Then in the last watch of the night, the Venerable Samiddhi rose and approached the Tapodā to bathe. Having bathed at Tapodā, he returned and stood with one robe on, drying his limbs. Then a certain devatā, radiant in the extreme, illuminating the entire Tapodā with her radiance, approached the Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, she stood in the air and addressed the Venerable Samiddhi in verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: "Do not be a bhikkhu without truly being one, for merely being doesn't make you a bhikkhu. Be a bhikkhu who truly is; let not time overtake you."
translations.sn1.20:20: "Beings are intent on what should not be spoken, fixed upon what should not be spoken. Without fully understanding what should not be spoken, they are bound by the bonds of death."
translations.sn1.20:21: "Having fully understood what should not be spoken, one does not regard the speaker. For that person there is no such thing, by which one could bind or condemn him. If you understand, speak up, O yakkha."
translations.sn1.20:22: "I do not, venerable sir, understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement made by the Blessed One. Please, venerable sir, may the Blessed One explain it so that I may understand its meaning in detail."
translations.sn1.20:23: "Whether equal, superior, or inferior — whoever thinks thus disputes with it. One who remains unshaken in these three ways, for him there is no notion of equal or superior. If you understand, speak up, O yakkha."
translations.sn1.20:25: "He has abandoned doubt, has not entered into conceit, has cut craving for name-and-form here. Him, with bonds severed, unobstructed, without hope, seekers do not find — neither devas nor humans here or beyond, nor in any abode in the heavens."
translations.sn1.20:3: "I do not know the time, the hour is not apparent. Therefore I practice as a bhikkhu without delay, lest time overtake me."
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that devatā, standing on the ground, said to the Venerable Samiddhi: "Young are you, bhikkhu, newly gone forth, with dark hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, not yet indulging in sensual pleasures. Enjoy, bhikkhu, human pleasures; do not chase after the future, abandoning the present."
translations.sn1.20:5: "No, friend, I do not chase after the future having abandoned the present. Rather, having abandoned the future, I pursue the present. For sensual pleasures, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One to be full of suffering, full of distress, with greater danger. This Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, effective here and now, to be realized individually by the wise."
translations.sn1.20:6: "But how, bhikkhu, have sensual pleasures been declared by the Blessed One to be full of suffering, full of distress, with greater danger? And how is this Dhamma directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, effective here and now, to be realized individually by the wise?"
translations.sn1.20:7: "I am, friend, newly gone forth, recently arrived in this Dhamma and Discipline. I am not able to explain it in detail. The Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is dwelling in Rājagaha in the Tapodārāma. Approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it."
translations.sn1.20:8: "It is not easy, bhikkhu, for us to approach that Blessed One, surrounded as he is by great assemblies of devatās. But if you, bhikkhu, approach the Blessed One and ask him this matter, we too will come to hear the Dhamma." "Very well, friend," replied the Venerable Samiddhi, and having answered that devatā, he went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Samiddhi said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.21:2: "Like a man whose head is on fire, or whose turban is burning, let the bhikkhu, mindful, wander forth for the abandoning of sensual desire."
translations.sn1.21:3: "Like a man whose head is on fire, or whose turban is burning, let the bhikkhu, mindful, wander forth for the abandoning of self-view."
translations.sn1.25:1: "If a bhikkhu is an arahant, one who has done his task, whose taints are destroyed, bearing his final body — even if he says, 'I speak,' or 'They say of me,'"
translations.sn1.25:2: "If a bhikkhu is an arahant, one who has done his task, whose taints are destroyed, bearing his final body — even if he says, 'I speak,' or 'They say of me,' understanding worldly convention skillfully, he would use such expressions merely as a matter of convention."
translations.sn1.25:3: "If a bhikkhu is an arahant, one who has done his task, whose taints are destroyed, bearing his final body — would such a bhikkhu, having taken up conceit, say, 'I speak,' or 'They say of me'?"
translations.sn1.25:4: "For one whose conceit is destroyed, there are no bonds; all bonds of conceit are removed. The wise one, having transcended the notion of 'I am,' might say, 'I speak.'
translations.sn1.25:5: "Or 'They say of me,' understanding worldly convention skillfully; he would use such expressions merely as a matter of convention."
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain devatā, radiant in the extreme, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove with her radiance, approached the Blessed One in the last watch of the night; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that devatā said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.2:5: "With the fading away of delight in existence, with the cessation of perception and consciousness, with the cessation and calming of feelings, this, friend, is how I understand it: the release, liberation, and detachment of beings."
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then a number of devatās of the Satullapā group, radiant in the extreme, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove with their radiance, approached the Blessed One in the last watch of the night; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one devatā recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.36:2: "Faith is the second treasure for a man; if he does not lose faith, his fame and glory grow, and after laying down the body, he goes to heaven."
translations.sn1.36:4: "Abandon anger, abandon pride, transcend all bonds. For one who clings to name-and-form, associations do not adhere to one who is desireless."
translations.sn1.36:5: "Fools, unintelligent people, indulge in negligence. The wise guard heedfulness as the highest treasure.
translations.sn1.36:6: "Do not indulge in negligence, do not delight in sensual pleasures. For the heedful one who meditates attains the highest happiness."
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard — at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha, in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. At that time, the Blessed One's foot had been injured by a splinter. Indeed, bodily feelings that were painful, sharp, severe, harsh, unpleasant, and disagreeable arose in the Blessed One; yet the Blessed One endured them mindfully and clearly comprehending, without being distressed. Then the Blessed One arranged his outer robe into four layers, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, one foot placed on top of the other, mindful and clearly comprehending.
translations.sn1.38:10: Bound by craving and rigid morality, they practice rough austerities for a hundred years; their mind is not rightly liberated, they are of low attainment and do not reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: There is no restraint for one proud of conceit, nor is there concentration for one uncomposed; even if a heedless man dwells alone in the forest, he would not cross over the domain of death.
translations.sn1.38:12: Having abandoned conceit, well-concentrated, with a mind thoroughly purified and completely freed, if a man dwells alone in the forest, mindful and heedful, he would indeed cross over the domain of death.
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred goddesses of the Tusita heaven, radiant and beautiful, illuminated the entire Maddakucchi with their splendor and approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing there, one goddess uttered this exclamation in the presence of the Blessed One: 'Indeed, friend, the ascetic Gotama is a serpent; even though painful, sharp, severe, harsh, unpleasant, and disagreeable bodily feelings have arisen, he endures them mindfully and clearly comprehending, without being distressed.'
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another goddess uttered this exclamation in the presence of the Blessed One: 'Indeed, friend, the ascetic Gotama is a lion; even though painful, sharp, severe, harsh, unpleasant, and disagreeable bodily feelings have arisen, he endures them mindfully and clearly comprehending, without being distressed.'
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another goddess uttered this exclamation in the presence of the Blessed One: 'Behold the mind well-concentrated, well-liberated, neither inflated nor deflated, nor constrained by forced suppression. Who could think that such a man—this human bull, human lion, human hero, human bull among men, human thoroughbred, human tusker—could be surpassed, except through blindness?'
translations.sn1.38:9: The five Vedas are equal to a hundred, ascetic brahmins practice austerities; yet their mind is not rightly liberated, they are of low attainment and do not reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard — at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then a certain goddess, radiant and beautiful, illuminated the entire Jeta Grove with her splendor during the night and approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing there, that goddess recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.41:4: Giving bears pleasant fruit; not giving does not bear such fruit. Thieves steal it, kings confiscate it, fire burns it, it perishes.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then, at the end, one must abandon it, along with the body and all possessions. Understanding this, the wise person should both enjoy and give; having given and having enjoyed according to their means, blameless, they ascend to heaven.
translations.sn1.42:1: 'Who gives strength? Who gives beauty? Who gives happiness? Who gives sight? And who is the giver of all? Tell me, when asked.'
translations.sn1.42:2: 'Food gives strength, clothing gives beauty, vehicles give happiness, lamps give sight.'
translations.sn1.42:3: 'He who gives shelter is the giver of all; and he who teaches the Dhamma is the giver of the deathless.'
translations.sn1.51:1: 'What is good until old age? What is well established? What is the jewel of men? What is hard for thieves to steal?'
translations.sn1.51:2: 'Virtue is good until old age, faith is well established, wisdom is the jewel of men, merit is hard for thieves to steal.'
translations.sn1.55:1: 'What gives rise to a man? What drives him? What leads him into saṁsāra? What is his great fear?'
translations.sn1.55:2: 'Craving gives rise to a man, mind drives him, being leads him into saṁsāra, suffering is his great fear.'
translations.sn1.56:1: 'What gives rise to a man? What drives him? What leads him into saṁsāra? Why does he not gain release?'
translations.sn1.56:2: 'Craving gives rise to a man, mind drives him, being leads him into saṁsāra, suffering does not release him.'
translations.sn1.57:1: 'What gives rise to a man? What drives him? What leads him into saṁsāra? What is his destination?'
translations.sn1.57:2: 'Craving gives rise to a man, mind drives him, being leads him into saṁsāra, kamma is his destination.'
translations.sn1.59:1: 'What is a man's second companion? What delights him? What does a mortal delight in, by which he is freed from all suffering?'
translations.sn1.59:2: 'Faith is a man's second companion, wisdom delights him; a mortal who delights in Nibbāna is freed from all suffering.'
translations.sn1.62:1: 'By what is the world led? By what is it drawn? By the power of what single thing are all things bent?'
translations.sn1.62:2: 'The world is led by mind, drawn by mind; by the power of mind, all things are bent.'
translations.sn1.63:2: 'The world is led by craving, drawn by craving; by the power of craving, all things are bent.'
translations.sn1.64:1: 'What binds the world? What is its movement? By the abandoning of what is Nibbāna said to be?'
translations.sn1.64:2: 'The world is bound by delight, thought is its movement; by the abandoning of craving, Nibbāna is said to be.'
translations.sn1.65:1: 'What binds the world? What is its movement? By the abandoning of what does one cut all bonds?'
translations.sn1.65:2: 'The world is bound by delight, thought is its movement; by the abandoning of craving, one cuts all bonds.'
translations.sn1.69:1: 'By what is the world confined? By the removal of what is it freed? By the abandoning of what does one cut all bonds?'
translations.sn1.69:2: 'The world is confined by desire, freed by the removal of desire; by the abandoning of desire, one cuts all bonds.'
translations.sn1.71:2: 'Having cut what does one sleep happily? Having cut what does one not grieve? For the destruction of what single thing did you, Gotama, approve?'
translations.sn1.71:3: 'Having cut anger, one sleeps happily; having cut anger, one does not grieve. O deity, anger is the root of poison, sharp and bitter; the noble ones praise its destruction, for having cut it, one does not grieve.'
translations.sn1.73:1: 'What wealth is best for a man? What, when well practiced, brings happiness? What taste is superior to all tastes? How is life said to be the best?'
translations.sn1.73:2: “Wealth is the best thing for a man here; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness; Truth indeed is the highest of tastes; Life guided by wisdom is said to be the best.”
translations.sn1.7:2: “Those for whom the Dhammas are not clearly understood, are led into the views of others; They do not awaken from sleep; The time for their awakening has not come.”
translations.sn1.7:3: “Those for whom the Dhammas are well understood, are not led into the views of others; They are fully awakened, rightly knowing; They dwell in equanimity even in uneven situations.”
translations.sn1.8:2: “Those for whom the Dhammas are well obscured, are led into the views of others; They do not awaken from sleep; The time for their awakening has not come.”
translations.sn1.8:3: “Those for whom the Dhammas are not obscured, are not led into the views of others; They are fully awakened, rightly knowing; They dwell in equanimity even in uneven situations.”
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, the lord of devas, addressed the devas of the Tāvatiṁsa heaven: ‘Do not, gentlemen, disparage this devaputta. For indeed, gentlemen, this devaputta formerly was a human being who, while human, acquired faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Having acquired faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Tathāgata’s well-proclaimed Dhamma discipline, upon the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world, among the devas of the Tāvatiṁsa. He outshines other devas in beauty and fame.’ Then, bhikkhus, as Sakka, the lord of devas, was encouraging the devas of the Tāvatiṁsa, he spoke these verses at that moment:
translations.sn11.14:6: “Therefore, the wise should cultivate faith and virtue, confidence and vision of Dhamma, ever mindful of the Buddha’s dispensation.”
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove. Then Sakka, the lord of devas, approached the Blessed One, and having approached, paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, the lord of devas, said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the source of a delightful land?”
translations.sn11.15:2: “Gardens and groves, well-planted lotus ponds; These are delightful to humans, but they do not surpass the sixteenfold excellence.”
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove. There the Blessed One said this: “Once in the past, bhikkhus, a certain ugly, misshapen yakkha was seated on the seat of Sakka, the lord of devas. Then, bhikkhus, the Tāvatiṁsa devas complained, grumbled, and criticized: ‘Amazing indeed, sir! Astonishing indeed, sir! This ugly, misshapen yakkha is seated on the seat of Sakka, the lord of devas!’ And, bhikkhus, as the Tāvatiṁsa devas complained, grumbled, and criticized, that yakkha became even more beautiful, more pleasing, and more radiant.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, the lord of devas, approached that angry yakkha; having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and, raising his folded hands toward that angry yakkha, declared his name three times: ‘I am Sakka, sir, the lord of devas; I am Sakka, sir, the lord of devas.’ And, bhikkhus, as Sakka, the lord of devas, declared his name, that yakkha became uglier, more misshapen, and more deformed. Having become uglier and more misshapen, he vanished right there. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, the lord of devas, sat down on his own seat and, as he encouraged the Tāvatiṁsa devas, spoke these verses at that moment:
translations.sn11.22:4: ‘My mind is not struck down, nor am I easily provoked; I will not be angry with you for long; anger does not remain in me.’
translations.sn11.22:5: ‘Though angry, I do not speak harshly, nor do I proclaim the Dhamma; I restrain myself, I watch over my own good.’
translations.sn11.24:2: “These two, bhikkhus, are foolish: one who does not see an offense as an offense, and one who does not accept in accordance with the Dhamma from one who points out an offense. These two, bhikkhus, are wise: one who sees an offense as an offense, and one who accepts in accordance with the Dhamma from one who points out an offense.”
translations.sn11.24:3: “Once in the past, bhikkhus, Sakka, the lord of devas, as he encouraged the Tāvatiṁsa devas in the Sudhammā assembly, spoke this verse at that moment:
translations.sn11.24:4: ‘May anger not overcome you, may old age not come upon your friends; Do not blame the blameless, nor speak maliciously; Then anger toward evil people will crush them like a mountain.’
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: “If you do not recollect me, then recollect the Dhamma: ‘Well proclaimed by the Blessed One is the Dhamma, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, effective, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ For, bhikkhus, when you recollect the Dhamma, any fear, dread, or horripilation that may arise will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: “If you do not recollect the Dhamma, then recollect the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples who have practiced well, who have practiced straightforwardly, who have practiced rightly, who have practiced properly—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals; this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ For, bhikkhus, when you recollect the Saṅgha, any fear, dread, or horripilation that may arise will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: “Why is that? Because the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an arahant, perfectly enlightened one, free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, fearless, without anxiety, unshakable, and does not flee.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said:
translations.sn11.3:13: “In the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, bhikkhus, recollect the Fully Enlightened One; fear will not come upon you.
translations.sn11.3:14: “If you cannot recollect the Buddha, the chief of the world, the bull among men, then recollect the Dhamma, the well-taught path leading out.
translations.sn11.3:15: “If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, the well-taught path leading out, then recollect the Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: “Thus, bhikkhus, for those who recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, fear, dread, or horripilation will not arise.”
translations.sn11.3:2: “Once upon a time, monks, a battle between the devas and asuras arose. Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas, addressed the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven:
translations.sn11.3:3: ‘If, gentlemen, fear, trembling, or horripilation should arise in any of the devas who have entered the battle, let them look to my banner-top. For when you look to my banner-top, any fear, trembling, or horripilation that has arisen will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look to my banner-top, then look to the banner-top of Pajāpati, the king of the devas. For when you look to the banner-top of Pajāpati, the king of the devas, any fear, trembling, or horripilation that has arisen will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: Why is that? Because, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas, is not free from lust, hatred, and delusion; he is fearful, trembling, and terrified, and runs away.
translations.sn11.3:9: And I, monks, say this: ‘If fear, trembling, or horripilation should arise in any of you who are gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, then at that time remember me: “Indeed, the Blessed One is arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, awakened, and blessed.” For when you remember me, any fear, trembling, or horripilation that has arisen will be abandoned, monks.'
translations.sn11.5:12: He moves for the good of both, his own and others'; knowing that another is upset, the mindful one calms down.
translations.sn11.5:14: Then, monks, after Sakka, the lord of the devas, had spoken these verses, the devas approved, but the asuras were silent. Then, monks, the retinues of the devas and asuras said this: ‘These verses were spoken by Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras. And they are violent in speech, aggressive in tone—indeed, quarreling, dispute, and conflict. These verses were spoken by Sakka, the lord of the devas. And they are non-violent in speech, non-aggressive in tone—indeed, no quarreling, no dispute, no conflict. Victory belongs to Sakka, the lord of the devas, through his well-spoken words.’ Thus, monks, victory belonged to Sakka, the lord of the devas, through his well-spoken words.
translations.sn11.5:2: ‘Let fools be struck more and more, since there is no one to restrain them; therefore, the wise should restrain the fool thoroughly with punishment.'
translations.sn11.5:3: Then, monks, after Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, had spoken this verse, the asuras approved, but the devas were silent. Then, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, said to Sakka, the lord of the devas: ‘Speak, lord of the devas, a verse.’ When this was said, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: ‘This alone I consider the restraint of a fool: when, knowing that another is angry, the mindful one remains calm.'
translations.sn11.5:5: Then, monks, after Sakka, the lord of the devas, had spoken this verse, the devas approved, but the asuras were silent. Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas, said to Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras: ‘Speak, Vepacitti, a verse.’ When this was said, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: ‘By forbearance alone, Vāsava, I see a fault: when the fool thinks, “He endures out of fear”; the foolish one becomes more arrogant, like a bull that runs away more frequently.'
translations.sn11.5:8: ‘Let him think what he will, or not think at all—he endures out of fear; there is no higher good than a beneficial companion, and nothing surpasses patience.'
translations.sn12.11:1: So I have heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. “Monks, these four kinds of nutriment support the existence or help the continuation of beings who have come to be or those seeking birth. What four? Coarse or fine material food as the first, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These four kinds of nutriment support the existence or help the continuation of beings who have come to be or those seeking birth.
translations.sn12.12:1: He was staying in Sāvatthī. “Monks, these four kinds of nutriment support the existence or help the continuation of beings who have come to be or those seeking birth. What four? Coarse or fine material food as the first, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These four kinds of nutriment support the existence or help the continuation of beings who have come to be or those seeking birth.'
translations.sn12.15:1: He was staying in Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down at one side. Seated there, Venerable Kaccānagotta said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, they say ‘right view, right view.’ In what way, venerable sir, is there right view?”
translations.sn12.15:2: “The world, Kaccāna, is for the most part dependent on a duality—existence and non-existence. But, Kaccāna, when one sees the origin of the world as it really is with right wisdom, the view of non-existence in the world does not arise. And, Kaccāna, when one sees the cessation of the world as it really is with right wisdom, the view of existence in the world does not arise. The world, Kaccāna, is for the most part bound by attachment, clinging, and insistence. But one who does not attach, cling, or insist, who does not determine ‘self is mine,’ does not doubt or waver about ‘suffering arises as suffering arises, suffering ceases as suffering ceases’—knowledge arises in him without dependence on others. This, Kaccāna, is how there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: So I have heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying in Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel’s Sanctuary. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then the naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings. After cordial greetings and polite conversation, he stood at one side. Standing there, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: ‘May we ask the Venerable Gotama a question, if the Venerable Gotama grants us permission to ask?’ ‘It is not the right time now, Kassapa; I have entered a private dwelling.’
translations.sn12.17:5: "'He who does, he who feels'—this, Kassapa, when one is attached to existence, leads to the view 'suffering is self-made,' and thus one falls into eternalism. 'Another does, another feels'—this, Kassapa, when one is overwhelmed by feeling, leads to the view 'suffering is made by another,' and thus one falls into annihilationism. Avoiding both extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness... Thus arises this whole mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness... Thus ceases this entire mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the wanderer Acela Kassapa said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, sir, excellent! Just as one might set upright what has been overturned, reveal what has been hidden, show the way to one who is lost, or bring an oil lamp into the dark so that those with eyes can see forms—so too has the Dhamma been explained in many ways by the Blessed One. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive ordination under the Blessed One, may I receive full admission?"
translations.sn12.17:7: "Whoever, Kassapa, previously belonging to another sect desires ordination and full admission in this Dhamma and Discipline, must undergo a probation period of four months. After four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied, they ordain him and grant full admission into bhikkhuhood. However, I recognize individual temperaments."
translations.sn12.18:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One, and after exchanging courteous greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: "'This feeling, this one feels'—this, Timbaruka, when one is attached to existence, leads to the view 'pleasure and pain are self-made,' but I do not say this. 'Another feeling, another feels'—this, Timbaruka, when one is overwhelmed by feeling, leads to the view 'pleasure and pain are made by another,' but I do not say this. Avoiding both extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness... Thus arises this whole mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness... Thus ceases this entire mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.19:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. "Due to being enveloped by ignorance, bhikkhus, and bound by craving, this body has come into being. Thus this body here, and external name-and-form, constitute this duality. Dependent on this duality, contact at the six sense bases arises, by which the fool feels pleasure and pain, or one of these."
translations.sn12.19:2: "Due to being enveloped by ignorance, bhikkhus, and bound by craving, this body has come into being. Thus this body here, and external name-and-form, constitute this duality. Dependent on this duality, contact at the six sense bases arises, by which the wise person feels pleasure and pain, or one of these."
translations.sn12.19:3: "Now, bhikkhus, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what makes the wise person different from the fool?" "Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, taking refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it."
translations.sn12.19:5: "The ignorance that envelops the fool and the craving with which he is bound—by this this body has come into being—this ignorance in the fool is not abandoned, and this craving is not destroyed. Why is that? The fool, bhikkhus, has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, at the breakup of the body, the fool becomes embodied again; being embodied, he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. 'He is not freed from suffering,' I say."
translations.sn12.23:5: "And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for craving? 'Feeling' should be said... 'Contact' should be said... 'The six sense bases' should be said... 'Name-and-form' should be said... 'Consciousness' should be said... 'Volitional formations' should be said. Volitional formations, bhikkhus, I say have a supporting condition, not that they are without one. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for volitional formations? 'Ignorance' should be said."
translations.sn12.23:6: "Thus, bhikkhus, ignorance is the supporting condition for volitional formations; volitional formations are the supporting condition for consciousness; consciousness is the supporting condition for name-and-form; name-and-form is the supporting condition for the six sense bases; the six sense bases are the supporting condition for contact; contact is the supporting condition for feeling; feeling is the supporting condition for craving; craving is the supporting condition for clinging; clinging is the supporting condition for existence; existence is the supporting condition for birth; birth is the supporting condition for suffering; suffering is the supporting condition for faith; faith is the supporting condition for joy; joy is the supporting condition for rapture; rapture is the supporting condition for tranquility; tranquility is the supporting condition for happiness; happiness is the supporting condition for concentration; concentration is the supporting condition for knowledge and vision of things as they really are; knowledge and vision of things as they really are is the supporting condition for disenchantment; disenchantment is the supporting condition for dispassion; dispassion is the supporting condition for liberation; liberation is the supporting condition for the knowledge of destruction."
translations.sn12.23:7: "Just as, bhikkhus, when heavy rain falls on a mountain peak, the water flows down along the slope, filling the clefts, gullies, and creeks. When the clefts, gullies, and creeks are full, they fill the small pools. The small pools being full, they fill the large pools. The large pools being full, they fill the small streams. The small streams being full, they fill the great rivers. The great rivers being full, they fill the great ocean."
translations.sn12.25:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then, in the evening, Venerable Bhūmija emerged from seclusion and went to Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous greetings, he sat down to one side and said to Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: "With the body, Hānanda, due to bodily intention, internal pleasure and pain arise. With speech, Hānanda, due to verbal intention, internal pleasure and pain arise. With the mind, Hānanda, due to mental intention, internal pleasure and pain arise, conditioned by ignorance."
translations.sn12.25:11: Either, Ānanda, one fabricates that bodily formation oneself, on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally. Or others fabricate that bodily formation, on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally. Or, Ānanda, one fabricates that bodily formation with full awareness, on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally. Or, Ānanda, one fabricates that bodily formation without full awareness, on account of which that pleasant or painful feeling arises internally.
translations.sn12.25:2: "There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action, who declare pleasure and pain to be self-made. There are others, friend Sāriputta, who are proponents of action, who declare pleasure and pain to be made by another. There are others, friend Sāriputta, who are proponents of action, who declare pleasure and pain to be both self-made and made by another. And there are others, friend Sāriputta, who are proponents of action, who declare pleasure and pain to be arisen fortuitously, neither self-made nor made by another. Now, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One say about this? How does he explain it, so that we may speak in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, without misrepresenting him with what is false, and so that we may explain the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, and no legitimate criticism or reproach should come our way?"
translations.sn12.25:3: "Dependent arising, friend, is what the Blessed One has declared regarding pleasure and pain. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who speaks thus speaks in accordance with what has been said by me, does not misrepresent me with what is false, explains the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, and no legitimate criticism or reproach should come their way."
translations.sn12.25:4: Now, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and declare pleasure and pain to be self-made— even that is dependent on contact. And those who declare it to be made by another... those who declare it to be both self-made and made by another... those who declare pleasure and pain to be arisen fortuitously, neither self-made nor made by another— even that is dependent on contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: Now, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and declare pleasure and pain to be self-made— to say that they would experience it apart from contact is not possible. And those who declare it to be made by another... those who declare it to be both self-made and made by another... those who declare pleasure and pain to be arisen fortuitously, neither self-made nor made by another— to say that they would experience it apart from contact is not possible.
translations.sn12.25:6: Venerable Ānanda heard the conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and the bhikkhu Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One, and having approached, paid homage and sat down to one side. Seated there, Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had heard with Venerable Sāriputta.
translations.sn12.25:7: "Well said, well said, Ānanda! Sāriputta has rightly explained it. Dependent arising, Ānanda, is what I have declared regarding pleasure and pain. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who speaks thus speaks in accordance with what has been said by me, does not misrepresent me with what is false, explains the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, and no legitimate criticism or reproach should come their way."
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, bhikkhus, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention— this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements— this is called form. Thus, this name and this form: this is called, bhikkhus, name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? These six, bhikkhus, are classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called, bhikkhus, consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, bhikkhus, are formations? These three, bhikkhus, are formations: bodily formation, verbal formation, mental formation. These are called, bhikkhus, formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, not knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering— this is called, bhikkhus, ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is existence? These three, bhikkhus, are kinds of existence: sense-desire existence, form existence, formless existence. This is called, bhikkhus, existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? These four, bhikkhus, are kinds of clinging: clinging to sense pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, clinging to a doctrine of self. This is called, bhikkhus, clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: "This has been said, Sāriputta, in the Ajita Questions in the Pārāyana:
translations.sn12.31:2: 'Those conditioned things, and those noble ones here numerous; Explain to me, sir, the wise one's conduct when questioned.'"
translations.sn12.31:3: "How should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail, Sāriputta?" When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: "Do you see, Sāriputta, 'This is real'"? "Yes, bhante, one who sees 'This is real' sees it truly with right wisdom. Seeing 'This is real' truly with right wisdom, one proceeds towards disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is real. One who sees truly with right wisdom the origin dependent on nutriment, seeing the origin dependent on nutriment truly with right wisdom, proceeds towards disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding that origin by nutriment. With the cessation of nutriment, one who sees truly with right wisdom that 'What is real is subject to cessation', seeing that 'What is real is subject to cessation' truly with right wisdom, proceeds towards disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation. Thus, bhante, is a noble one. "
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, sir, is the conditioned state? One truly understands, 'This is the real thing,' with right wisdom as it actually is. Having seen truly with right wisdom as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted, dispassionate, and ceases with regard to the real thing, and is liberated without clinging. One truly understands with right wisdom as it actually is, 'This arises dependent on nutriment.' Having seen truly with right wisdom as it actually is, 'This arises dependent on nutriment,' one becomes disenchanted, dispassionate, and ceases with regard to the arising dependent on nutriment, and is liberated without clinging. With the cessation of nutriment, one truly understands with right wisdom as it actually is, 'Whatever was real, that is subject to cessation.' Having seen truly with right wisdom as it actually is, 'Whatever was real, that is subject to cessation,' one becomes disenchanted, dispassionate, and ceases with regard to the state of cessation, and is liberated without clinging. Thus, sir, is the conditioned state. Thus, sir, was it said in the Pārāyana, in the Ajita’s Questions:
translations.sn12.35:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness... Thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.' When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: 'But what, sir, is aging-and-death, and to whom does this aging-and-death belong?' 'It is not appropriate to ask that,' said the Blessed One. 'To say, “What is aging-and-death, and to whom does this aging-and-death belong?” or to say, bhikkhu, “Another is aging-and-death, and another to whom this aging-and-death belongs,”—both these expressions are merely different ways of stating the same thing. With the view, “The soul is the same as the body,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. With the view, “The soul is one thing, the body another,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: “With birth as condition, aging-and-death.”'
translations.sn12.35:2: 'But what, sir, is birth, and to whom does this birth belong?' 'It is not appropriate to ask that,' said the Blessed One. 'To say, “What is birth, and to whom does this birth belong?” or to say, bhikkhu, “Another is birth, and another to whom this birth belongs,”—both these expressions are merely different ways of stating the same thing. With the view, “The soul is the same as the body,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. With the view, “The soul is one thing, the body another,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: “With existence as condition, birth.”'
translations.sn12.35:3: 'But what, sir, is existence, and to whom does this existence belong?' 'It is not appropriate to ask that,' said the Blessed One. 'To say, “What is existence, and to whom does this existence belong?” or to say, bhikkhu, “Another is existence, and another to whom this existence belongs,”—both these expressions are merely different ways of stating the same thing. With the view, “The soul is the same as the body,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. With the view, “The soul is one thing, the body another,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: “With clinging as condition, existence”... “With craving as condition, clinging”... “With feeling as condition, craving”... “With contact as condition, feeling”... “With the six sense bases as condition, contact”... “With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases”... “With consciousness as condition, name-and-form”... “With volitional formations as condition, consciousness.”'
translations.sn12.35:4: 'But what, sir, are volitional formations, and to whom do these volitional formations belong?' 'It is not appropriate to ask that,' said the Blessed One. 'To say, “What are volitional formations, and to whom do these volitional formations belong?” or to say, bhikkhu, “Others are volitional formations, and another to whom these volitional formations belong,”—both these expressions are merely different ways of stating the same thing. With the view, “The soul is the same as the body,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. With the view, “The soul is one thing, the body another,” bhikkhu, there is no holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations.”'
translations.sn12.35:5: 'With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, bhikkhu, all those speculative views that were pursued, indulged in, and agitated about—such as “What is aging-and-death? To whom does this aging-and-death belong?” or “Another is aging-and-death, another to whom this aging-and-death belongs,” or “The soul is the same as the body,” or “The soul is one thing, the body another”—all these will be abandoned, their root cut off, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and will no longer be subject to future arising.'
translations.sn12.35:7: 'With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, bhikkhu, all those speculative views that were pursued, indulged in, and agitated about—such as “What is existence?”... “What is clinging?”... “What is craving?”... “What is feeling?”... “What is contact?”... “What are the six sense bases?”... “What is name-and-form?”... “What is consciousness?”—all these will be abandoned, their root cut off, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and will no longer be subject to future arising.'
translations.sn12.38:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'Whatever one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one has underlying tendencies toward—this becomes an object for the establishing of consciousness. When there is an object, consciousness becomes established. When consciousness is established and grows, there is future renewed existence in the future. With the presence of future renewed existence, future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.38:2: 'If one does not intend, does not plan, but still has underlying tendencies, this becomes an object for the establishing of consciousness. When there is an object, consciousness becomes established. When consciousness is established and grows, there is future renewed existence in the future. With the presence of future renewed existence, future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.44:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'I will teach you, bhikkhus, the origin and the passing away of the world. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: And what, monks, is the origin of the world? With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is the condition for feeling; feeling is the condition for craving; craving is the condition for clinging; clinging is the condition for existence; existence is the condition for birth; birth is the condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair to arise. This, monks, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:3: With the ear and sounds as conditions, ear-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is the condition for feeling. Feeling is the condition for craving. Craving is the condition for clinging. Clinging is the condition for existence. Existence is the condition for birth. Birth is the condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair to arise. This, monks, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, monks, is the passing away of the world? With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is the condition for feeling; feeling is the condition for craving. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all cease. Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is the passing away of the world.
translations.sn12.46:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin went to the Blessed One, and on arrival exchanged courteous greetings with him. After exchanging polite and friendly talk, he sat down to one side. Seated there, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: "Who is it, Master Gotama, that performs the action and who is it that experiences the result?"
translations.sn12.46:3: "'He who acts is the one who experiences the result,' brahmin, this is one extreme. 'Another performs the action, another experiences the result,' brahmin, this is the second extreme. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma: 'With ignorance as condition, formations [come to be]; with formations as condition, consciousness... Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations... Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.'"
translations.sn12.51:10: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he knows it as impermanent, as not clung to, as not delighted in. If he feels a painful feeling, he knows it as impermanent, as not clung to, as not delighted in. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows it as impermanent, as not clung to, as not delighted in. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it disjoined [from attachment]. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it disjoined. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it disjoined.
translations.sn12.51:11: When feeling feelings that extend to the body, he knows: 'I am feeling feelings that extend to the body.' When feeling feelings that extend to life, he knows: 'I am feeling feelings that extend to life.' He knows: 'With the breakup of the body, after the termination of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will grow cold right here; the body will remain, discarded like a lifeless log.'
translations.sn12.51:12: Suppose, monks, a man were to lift a heated potsherd from a potter’s kiln and place it on level ground. The heat in it would subside right there, and the shards would remain. So too, monks, when a bhikkhu is feeling feelings that extend to the body, he knows: 'I am feeling feelings that extend to the body.' When feeling feelings that extend to life, he knows: 'I am feeling feelings that extend to life.' He knows: 'With the breakup of the body, after the termination of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will grow cold right here; the body will remain, discarded like a lifeless log.'
translations.sn12.51:13: "What do you think, monks? Would a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed generate meritorious formations, or demeritorious formations, or imperturbable formations?"
translations.sn12.51:14: "Or, with the complete non-existence of all formations, would consciousness still be discernible due to the cessation of formations?"
translations.sn12.51:2: "To what extent, monks, should a bhikkhu investigate thoroughly so as to rightly reach the complete ending of suffering?"
translations.sn12.51:3: "Here, monks, a bhikkhu investigates thoroughly: 'This various and manifold suffering that arises in the world—old age and death—what is the source of this suffering? What is its origin, its cause, its condition? When what exists does old age and death arise? When what does not exist do they not arise?' Investigating thoroughly, he understands: 'This various and manifold suffering that arises in the world—old age and death—has birth as its source, birth as its origin, birth as its cause, birth as its condition. When birth exists, old age and death arise; when birth does not exist, old age and death do not arise.'
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands old age and death, he understands the origin of old age and death, he understands the cessation of old age and death, and he understands the path leading to the cessation of old age and death.
