He practices accordingly, in accordance with the Dhamma. He is called, monks, a bhikkhu who rightly practices for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of old age and death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then, further investigating, he reflects: 'But this birth—what is its source, what is its origin, what is its cause, what is its condition? When what exists does birth arise? When what does not exist does it not arise?' Investigating thoroughly, he understands: 'Birth has existence as its source, existence as its origin, existence as its cause, existence as its condition. When existence exists, birth arises; when existence does not exist, birth does not arise.'
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands birth, he understands the origin of birth, he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the path leading to the cessation of birth; and he practices accordingly, in harmony with the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who practices rightly for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, further examining, he investigates: 'But this becoming—what is its source? ... And this clinging—what is its source? ... And this craving—what is its source? ... Feeling ... contact ... the six sense bases—what are they dependent on? ... Name-and-form—what are they dependent on? ... Consciousness—what is it dependent on? ... And these formations—what are they dependent on, from what do they arise, what is their source, what is their origin? On the presence of what do formations come to be? On the absence of what do formations not come to be?' Investigating thus, he understands: 'These formations have ignorance as their source, arise with ignorance, originate from ignorance, and are born of ignorance. With the presence of ignorance, formations come to be; with the absence of ignorance, formations do not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands formations, he understands the origin of formations, he understands the cessation of formations, and he understands the path leading to the cessation of formations; and he practices accordingly, in harmony with the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who practices rightly for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of formations.
translations.sn12.51:9: When, bhikkhus, a person in the grip of ignorance performs meritorious volitional activity, consciousness becomes bound to merit. If he performs demeritorious volitional activity, consciousness becomes bound to demerit. If he performs imperturbable volitional activity, consciousness becomes bound to the imperturbable. But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu's ignorance has been abandoned and true knowledge has arisen, then due to dispassion towards ignorance and arising of knowledge, he neither performs meritorious volitional activity, nor demeritorious, nor imperturbable. Not fabricating, not intending, he does not cling to anything in the world. Without clinging, he is not agitated; being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, lived is the holy life, done is what had to be done, there is no more of this state of being.'
translations.sn12.52:2: Just as, bhikkhus, a great mass of fire would keep burning in the case of ten, twenty, thirty, or forty cartloads of wood, and a man from time to time would throw dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood upon it, so that great mass of fire, being sustained by that fuel and nourishment, would burn for a long time. So too, bhikkhus, when one dwells contemplating the gratification in things that are objects of clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging ... Thus this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.52:3: When one dwells, bhikkhus, contemplating the danger in things that are objects of clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all cease. Thus there is cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'When one dwells, bhikkhus, contemplating the gratification in things that are objects of clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging ... Thus this entire mass of suffering originates.'
translations.sn12.55:2: Just as, bhikkhus, a great tree: all its roots, whether going downwards or spreading sideways, continually draw up sap and nourishment upwards. So too, that great tree, being sustained by that nourishment and support, would stand for a long time. So too, bhikkhus, when one dwells contemplating the gratification in things that are objects of clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging ... Thus this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.55:3: When one dwells, bhikkhus, contemplating the danger in things that are objects of clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases ... Thus there is cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. 'An unlearned ordinary person, bhikkhus, might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated with regard to this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because this body composed of the four great elements is seen to increase and decrease, to be taken up and put down. Therefore, in this regard, the unlearned ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated.'
translations.sn12.61:2: But with regard to what is called mind, thought, or consciousness, the unlearned ordinary person is incapable of becoming disenchanted, dispassionate, or liberated. Why is that? Because this has long been appropriated, cherished, and grasped by the unlearned ordinary person as 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self.' Therefore, in this regard, the unlearned ordinary person is incapable of becoming disenchanted, dispassionate, or liberated.
translations.sn12.61:3: Better, bhikkhus, is it for the unlearned ordinary person to regard this body composed of the four great elements as self rather than the mind. Why is that? Because this body composed of the four great elements may last one year, two years, three years, four years, five years, ten years, twenty years, thirty years, forty years, fifty years, a hundred years, or even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: There, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple carefully and wisely attends to dependent origination: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness … Thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.62:3: There, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple carefully and wisely attends to dependent origination: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' Bhikkhus, with pleasant contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same pleasant contact, the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that pleasant contact ceases and subsides. Bhikkhus, with painful contact as condition, painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that same painful contact, the painful feeling that arose dependent on that painful contact ceases and subsides. Bhikkhus, with neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Bhikkhus, suppose that with the rubbing together and joining of two sticks, heat arises and fire is produced. When those same two sticks are separated and laid aside, the heat that arose from them ceases and subsides. So too, bhikkhus, with pleasant contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same pleasant contact, the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that pleasant contact ceases and subsides … with painful contact … with neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: "What do you think, bhikkhus, would those people eat food for the sake of intoxication, for the sake of drunkenness, for adornment, or for beautification?" "No indeed, sir." "Would they not rather eat food merely for the sake of crossing the wilderness?" "Yes, sir." "So too, bhikkhus, I say that coarse food should be regarded in this way. With coarse food fully understood, the lust for the five sense pleasures is fully understood. With lust for the five sense pleasures fully understood, there is no fetter by which a noble disciple would return again to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, bhikkhus, should contact be regarded? Suppose, bhikkhus, a cow with bare hide were standing leaning on a thornbush. The creatures living in the thornbush would feed on her. If she were standing leaning on a tree, the creatures living in the tree would feed on her. If she were standing leaning on water, the creatures living in the water would feed on her. If she were standing leaning on the air, the creatures living in the air would feed on her. Whichever support that cow with bare hide would lean on, the creatures dependent on that support would feed on her. So too, bhikkhus, I say that contact should be regarded in this way. With contact fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. With the three feelings fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, bhikkhus, should mental volition as nutriment be regarded? Suppose, bhikkhus, a pit of glowing embers were full of coals, without flames, without smoke. Then a man would come, desiring life, recoiling from death, desiring pleasure, averse to pain. Two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him towards that pit of glowing embers. Then, bhikkhus, that man would have the intention to move away, the wish to move away, the determination to move away. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that man would think: 'If I fall into this pit of embers, I shall either die or suffer pain equal to death.' So too, bhikkhus, I say that mental volition as nutriment should be regarded in this way. With mental volition as nutriment fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. With the three cravings fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: If, bhikkhus, there is lust, delight, and craving for coarse food, consciousness becomes established and grows there. Wherever consciousness becomes established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Wherever there is the descent of name-and-form, there is growth in the formations. Wherever there is growth in the formations, there is future renewed existence. Wherever there is future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Wherever there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, bhikkhus.
translations.sn12.64:4: Just as, bhikkhus, a dyer or painter might create on a well-polished board, wall, or piece of cloth a likeness of a woman or a man, complete with all limbs and features, so too, bhikkhus, when there is lust, delight, and craving for coarse nutriment, consciousness becomes established and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is growth in the formations. Where there is growth in the formations, there is future renewed existence. Where there is future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say, bhikkhus, that is accompanied by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: But if, bhikkhus, there is no lust, no delight, no craving for coarse nutriment, then consciousness is not established and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth in the formations. Where there is no growth in the formations, there is no future renewed existence. Where there is no future renewed existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, I say, bhikkhus, that is without sorrow, without lamentation, without pain, without grief, without despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Just as, bhikkhus, in a roofed hall or a roofed pavilion, when the sun rises, the sunbeam enters through a window: 'On what is it based?' 'On the western wall, sir.' 'But if it is not based on the western wall?' 'On the earth, sir.' 'But if it is not based on the earth?' 'On the water, sir.' 'But if it is not based on the water?' 'It is not based, sir.' So too, bhikkhus, when there is no lust, no delight, no craving for coarse nutriment ….
translations.sn12.65:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. 'Before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened bodhisatta, this occurred to me: “How wretched is this world! It is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn, yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from old age and death. When will the escape from this suffering, from old age and death, be discerned?” To me, bhikkhus, this occurred: “With what as condition is old age and death? On account of what does old age and death come to be?” By careful attention, bhikkhus, there came the breakthrough by wisdom: “With birth as condition, old age and death come to be.”'
translations.sn12.65:3: To me, bhikkhus, this occurred: 'This consciousness turns back; it does not go beyond name-and-form. As far as one is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn, that is, dependent on name-and-form, consciousness; dependent on consciousness, name-and-form; dependent on name-and-form, the six sense bases; dependent on the six sense bases, contact … Thus arises this whole mass of suffering. “Arising, arising,” bhikkhus, to me in regard to things never heard before, there arose vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.'
translations.sn12.65:5: To me, bhikkhus, this occurred: 'With the absence of what does consciousness not come to be? With the cessation of what does the cessation of consciousness occur?' By careful attention, bhikkhus, there came the breakthrough by wisdom: 'With name-and-form absent, consciousness does not come to be; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of consciousness.'
translations.sn12.65:6: To me, bhikkhus, this occurred: 'I have discovered the path to enlightenment, namely: with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact … Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. “Cessation, cessation,” bhikkhus, to me in regard to things never heard before, there arose vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.'
translations.sn12.65:7: Just as, bhikkhus, a man wandering and traveling in a forest might see an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of old. He would follow along that path. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people of old, with parks, groves, ponds, and ramparts, delightful. Then, bhikkhus, that man would inform the king or a royal minister: 'Know this, sir: I, while wandering and traveling in the forest, saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of old. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people of old, with parks, groves, ponds, and ramparts, delightful. Let that city be restored, sir.' Then, bhikkhus, the king or royal minister would restore that city. After some time, that city would become prosperous, thriving, crowded with people, and well-developed. So too, bhikkhus, I saw the ancient path, the ancient road traveled by the fully enlightened ones of old.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kuru people in a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadamma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Do you contemplate, bhikkhus, the internal contemplation?' When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: 'I do contemplate, sir, the internal contemplation.' 'But how, bhikkhu, do you contemplate the internal contemplation?' Then that bhikkhu explained. But his explanation did not satisfy the mind of the Blessed One.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Now is the time, Blessed One; now is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to explain this in detail. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.' 'Then listen, Ānanda, and apply your mind well, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' the bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, contemplating further, one contemplates the intermediate: 'Where does this craving arise and where does it settle?' Contemplating thus, one knows: 'Whatever in the world is pleasing and delightful, it is there that craving arises and settles. And what in the world is pleasing and delightful? The eye in the world is pleasing and delightful; it is there that craving arises and settles. The ear in the world is pleasing and delightful... The nose in the world is pleasing and delightful... The tongue in the world is pleasing and delightful... The body in the world is pleasing and delightful... The mind in the world is pleasing and delightful; it is there that craving arises and settles.'
translations.sn12.66:6: For whoever, bhikkhus, in past times—whether ascetics or brahmins—regarded whatever in the world is pleasing and delightful as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure, they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased clinging. Those who increased clinging increased suffering. Those who increased suffering did not escape birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and anxieties. I say they did not escape suffering.
translations.sn12.66:7: And whoever, bhikkhus, in future times—whether ascetics or brahmins—will regard whatever in the world is pleasing and delightful as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure, they will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase clinging. Those who increase clinging will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not escape birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and anxieties. I say they will not escape suffering.
translations.sn12.66:8: And whoever, bhikkhus, at present—whether ascetics or brahmins—regard whatever in the world is pleasing and delightful as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure, they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase clinging. Those who increase clinging increase suffering. Those who increase suffering do not escape birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and anxieties. I say they do not escape suffering.
translations.sn12.67:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Benares, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from seclusion and went to Venerable Sāriputta; and having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous and amiable talk, he sat down at one side. Seated there, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, is aging and death self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or is it without cause, spontaneously arisen?' 'Friend Koṭṭhika, aging and death is neither self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without cause, spontaneously arisen. Rather, aging and death is dependent on birth.'
translations.sn12.67:2: 'Friend Sāriputta, is birth self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or is it without cause, spontaneously arisen?' 'Friend Koṭṭhika, birth is neither self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without cause, spontaneously arisen. Rather, birth is dependent on existence.'
translations.sn12.67:4: 'Friend Sāriputta, is consciousness self-made, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or is it without cause, spontaneously arisen?' 'Friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is neither self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without cause, spontaneously arisen. Rather, consciousness is dependent on name-and-form.'
translations.sn12.67:5: 'Now we understand the Venerable Sāriputta’s statement thus: 'Friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is neither self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without cause, spontaneously arisen. Rather, name-and-form is dependent on consciousness.'
translations.sn12.67:7: How, friend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be understood?" "Therefore, friend, I will give you a simile. Wise men understand the meaning of a statement through similes. Just as, friend, two bundles of reeds might stand leaning against each other, so too, with nāmarūpa as condition, there is viññāṇa; with viññāṇa as condition, nāmarūpa; with nāmarūpa as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact... Thus there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering. And if, friend, one of those bundles of reeds were to be pulled away, the other would fall; if the other were to be pulled away, the one would fall. So too, with the cessation of nāmarūpa, viññāṇa ceases; with the cessation of viññāṇa, nāmarūpa ceases; with the cessation of nāmarūpa, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases... Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."
translations.sn12.67:8: "Amazing, friend Sāriputta! Astounding, friend Sāriputta! Well said indeed by the Venerable Sāriputta. And we approve of this statement of the Venerable Sāriputta in these thirty-two ways:"
translations.sn12.68:13: "Therefore, is the Venerable Nārada an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?" "Friend, 'cessation of existence is nibbāna'—this has been clearly seen with right wisdom as it actually is, yet I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. Just as, friend, a pool in a desert path, where there is neither rope nor water-bucket. Then a man would come, oppressed by heat, weary, exhausted, thirsty, and he would see that pool. He would know 'there is water', but he would not experience it directly with his body. So too, friend, 'cessation of existence is nibbāna'—this has been clearly seen with right wisdom as it actually is, yet I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed."
translations.sn12.68:6: "Therefore, is the Venerable Musīla an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?" When this was said, the Venerable Musīla remained silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, the great ocean draws the great rivers towards it; the great rivers draw the smaller rivers towards them; the smaller rivers draw the large streams towards them; the large streams draw the small streams towards them. So too, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, nāmarūpa; with nāmarūpa as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death."
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel's Sanctuary. At that time, the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and received abundant offerings of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines. The bhikkhu Saṅgha too was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and received abundant offerings. But the wanderers of other sects were unhonored, disrespected, unrevered, unvenerated, and received no offerings of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines.
translations.sn12.70:10: "But do you, venerable sirs, who know and see in this way, dwell having directly touched with the body those liberations that transcend form, the formless attainments?" "No, indeed, friend."
translations.sn12.70:11: "Then now, venerable sirs, there is this declaration and non-attainment of these states; what is your position, friend?" "We are liberated by wisdom, friend Suvimā."
translations.sn12.70:12: "I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement made by the venerable ones. Please, venerable sirs, speak in such a way that I may understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement made by the venerable ones." "Whether you understand it or not, friend Susīma, we are liberated by wisdom."
translations.sn12.70:13: Then the Venerable Susīma rose from his seat, went to the Blessed One, and having paid homage to him, sat down at one side. The Venerable Susīma then reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with those bhikkhus. "First comes knowledge of the fixed nature of dhammas, Susīma, then knowledge of nibbāna."
translations.sn12.70:14: "I do not understand, venerable sir, the detailed meaning of this brief statement made by the Blessed One. Please, venerable sir, speak in such a way that I may understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement made by the Blessed One." "Whether you understand it or not, Susīma, first comes knowledge of the fixed nature of dhammas, then knowledge of nibbāna."
translations.sn12.70:16: "Therefore, Susīma, whatever kind of form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—every form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Whatever kind of feeling there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—every feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Whatever kind of perception there is... Whatever kind of formations there are, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all formations should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Whatever kind of consciousness there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—every consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'"
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, Susima, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with fabrications, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, passion fades away. With the fading of passion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: 'I am liberated.' He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, lived is the holy life, done is what had to be done, there is no more of this state of being.'
translations.sn12.70:18: 'With birth as condition, aging and death,' Susima, do you see this?
translations.sn12.70:25: 'But, Susima, do you, knowing thus and seeing thus, dwell having personally touched with the body and abiding in those liberations that are formless, transcending form?'
translations.sn12.70:6: 'But do you, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, hear with the purified divine ear-element, surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?'
translations.sn12.70:8: 'But do you, venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, recollect various past lives, with their details and characteristics? For instance: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand births; many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of both world-contraction and expansion: “There I was named so, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn here. Here I was named so, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; passing away from here, I was reborn there.” Thus do you recollect various past lives with their details and characteristics?'
translations.sn12.70:3: Then the Venerable Ānanda, taking Susima the wanderer, went to the Blessed One; and on arriving, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. The Venerable Ānanda seated at one side said to the Blessed One: 'This Susima the wanderer says: “I wish, friend Ānanda, to lead the spiritual life in this Dhamma and discipline.”' 'Then, Ānanda, ordain Susima.' And Susima the wanderer obtained ordination from the Blessed One, and received full admission.
translations.sn12.70:27: Then the Venerable Susima prostrated himself at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One: 'I have erred, venerable sir, I have transgressed, being foolish, being stupid, being unskilful, that I, a Dhamma-seeker, have gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and discipline. May the Blessed One accept my offence as an offence, for the future restraint.'
translations.sn12.70:2: At that time Susima the wanderer was dwelling at Rājagaha together with a large company of wanderers. Then the company of wanderers said to Susima the wanderer: 'Come, friend Susima, go forth into the ascetic Gotama's order and lead the spiritual life. When you have learned the Dhamma, you can teach us. Then we too, having learned the Dhamma, will teach householders. Thus we too will be honoured, respected, esteemed, revered, and saluted, and will obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines for the sick.' 'Very well, friends,' replied Susima the wanderer, accepting the instruction of his company; and he went to the Venerable Ānanda. On arriving, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. Seated at one side, Susima the wanderer said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'I wish, friend Ānanda, to lead the spiritual life in this Dhamma and discipline.'
translations.sn12.70:21: "But, Susima, do you, knowing thus, seeing thus, hear with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether near or far?" "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn12.70:5: "But do you, venerable ones, knowing thus, seeing thus, experience various kinds of psychic powers: being one, become many; being many, become one; appear and vanish; go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains, as if through space; dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; walk on water without sinking as if on earth; fly cross-legged through the air like a bird; with your hand touch and stroke the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; and exercise bodily mastery even up to the Brahmā world?" "No, friend."
translations.sn12.70:7: "But do you, venerable ones, knowing thus, seeing thus, understand the minds of other beings, of other persons, with your own mind? Do you understand a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust'; a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust'; a mind with hate as 'a mind with hate'; a mind without hate as 'a mind without hate'; a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion'; a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion'; a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind'; a distracted mind as 'a distracted mind'; a lofty mind as 'a lofty mind'; a lowly mind as 'a lowly mind'; a superior mind as 'a superior mind'; an incomparable mind as 'an incomparable mind'; a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind'; an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind'; a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind'; an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind'?" "No, friend. "
translations.sn12.70:9: “But do you, venerable ones, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand beings according to their actions: ‘These beings, endowed with bad bodily conduct, bad verbal conduct, and bad mental conduct, revilers of noble ones, holding wrong view, performing deeds rooted in wrong view, after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell; or these beings, endowed with good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct, not revilers of noble ones, holding right view, performing deeds rooted in right view, after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world’? Do you thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand beings according to their actions?” “No, indeed, friend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrel’s Feeding Place. At that time Venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills with a large community of bhikkhus.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘My sense of urgency and heedfulness will be established toward senior, middle, and junior bhikkhus.’ This is how you should train.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Whatever Dhamma I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will bear it in mind, attend to it with the whole mind, and listen with a heart set on giving it up.’ This is how you should train.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘My mindfulness of the body accompanied by rapture will not be abandoned.’ This is how you should train.”
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, the Blessed One, having instructed me with this exhortation, rose from his seat and departed. Within seven days, friend, I became one who remembers; I attained enlightenment on the eighth day.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Blessed One, having left the path, approached a certain foot of a tree. Then, friend, I folded my outer robe fourfold and said to the Blessed One: ‘Let the Blessed One sit here, for my long-term welfare and happiness.’ The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then, friend, the Blessed One said to me: ‘This outer robe of yours, Kassapa, is indeed soft.’ ‘Let the Blessed One accept this outer robe of mine, out of compassion,’ I said. ‘But you, Kassapa, will wear rag-robes, cast-off cloth, and discarded shrouds.’ ‘I will wear, sir, the Blessed One’s rag-robes, cast-off cloth, and discarded shrouds.’ So, friend, I offered my outer robe to the Blessed One. And I myself took up the rag-robes, cast-off cloth, and discarded shrouds of the Blessed One.
translations.sn16.11:17: Indeed, friend, with the destruction of the taints, I dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom. Let him who will, consider me as concealing the seven treasures, or even an elephant seven or eight ratanas long under a palm-leaf roof—let him who will consider me as concealing the six direct knowledges.
translations.sn16.11:2: At that time, thirty of Venerable Ānanda’s companions, bhikkhus who were mostly young men newly ordained, had given up the training and reverted to the lower life. Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered at will in the Southern Hills, approached Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel’s Feeding Place, where Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling. Having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. Then Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: “For how many reasons, friend Ānanda, did the Blessed One institute the rule of taking meals in three households within a village?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “Three reasons, venerable Kassapa, are why the Blessed One instituted the rule of taking meals in three households within a village: for restraining difficult individuals, for the comfortable abiding of capable bhikkhus, so that the malicious party might not split the Saṅgha relying on that, and for the welfare of families. These three reasons, venerable Kassapa, are why the Blessed One instituted the rule of taking meals in three households within a village.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “And how is it, friend Ānanda, that you wander on tour with these new bhikkhus who are unrestrained in the sense faculties, immoderate in eating, and unmindful of wakefulness? I think you are causing harm to the herd, causing harm to the families. Indeed, your community is being corrupted, friend Ānanda; your young bhikkhus are becoming spoiled. Surely this young man does not consider himself even slightly at fault.”
translations.sn16.11:6: Then the bhikkhunī Thullanandā heard: “It seems the Venerable Mahākassapa has discredited the Venerable Ānanda, the Vedehan sage, by calling him a ‘youngster’.”
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, displeased, expressed her displeasure: “How can the Venerable Mahākassapa, who was formerly of another sect, think that the Venerable Ānanda, the Vedehan sage, should be discredited by calling him a ‘youngster’?” Venerable Mahākassapa heard the bhikkhunī Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Just now, friend Ānanda, an unconsidered and hasty statement was made by the bhikkhunī Thullanandā. Friend, since I shaved my head and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness, I know of no other teacher whom I have acknowledged, apart from the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. Before, friend, while I was still a householder, this thought occurred to me: “The household life is crowded and dusty; the life gone forth is spacious. It's not easy, while living in a house, to lead a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?” Then, friend, some time later, having made a patched outer robe, I went forth from the household life into homelessness, directing my heart towards those who in the world are arahants.'
translations.sn16.13:2: Just as, Kassapa, gold does not disappear so long as no counterfeit made to resemble gold has arisen in the world. But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit made to resemble gold arises in the world, then gold disappears. So too, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear so long as no counterfeit of the true Dhamma has arisen in the world. But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.
translations.sn16.13:4: Five, Kassapa, are the declining factors that lead to the deterioration and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen dwell without respect and without confidence towards the Teacher, without respect and without confidence towards the Dhamma, without respect and without confidence towards the Saṅgha, without respect and without confidence towards the training, and without respect and without confidence towards concentration. These, Kassapa, are the five declining factors that lead to the deterioration and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Benares in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākassapa. When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. As he sat to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Mahākassapa: 'It is said, friend Kassapa: “one devoid of zeal, devoid of shame, incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.” But one with zeal and with shame is capable of awakening, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.'
translations.sn16.2:3: And how, friend, is one devoid of shame? Here, friend, a bhikkhu feels no shame that unarisen bad unwholesome qualities might arise for his own harm; feels no shame that arisen bad unwholesome qualities might not be abandoned for his own harm; feels no shame that unarisen wholesome qualities might not arise for his own harm; feels no shame that arisen wholesome qualities might not be maintained, not decrease, not grow, not reach fulfillment by development for his own harm. Thus, friend, is one devoid of shame. Thus, friend, one devoid of zeal and devoid of shame is incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how, friend, has one zeal? Here, friend, a bhikkhu exerts zeal that unarisen bad unwholesome qualities do not arise for his own harm; exerts zeal that arisen bad unwholesome qualities are abandoned for his own harm; exerts zeal that unarisen wholesome qualities arise for his own harm; exerts zeal that arisen wholesome qualities are maintained, do not decrease, but grow and reach fulfillment by development for his own harm. Thus, friend, one has zeal.
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel's Sanctuary. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the Venerable Mahākassapa, who was seated there: 'You are now old, Kassapa, and these coarse rag-robes you wear are heavy. Therefore, you should now wear robes offered by householders, accept invitations to meals, and dwell near me.'
translations.sn21.10:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel's Sanctuary. At that time a certain bhikkhu named Thera was a solitary dweller and an advocate of solitary dwelling. He would enter a village alone for alms, return alone, sit alone in seclusion, and pace alone in meditation. Then several bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As they sat there, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, a certain bhikkhu named Thera is a solitary dweller and an advocate of solitary dwelling.'
translations.sn21.10:3: 'There is such a one, Thera, who is a solitary dweller—I do not deny it. But, Thera, I say that a solitary dweller is one who is fully filled with spaciousness. Listen, pay close attention; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' ... 'And how, Thera, is a solitary dweller fully filled with spaciousness? Here, Thera, what is past is abandoned, what is future is relinquished, and in regard to present personal acquisitions, craving and delight are well restrained. Thus, Thera, is a solitary dweller fully filled with spaciousness.'
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus!' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāno said: 'Friends, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought occurred to my mind: “The noble silence, the noble silence is spoken of. What then is the noble silence?” And it occurred to me: “Here, a monk, with the stilling of thought and examination, gains internal confidence, unification of mind, without thought, without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and happiness, and dwells in the second jhāna. This is called the noble silence.” So indeed, friends, I attained and dwelled in the second jhāna, with the stilling of thought and examination, gaining internal confidence, unification of mind, without thought, without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and happiness. While I was dwelling in this abiding, perception and mental attention associated with thought arose in me.'
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus!' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: 'Friends, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought occurred to my mind: “Is there anything in the world, such that when it changes and alters, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in me?” And it occurred to me: “There is nothing in the world such that when it changes and alters, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in me.”'
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Now at that time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno were dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel's Sanctuary, in a single dwelling. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno. When they had exchanged greetings and cordial talk, he sat down at one side. Seated at one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno:
translations.sn21.3:2: 'Your faculties are clearly serene, friend Moggallāna, your complexion is pure and bright. Surely, friend Mahāmoggallāna, you have dwelled today in a peaceful abiding.' 'I have dwelled today, friend, in a coarse abiding. But still, I had a Dhamma discussion.' 'With whom did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma discussion?' 'With the Blessed One, friend, I had a Dhamma discussion.' 'But, friend, the Blessed One is now dwelling far away at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno go to the Blessed One by means of psychic power, or did the Blessed One come to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno by means of psychic power?' 'I did not go to the Blessed One by means of psychic power, friend, nor did the Blessed One come to me by means of psychic power. But as far as the Blessed One is concerned, so far my divine eye became purified and my divine ear. And the Blessed One, as far as I am concerned, so far his divine eye became purified and his divine ear.' 'But how, friend, did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāno have a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One?'
translations.sn21.3:3: 'Here, friend, I said to the Blessed One: “The energetic one, the energetic one is spoken of, sir. In what way, sir, is one energetic?” When this was said, the Blessed One said to me: “Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused: “Let the skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood of my body dry up; yet, without attaining what can be attained by human strength, human energy, human striving, I will not relax my effort.” It is in this way, Moggallāna, that one is energetic.” This, friend, is how I had a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One.'
translations.sn21.3:6: 'Sāriputta indeed through wisdom, through virtue and calm; even a bhikkhu who has reached the far shore would not surpass him.'
translations.sn21.6:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya coming from afar. Seeing him, he addressed the bhikkhus: 'Do you see, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu coming, dark-complexioned, ugly, misshapen, deformed in appearance?' 'Yes, sir.' 'This bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is mighty in psychic power, great in influence, and there is no attainment as easily accessible to him as the one he has not yet attained. For the sake of which goal noble sons rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge and dwells in it in this very life.' This is what the Blessed One said ... the Teacher:
translations.sn21.6:2: 'Geese, swans, peacocks, elephants, horses, deer—all fear the lion; there is no bodily likeness equal to his.'
translations.sn21.8:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One's maternal cousin, having folded and refolded his robe, applied eye ointment, and holding a clean bowl, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Nanda, seated at one side: 'It is not fitting for you, Nanda, a son of good family who has gone forth in faith from home to homelessness, to wear robes that are folded and refolded, to apply eye ointment, and to carry a clean bowl. It is fitting for you, Nanda, a son of good family who has gone forth in faith from home to homelessness, to dwell as a forest dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and uninterested in sensual pleasures.' This is what the Blessed One said ... the Teacher:
translations.sn21.8:2: 'When shall I see Nanda, a forest dweller, a rag-robe wearer, living content with anything, uninterested in sensual pleasures?'
translations.sn21.9:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Tissa, the Buddha's nephew, went to the Buddha, and on arrival, having bowed down to the Buddha, he sat down to one side, sorrowful, dejected, with tears flowing. Then the Buddha said to the Venerable Tissa: 'Why is it, Tissa, that you are sitting there sorrowful, dejected, with tears flowing?' 'Indeed, sir, the bhikkhus are reproaching me with harsh words.' 'But you, Tissa, should be one who speaks and is patient in speech. It is not fitting for a clansman who has gone forth in faith from the household life to homelessness, Tissa, that you should be one who speaks and is not patient in speech. It is fitting for a clansman who has gone forth in faith from the household life to homelessness that you should be one who speaks and is patient in speech.'
translations.sn22.100:2: Do you see, bhikkhus, this thing called mind as it really is?
translations.sn22.100:3: I do not see, bhikkhus, any other single group as having such a mind as these beings in the animal realm. Even those, bhikkhus, beings in the animal realm are known by the mind through the mind. Even with those beings in the animal realm, one mind is even more known by another mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, one should frequently examine one's own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion.' Beings are defiled by mental defilements; beings are purified by mental purity.
translations.sn22.101:1: At Sāvatthī. 'I speak of the destruction of the taints, bhikkhus, knowing and seeing, not without knowing and seeing. And what is it, bhikkhus, that one knows and sees when the destruction of the taints occurs? 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling ... such is perception ... such are volitional formations ... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness'—thus, bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, the destruction of the taints occurs.
translations.sn22.101:2: For a bhikkhu who dwells without devoting himself to the practice of meditation, even if such a wish arises: 'Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!' still his mind is not liberated from the taints without clinging. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of lack of development.' Lack of development of what? Lack of development of the four establishments of mindfulness, lack of development of the four right efforts, lack of development of the four bases of psychic power, lack of development of the five faculties, lack of development of the five powers, lack of development of the seven factors of enlightenment, lack of development of the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Suppose, bhikkhus, a hen has eight, ten, or twelve eggs, but she does not properly sit on them, warm them, or incubate them. Even if she has such a wish: 'Oh, that my chicks might break through the eggshells with their claws and beaks and emerge safely!' still those chicks are unable to break through the eggshells with their claws and beaks and emerge safely. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, those eggs—eight, ten, or twelve—are not properly sat on, warmed, or incubated by the hen. So too, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who dwells without devoting himself to the practice of meditation, even if such a wish arises: 'Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!' still his mind is not liberated from the taints without clinging. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of lack of development.' Lack of development of what? Lack of development of the four establishments of mindfulness ... the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas in the Bhesakaḷā Grove at Suṁsumāragira. Then Nakulapitā the householder went to the Blessed One, and on arrival, having bowed down to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Nakulapitā the householder said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.1:10: He regards feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. He is obsessed by the notion: 'I am feeling, feeling is mine.' When he is obsessed by the notion 'I am feeling, feeling is mine,' that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of that feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise in him.
translations.sn22.1:11: He regards perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. He is obsessed by the notion: 'I am perception, perception is mine.' When he is obsessed by the notion 'I am perception, perception is mine,' that perception changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of that perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise in him.
translations.sn22.1:12: He regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessed of volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations. He is obsessed by the notion: 'I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine.' When he is obsessed by the notion 'I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine,' those volitional formations change and become otherwise. With the change and alteration of those volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair arise in him.
translations.sn22.1:13: They perceive consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness; or they perceive consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. They are obsessed with the notion: 'I am consciousness, this is mine.' When one obsessed with 'I am consciousness, this is mine,' that consciousness changes and alters. Due to the change and alteration of consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. Thus, householder, one has a diseased body and a diseased mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, does one have a diseased body but not a diseased mind? Here, a well-instructed noble disciple, who sees the noble ones and is skilled in their Dhamma, well-trained in the noble Dhamma, who sees the good persons and is skilled in their Dhamma, well-trained in the Dhamma of good persons, does not perceive form as self, nor self as possessing form; nor does he perceive form in self, or self in form. He is not obsessed with the notion: 'I am form, this is mine.' When one not obsessed with 'I am form, this is mine,' that form changes and alters. Due to the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.
translations.sn22.1:2: "I am, venerable sir, aged, old, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, burdened with illness, frail. I am one who sees impermanence, venerable sir, and I have listened to the teachings of the Blessed One and the bhikkhus devoted to the mind. Please instruct me, venerable sir; please advise me, venerable sir; for my long-term welfare and happiness."
translations.sn22.1:3: "Indeed so, householder, indeed so, householder. Diseased indeed is this body, householder, born from a womb, conditioned, fragile. Whoever, householder, while maintaining this body, would claim even for a moment to be free from illness—what else but childishness? Therefore, you should train yourself thus: 'Though my body may be diseased, my mind will remain healthy.' Thus should you train yourself, householder."
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakulapita, having approved and welcomed the words of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and went to where Venerable Sāriputta was; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. Seeing him seated there, Venerable Sāriputta said to the householder Nakulapita: "Your faculties are serene, householder, your complexion is clear and pure. Have you today heard a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One?"
translations.sn22.1:7: "But did it not occur to you, householder, to ask the Blessed One further: 'To what extent, venerable sir, does one have both a diseased body and a diseased mind, and to what extent does one have a diseased body but not a diseased mind?'" "Even if I had to travel far, venerable sir, I would come to the presence of Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. May Venerable Sāriputta himself explain the meaning of this statement."
translations.sn22.1:8: "Then listen well, householder, apply your mind carefully; I will speak."
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha. Then a number of bhikkhus from the western region approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Those bhikkhus seated to one side said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, we wish to go to the western region, to establish residence there.'
translations.sn22.22:6: "The five aggregates are indeed the burden, the person is the bearer of the burden; Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, laying down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, bhikkhus, is laying down the burden? It is the complete fading away and cessation, giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment to that same craving. This, bhikkhus, is called laying down the burden.
translations.sn22.22:2: And who, bhikkhus, is the burden-bearer? The person is meant by this term. This venerable one, of such a name, of such a clan—this, bhikkhus, is called the burden-bearer.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, bhikkhus, is taking up the burden? It is that craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called taking up the burden.
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friends, one were to dwell having taken up unwholesome states, and if in the present life there were happiness in living, without obstruction, without distress, without fever, and after the breakup of the body, following death, a favorable destination could be expected, then the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But since, friends, one who dwells having taken up unwholesome states experiences suffering in the present life, with obstruction, distress, and fever, and after the breakup of the body, following death, an unfavorable destination is to be expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:2: "Have you, bhikkhus, informed Sāriputta?" "No, venerable sir, we have not informed the Venerable Sāriputta." "Then inform Sāriputta, bhikkhus. Sāriputta, bhikkhus, is wise, a helper of his fellow bhikkhus, one who benefits his companions in the holy life." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.1:9: "And how, householder, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind? Here, householder, an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble teaching, untrained in the noble teaching; who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the teaching of good persons, untrained in the teaching of good persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He is obsessed with the idea: 'I am form, this is mine.' When he is obsessed with 'I am form, this is mine,' that form changes and alters. Due to the change and alteration of form, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.sn22.2:3: At that time, Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a certain leaf hut. Then those monks, having approved and agreed with what the Blessed One had said, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and went to Venerable Sāriputta; and approaching him, they exchanged greetings with him. After exchanging courteous and amiable talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'We wish, friend Sāriputta, to go to the western region, to establish residence in the western countryside. We have taken leave of the Teacher.'
translations.sn22.2:5: 'Even from afar, friend, we would come to the venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good indeed if the venerable Sāriputta would explain the meaning of this statement.' 'Then, friends, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One … and sitting down to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: 'May the Blessed One please teach me the Dhamma briefly, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I may dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.' 'Whatever one clings to, one conceives accordingly; whatever one conceives, one is bound thereby. One who does not cling to anything does not conceive it; one who does not conceive it is not bound thereby.' 'I have come to know it, Blessed One, I have come to know it, Sugata.'
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantī people in the Kuraraghara mountain at Papāta. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached Venerable Mahākaccāna, and having approached, paid homage to him and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: 'The Blessed One has said this in the Aṭṭhaka Vagga, in the Māgaṇḍiya Question: '
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one dispassionate towards sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone is free from lust, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from fever, and free from craving for sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, one is dispassionate towards sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one passionate towards sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone is not free from lust, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, and not free from craving for sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, one is passionate towards sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, is one aspiring? Here, householder, someone has such a thought: 'May I become such in the future life, may my feeling be such, may my perception be such, may my formations be such, may my consciousness be such.' Thus, householder, one is aspiring.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, is one a speaker of quarrelsome speech among people? Here, householder, someone speaks in this way: 'You don’t understand this Dhamma and discipline; I understand it. What do you understand about this Dhamma and discipline? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. What I say should be said first, what I say should be said later. My views are consistent; yours are inconsistent. Your doctrine has been refuted; go forth to defend it, or if you can, abandon it.' Thus, householder, one is a speaker of quarrelsome speech among people.
translations.sn22.3:17: 'Having abandoned the home, homeless, not dwelling in the village, dispassionate towards sensual pleasures, not aspiring, how could one engage in quarrelsome speech among people?'
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, is one dwelling in attachments? One who is attached and bound to the signs of form, householder, is called 'dwelling in attachments.' One who is attached and bound to the signs of sound … smell … taste … touch … mental phenomena, householder, is called 'dwelling in attachments.' Thus, householder, one is dwelling in attachments.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, is one involved in village affairs? Here, householder, someone lives associated with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows, happy when they are happy, suffering when they are suffering, and personally involved in whatever duties and tasks arise. Thus, householder, one is involved in village affairs.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, is one not involved in village affairs? Here, householder, a bhikkhu lives unassociated with householders, not sharing their joys and sorrows, not happy when they are happy, not suffering when they are suffering, and not personally involved in whatever duties and tasks arise. Thus, householder, one is not involved in village affairs.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. 'Monks, whoever among ascetics or brahmins who perceive the self in various ways, all of them perceive the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one among them. What five? Here, monks, an unlearned ordinary person, unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the noble Dhamma, undisciplined in the noble Dhamma, unseeing of good persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of good persons, perceives form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. He perceives feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: If this perception is not abandoned in him, it is said to be 'I am.' And when 'I am' is not abandoned, bhikkhus, the faculties of the five senses find an opening—of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. There is, bhikkhus, mind, there are mental objects, there is the element of ignorance. When an unlearned ordinary person is contacted by feeling born of ignorance-contact, there arises in him 'I am'; 'I am this'; 'I shall be'; 'I shall not be'; 'I shall be material'; 'I shall be immaterial'; 'I shall be percipient'; 'I shall be non-percipient'; 'I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient.'
translations.sn22.48:1: Discourse from Sāvatthī. 'I will teach you the five aggregates, bhikkhus, and the five aggregates subject to clinging. Listen to this. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever there is, bhikkhus, of form, past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the form aggregate. Whatever there is of feeling … of perception … of volitional formations, past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the aggregate of volitional formations. Whatever there is, bhikkhus, of consciousness, past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the consciousness aggregate. These, bhikkhus, are called the five aggregates.
translations.sn22.53:1: Discourse from Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, with fuel, consciousness would remain established; without fuel, it would not continue. If, bhikkhus, consciousness were established with form as fuel, with form as its object, supported by form, delighting in form, it would increase, grow, and expand. If with feeling as fuel … with perception as fuel … if, bhikkhus, consciousness were established with volitional formations as fuel, with volitional formations as its object, supported by volitional formations, delighting in volitional formations, it would increase, grow, and expand.
translations.sn22.53:2: If, bhikkhus, someone were to say: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from volitional formations, I will describe the coming, going, decease, rebirth, increase, growth, or expansion of consciousness,' that would not be possible.
translations.sn22.54:2: If, bhikkhus, consciousness were established with form as fuel, with form as its object, supported by form, delighting in form, it would increase, grow, and expand. If, bhikkhus, consciousness were established with feeling as fuel … with perception as fuel … if, bhikkhus, consciousness were established with volitional formations as fuel, with volitional formations as its object, supported by volitional formations, delighting in volitional formations, it would increase, grow, and expand.
translations.sn22.55:1: Discourse from Sāvatthī. Then the Blessed One uttered this exclamation: 'A bhikkhu who is firmly resolved thus: 'I am not this, nor shall I ever be; it was not mine, nor shall it ever be mine'—such a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters.' When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: 'But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu who is firmly resolved thus: 'I am not this, nor shall I ever be; it was not mine, nor shall it ever be mine'—how does such a bhikkhu cut off the lower fetters?'
translations.sn22.55:10: 'But how, venerable sir, does one know and see so that the destruction of the taints occurs immediately?' 'Here, bhikkhu, an unlearned worldling experiences fear in a certain situation. This fear of the unlearned worldling is: 'I am not this, nor shall I ever be; it was not mine, nor shall it ever be mine.'
translations.sn22.55:4: He does not understand form, which is suffering, as 'suffering form' as it really is; he does not understand feeling, which is suffering … perception, which is suffering … volitional formations, which are suffering … consciousness, which is suffering, as 'suffering consciousness' as it really is.
translations.sn22.55:5: He does not understand form, which is not-self, as 'not-self form' as it really is; he does not understand feeling, which is not-self, as 'not-self feeling' as it really is; he does not understand perception, which is not-self, as 'not-self perception' as it really is; he does not understand volitional formations, which are not-self, as 'not-self volitional formations' as it really is; he does not understand consciousness, which is not-self, as 'not-self consciousness' as it really is.
translations.sn22.55:6: He does not understand form, which is conditioned, as 'conditioned form' as it really is; he does not understand feeling, which is conditioned … perception, which is conditioned … volitional formations, which are conditioned … consciousness, which is conditioned, as 'conditioned consciousness' as it really is. He does not understand as it really is that 'form will cease.' He does not understand as it really is that 'feeling will cease … perception will cease … volitional formations will cease … consciousness will cease.'
translations.sn22.55:8: He truly understands impermanent form as 'impermanent form.' He truly understands impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent volitional formations … impermanent consciousness as 'impermanent consciousness.' He truly understands suffering form … suffering consciousness … not-self form … not-self consciousness … conditioned form … conditioned consciousness as 'conditioned consciousness.' He truly understands that 'form will cease.' He truly understands that 'feeling will cease … perception will cease … volitional formations will cease … consciousness will cease.'
translations.sn22.55:9: With the cessation of form, with the cessation of feeling, with the cessation of perception, with the cessation of volitional formations, with the cessation of consciousness—thus, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu who is firmly resolved: 'I am not this, nor shall I ever be; it was not mine, nor shall it ever be mine'—such a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters.' 'Indeed, venerable sir, a bhikkhu who is firmly resolved thus would cut off the lower fetters.'
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? These six, bhikkhus, are classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness. With the arising of name-and-form, consciousness arises; with the cessation of name-and-form, consciousness ceases. This very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, namely: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.56:14: For whoever, monks, ascetics or brahmins, having fully understood consciousness, having fully understood the origin of consciousness, having fully understood the cessation of consciousness, having fully understood the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, have proceeded towards disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness—they are well-practiced. Those who are well-practiced are firmly established in this Dhamma-discipline.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? Form has been fully known, the origin of form has been fully known, the cessation of form has been fully known, the path leading to the cessation of form has been fully known; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness has been fully known, the origin of consciousness has been fully known, the cessation of consciousness has been fully known, the path leading to the cessation of consciousness has been fully known.
translations.sn22.56:5: And whoever, monks, ascetics or brahmins, having fully understood form … having fully understood the path leading to the cessation of form, through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, are liberated without clinging—these are well-liberated. Those who are well-liberated are consummate ones. For the consummate ones, there is no further round to be designated.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Sāvatthī. 'A monk who is skilled in the sevenfold method, monks, who has thoroughly examined, is called a consummate one, a perfected one, a supreme person in this Dhamma-discipline. And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the sevenfold method? Here, monks, a monk understands form, he understands the origin of form, he understands the cessation of form, he understands the path leading to the cessation of form; he understands the gratification in form, he understands the danger in form, he understands the escape from form; he understands feeling … perception … volitional formations … he understands consciousness, he understands the origin of consciousness, he understands the cessation of consciousness, he understands the path leading to the cessation of consciousness; he understands the gratification in consciousness, he understands the danger in consciousness, he understands the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, monks, are volitional formations? These six classes of intention, monks—intention regarding form … intention regarding phenomena. These, monks, are called volitional formations. With the origin of contact, volitional formations originate; with the cessation of contact, volitional formations cease. This very noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations, namely: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: That pleasure and joy which arise in dependence on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust in regard to consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: And whoever, monks, ascetics or brahmins, having fully understood consciousness, having fully understood the origin of consciousness, having fully understood the cessation of consciousness, having fully understood the path leading to the cessation of consciousness; having fully understood the gratification in consciousness, having fully understood the danger in consciousness, having fully understood the escape from consciousness, through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, are liberated without clinging—these are well-liberated. Those who are well-liberated are consummate ones. For the consummate ones, there is no further round to be designated. Thus, monks, a monk is skilled in the sevenfold method.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, monks, is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. This, monks, is called form. With the origin of nutriment, form originates; with the cessation of nutriment, form ceases. This very noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of form, namely: right view … right concentration.
