translations.sn56.11:5: 'This is the noble truth of suffering'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of suffering should be fully understood'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:6: 'This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be abandoned'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:7: 'This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:8: 'This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering should be developed'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. 'This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed'—in me, bhikkhus, from previously unheard teachings, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:9: As long as, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths in threefold turn with twelve aspects was not fully purified, I did not claim in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its samaṇas, brahmins, devas, and humans, to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
translations.sn56.20:1: "These four, bhikkhus, are true, not false, unchanging. What four? 'This is suffering'—this, bhikkhus, is true, not false, unchanging; 'this is the origin of suffering'—this is true, not false, unchanging; 'this is the cessation of suffering'—this is true, not false, unchanging; 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering'—this is true, not false, unchanging. These four, bhikkhus, are true, not false, unchanging.
translations.sn56.26:1: "Whoever, bhikkhus, you would have compassion for, whoever you would consider worthy of listening—whether friends, colleagues, relatives, or kin—those should be encouraged, established, and settled by you, bhikkhus, in the realization of the four noble truths as they really are.
translations.sn56.26:2: Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Whoever, bhikkhus, you would have compassion for, whoever you would consider worthy of listening—whether friends, colleagues, relatives, or kin—those should be encouraged, established, and settled by you, bhikkhus, in the realization of these four noble truths as they really are.
translations.sn56.27:1: "These four, bhikkhus, are the noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These four, bhikkhus, are true, not false, unchanging; therefore they are called 'noble truths'.
translations.sn56.28:1: "These four, bhikkhus, are the noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. The Tathāgata is noble in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its samaṇas and brahmins, with its devas and humans; therefore they are called 'noble truths'.
translations.sn56.30:1: On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Cetā, in the Sahañcana Grove. Then, when those elder bhikkhus had returned from their alms round after the meal and were sitting together in the pavilion, this conversation arose among them: 'Who, friends, sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, also sees the path leading to the cessation of suffering?'
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in Kosambi, in the Sīsapā Grove. Then the Buddha, having taken a few sīsapā leaves into his hand, addressed the bhikkhus: 'What do you think, bhikkhus? Which is more: the few sīsapā leaves I have taken into my hand, or those above in the Sīsapā Grove?' 'The leaves in your hand are few, venerable sir; but those above in the Sīsapā Grove are far more numerous,' they replied. 'So too, bhikkhus, much more has been known by me but not declared. And why have I not declared it? Because, bhikkhus, it is not beneficial, not fundamental to the holy life, does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna; therefore I have not declared it.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, have I declared? 'This is suffering,' bhikkhus, has been declared by me, 'this is the origin of suffering' has been declared by me, 'this is the cessation of suffering' has been declared by me, 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' has been declared by me.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why, bhikkhus, have I declared this? Because, bhikkhus, this is beneficial, fundamental to the holy life, leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; therefore I have declared it.
translations.sn56.35:1: 'Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a man with a lifespan of a hundred years. Someone would say to him: 'Come, good man, in the morning they will strike you with a hundred spears, at midday with a hundred spears, in the evening with a hundred spears. And you, good man, being struck daily with three hundred spears, living a hundred years, at the end of a hundred years will have directly realized the four noble truths that have not yet been realized.'
translations.sn56.35:2: It would be worthwhile, bhikkhus, for a wise householder to undergo this. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, beginningless is saṁsāra; no first point is found of beings roaming and wandering, shrouded by ignorance, bound by craving. So it might be. But I do not say, bhikkhus, that the realization of the four noble truths occurs together with suffering and sorrow; rather, I say, bhikkhus, that the realization of the four noble truths occurs together with happiness and joy. Which four? The noble truth of suffering … the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: 'Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to strip off all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa and bind them into a single bundle; having made a single bundle, he would make a spear. Having made a spear, he would impale the large creatures in the great ocean on large spears, the medium-sized creatures on medium spears, and the minute creatures on fine spears. Yet, bhikkhus, the large creatures in the great ocean would still not be exhausted.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa would be used up and gone. But, bhikkhus, far more numerous would be the minute creatures in the great ocean, which would be difficult to impale on spears. Why is that? Because of their extreme fineness, bhikkhus, of their nature. So vast, bhikkhus, is the woeful state. So thoroughly freed is a person endowed with right view, who truly understands: 'This is suffering' … 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.'
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in Rājagaha, on the Vulture's Peak Mountain. Then the Buddha addressed the bhikkhus: 'Come, bhikkhus, let us go to the Paṭibhānakūṭa for the day's abode.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' the bhikkhus replied. Then the Buddha together with a number of bhikkhus went to the Paṭibhānakūṭa. A certain bhikkhu saw a large precipice at the Paṭibhānakūṭa. Having seen it, he said to the Buddha: 'This precipice is vast, venerable sir, and fearsome. Is there, venerable sir, another precipice even vaster and more fearsome than this?' 'Yes, bhikkhu, there is another precipice vaster and more fearsome than this.'
translations.sn56.42:2: 'But what, venerable sir, is the precipice vaster and more fearsome than this?' 'Those, bhikkhus, whether ascetics or brahmins, who do not truly understand: "This is suffering," who do not truly understand: "This is the origin of suffering," who do not truly understand: "This is the cessation of suffering," who do not truly understand: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—they delight in formations that lead to birth, delight in formations that lead to aging, delight in formations that lead to death, delight in formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Delighting in formations that lead to birth, delighting in formations that lead to aging, delighting in formations that lead to death, delighting in formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, they continue to form kamma in formations that lead to birth, continue to form kamma in formations that lead to aging, continue to form kamma in formations that lead to death, continue to form kamma in formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Having formed kamma in formations that lead to birth, having formed kamma in formations that lead to aging, having formed kamma in formations that lead to death, having formed kamma in formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, they fall into the precipice of birth, fall into the precipice of aging, fall into the precipice of death, fall into the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say they are not freed from suffering.
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then in the morning Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. He saw some Licchavi youths in the assembly hall, performing acts of worship, stretching out a seat from afar with a fine reed mat, smooth and well-smoothed. Seeing this, it occurred to him: 'Indeed, these Licchavi youths are well trained, very well trained, who would stretch out a seat from afar with a fine reed mat, smooth and well-smoothed.'
translations.sn56.45:3: What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and harder to achieve—someone stretching out a seat from afar with a fine reed mat, smooth and well-smoothed, or someone piercing a hundred layers of leather with a hundred layers of iron?' 'This, sir, is more difficult and harder to achieve—someone piercing a hundred layers of leather with a hundred layers of iron.' 'Then, Ānanda, those who penetrate what is hard to penetrate, who truly understand: “This is suffering” … “This is the origin of suffering” … “This is the cessation of suffering” … “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,” truly understand.'
translations.sn56.46:1: There are, bhikkhus, intermediate worlds, evil, unguarded, dark, pitch-dark, where even the light of the sun and moon—so mighty and powerful—does not shine.
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: 'Great indeed, sir, is that darkness, very great indeed is that darkness. Is there, sir, another darkness greater and more fearful than that?' 'Yes, bhikkhu, there is another darkness greater and more fearful than that.'
translations.sn56.48:1: Suppose, bhikkhus, this great earth were all one mass of water. A man would throw a single-holed yoke into it. The eastern wind would carry it westward, the western wind eastward, the northern wind southward, the southern wind northward. There is a blind turtle. It would surface once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, insert its neck into that single hole in the yoke?' 'It would be extremely rare, sir, that the blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, would insert its neck into that single hole in the yoke.'
translations.sn56.48:2: So extremely rare, bhikkhus, is it to obtain human existence. So extremely rare, bhikkhus, is it for a Tathāgata to arise in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One. So extremely rare, bhikkhus, is it for the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata to shine in the world. You have obtained this human existence, the Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, and the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world.
